title: How to Read the Bible Without Making It Say What You Want
excerpt: Two sincere readers open the same page and find opposite gods. The problem is not that the Bible is unclear. It is that no one reads from nowhere.
body:
Two readers open the same page of Paul's letter to the Romans. One closes it certain that God has blessed the social order exactly as it stands, that submission to authority is the whole of Christian duty. The other closes it certain that God is the great leveler who would pull that order down and seat the poor at the head of the table. Both are sincere. Both are literate. Both have read the same words in the same order, and both have walked out of the room carrying a different god. This happens every Sunday, in every tradition, in every century the church has had a book. It is the oldest problem we have.

The problem is not that the Bible is unclear. The problem is that we are not neutral, and we have spent five hundred years pretending we are.

That pretense has a history, and like most of the things that own us, it began as something good. When the Reformers said sola scriptura and put the Bible into the hands of the plowboy, they were not handing out a license for everyone to invent a private faith. They were breaking a monopoly. Scripture, they insisted, was clear enough in the things that matter for salvation that an ordinary believer could read it and live. They called this perspicuity, and they were right about it. But the printing press and the centuries that followed did something the Reformers did not intend. They produced a new character who has haunted the Western mind ever since. The reader who believes he stands nowhere. The mind that imagines it can approach the text the way Descartes imagined he could approach everything, scrubbed clean of every inheritance, a neutral observer reporting only what is there.

There is no such reader. There never was.

Begin with the strongest case for the side I am about to disagree with, because it deserves it. The plain-reading instinct is not stupidity. It is reverence wearing work clothes. The person who says just tell me what the text says and I will do it is protecting something precious, the conviction that God has spoken and that his word stands over us rather than under us. Mark Noll has documented how this instinct, what he calls a Reformed, commonsense biblicism, built American evangelical religion and gave it its spine (Noll 1994). When a believer resists the scholar who seems to dissolve every command into context, that believer is guarding the possibility that the Bible can still tell him to do something he does not want to do. That is not a small thing to guard. A book you can interpret into anything is a book that can no longer command you.

Grant all of it. Then notice what the plain reading cannot account for.

The same Americans who held the plainest, highest view of the Bible in the world read it, in 1845, straight into the defense of human slavery. They were not lying. They were not, most of them, cynics looking for a proof-text to cover an evil they already loved. They opened the book, found Paul returning Onesimus to his master, found the household codes, found no explicit abolition, and concluded in good conscience that the plain sense of Scripture permitted what their economy required. The abolitionists, working from the same book, lost the exegetical argument in the eyes of most and won the moral one in the eyes of history. Noll calls this the theological crisis of the Civil War, and it is the permanent refutation of the myth of the innocent reader (Noll 2006). The plainest readers in the country read the plain text and baptized an atrocity. The text did not fail them. Their certainty that they brought nothing to it failed them.

There is no reading without a reader, and the reader is never empty.

Now the other side, and it gets its full weight too. The progressive instinct says exactly what I have just said. There is no neutral reading. Every interpretation is shaped by the community, the century, the wound, the interest of the one doing the interpreting. The patriarch reads patriarchy, the empire reads empire, the comfortable read comfort. Hans-Georg Gadamer gave this its most serious philosophical form. We never come to a text as blank minds, he argued. We come carrying what he called prejudices, prejudgments, the whole inheritance of language and history that makes understanding possible in the first place. Understanding is not the erasure of our horizon but the fusion of our horizon with the horizon of the text (Gadamer 1989). The reader who claims to have no lens is simply a reader who has not noticed his glasses.

This is true. It is so true that the church has known it for sixteen centuries and the modern skeptic is late to it. Augustine said it in the fourth century, that anyone who thinks he has understood the Scriptures but whose interpretation does not build up the love of God and neighbor has not yet understood them at all (Augustine 1997). He assumed what Gadamer rediscovered, that we read from somewhere, toward something, with our loves already engaged.

But watch what happens when this true observation is asked to do more work than it can bear. If every reading is only the projection of the reader's interest, then the slaveholder and the abolitionist are simply two communities with two preferences and no court above them to which either can appeal. The text becomes a mirror. You look in, and you find your own face, and you call it God. Kevin Vanhoozer named the danger precisely in the title of his great book, asking whether there is any meaning in the text at all, or only the meanings we bring (Vanhoozer 1998). If the answer is only what we bring, then Scripture cannot correct us, because there is nothing in it that is not already us. The prophet cannot indict the king, because the prophet is only the king's rival reading. The progressive who weaponizes interpretation against the fundamentalist has, without noticing, dismantled the one tool that could ever have been used against injustice. A book that can mean anything means nothing, and a book that means nothing has never once set a captive free.

So both certainties collapse. The plain reading collapses because there is no innocent reader. The everything-is-interpretation reading collapses because it leaves the reader trapped in the mirror with no word from outside. Each is half of a truth pretending to be the whole.

The honest fact that no one reads from nowhere does not drive us toward relativism. Followed all the way down, it drives us back to exactly the things the modern reader was trying to escape, the community, the tradition, and the rule of faith. If I cannot trust my own neutrality, then I cannot be my own magisterium. The recognition that I read through a lens is not permission to grind whatever lens I please. It is the reason I need other readers, dead ones and living ones, to grind it with me and to tell me when I have made the text into a flattering portrait of myself.

This is the move the buffered modern self resists most. Charles Taylor describes the self that emerged from the Enlightenment as one sealed off from outside influence, the sovereign individual who is his own authority and answers to no community he did not choose (Taylor 2007). That self reads the Bible alone, by definition, even when sitting in a crowded sanctuary, because it has already decided that no interpreter outside its own head has any claim on it. James K.A. Smith has spent his career pressing the point that we are not first thinkers but lovers, that our desires are trained by what we do long before our minds engage what we read, and so we arrive at the text already aimed (Smith 2009). The reader formed all week by the liturgies of self, the feed, the market, the nation, does not become neutral the moment he opens to the Gospel of Luke. The question was never whether you read through a lens. It is whose lens, ground by whom, and aimed at what.

There is a scene in the Old Testament that holds the whole of this, and the church has too often walked past it. In the eighth chapter of Nehemiah, the exiles have come home to a broken city, and they gather in the square, and they ask Ezra the scribe to bring the book. He reads it aloud from morning until midday, and the people stand the whole time. But the reading is not left to fall on the crowd unaided. The Levites moved among the people and helped them understand, and the phrase is worth its weight. They read from the book, from the law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading (Nehemiah 8:8 ESV).

They gave the sense. The word of God was read plainly, and it still required to be opened. There is no opposition here between the authority of the text and the labor of interpretation. The same scene holds both. The book stands over the people. The people cannot grasp the book without help. And the help is not a single expert descending with the answers. It is the whole company of teachers moving through the assembly, a community formed around the text, doing together what no one of them could do alone.

Then comes the part that exposes every reader's heart. When the people understand, they weep. The word has done its work, it has shown them the distance between the life they have lived and the life the law describes, and they break. And Nehemiah and Ezra tell them to stop weeping, to go and eat the fat and drink the sweet wine and send portions to those who have nothing, because the joy of the Lord is their strength. The right reading of the text moves through grief into grace, and out the far side into generosity toward the poor. A reading that ends in despair has stopped too soon. A reading that never passed through the grief was never serious. And a reading that does not finally send bread to the one who has none has not understood the book at all.

This is not a technique. It is the gospel applied to the act of reading, and the cross is what makes it possible.

The reason I cannot be trusted alone with the text is the same reason I cannot be trusted alone with anything, the simple fact named on the first pages of the book, that the human heart curves inward and bends every good gift back toward itself. I do not read the Bible from a neutral place because there is no neutral place in me. There is a will that wants to be justified, and it will go into the holiest book ever written and come out holding a verse that proves it was right all along. Left to myself, I will always find the God I came looking for. That is not a flaw in my method. It is the condition the cross exists to address.

To read Scripture as a Christian is to submit to a text that intends to put me to death before it raises me. It means going to the page expecting to be contradicted, not confirmed. It means treating the verse that wounds me as more likely to be God's word to me than the verse that flatters me, because the God of this book has never once been the projection of human desire and has always been its interruption. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, teaching his underground seminarians to read, pressed them to come to the page asking not how they would pass the word on to others but what it was saying to them, listening with the humility of a servant rather than standing over the text as its master (Bonhoeffer 1954). He was describing the death that has to happen on the way into the text. The reader who will not die over the page will only ever be reading himself.

I know this reader. I have been this reader. I have stood with a passage on a Saturday night that meant to break something in me and in my people, and I have felt my mind go to work softening it, finding the angle that would let me preach it without being indicted by it, the reading that would cost the congregation something and cost me nothing. That is not interpretation. It is the oldest evasion there is, the one the serpent taught in the garden when he asked the first hermeneutical question ever recorded, did God really say. Every dishonest reading of Scripture since has been a footnote to that sentence. We do not usually deny the word. We adjust it, until it agrees with us, and we call the adjustment study.

So the practices that follow are not tips. They are the shape of a death and a resurrection, worked out in the ordinary discipline of opening the book.

Read it with the dead and the living, never alone. The whole point of the rule of faith, the creeds, the long tradition of the church, is that they are the lens-grinders God has given you so that you do not have to trust your own eyes by themselves. When your reading of a passage is one that no Christian in two thousand years has ever held, the odds are not that you have finally seen clearly. The odds are that you have found your own face in the mirror. Read with your enemies too. Read the brother across the political aisle who finds in the text what you cannot find, because he is reading past your blind spot the way you are reading past his.

Read the parts that condemn you first. Go looking for the sentence you do not want, and when you find it, stay there. The verse that offends your politics, your appetite, your certainty, is the verse most likely to be doing the work the gospel sent it to do, because grace comes through the wound and not around it. A reading that never makes you weep in the square has not yet read you.

And then do the last thing Nehemiah commanded. Send a portion to the one who has none. The test of whether you have read the book rightly is never the elegance of your interpretation. It is whether the reading drove you out of the mirror and into your neighbor's need. The Scripture was never given so that you could be right about it. It was given so that you could be remade by it, and the proof of the remaking is bread in another person's hand.

The Bible is not a mirror, though we keep using it as one. It is a window, and on the far side of it stands a God who has never yet been the thing we wanted him to be, and has always been the thing we needed. You will spend your whole life learning the difference. The learning is the Christian life. And the day you are certain you have finally read it without bending it to yourself is the day you should be most afraid, because that is the day the mirror has won and you have not even noticed the glass.

Read like a person who expects to be told something true and unwelcome. It is the only way anyone has ever heard from God.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 1997. On Christian Teaching. Translated by R. P. H. Green. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Gadamer, Hans-Georg. 1989. Truth and Method. 2nd rev. ed. New York: Crossroad.

Noll, Mark A. 1994. The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Noll, Mark A. 2006. The Civil War as a Theological Crisis. Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press.

Smith, James K. A. 2009. Desiring the Kingdom. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

Vanhoozer, Kevin J. 1998. Is There a Meaning in This Text? Grand Rapids: Zondervan.

title: What the Gospel Actually Is
excerpt: The gospel is not advice about how to be good or how to feel loved. It is news about something God has done. And news is more demanding than advice.
body:
A man stops you on the street and tells you the war is over. He does not tell you to end the war. He does not give you seven steps for ending wars, or assure you that deep down the war was already over inside your heart. He tells you a thing that happened. The guns are silent. The enemy has surrendered. Go home.

That is what the word gospel means, and we have nearly lost it. Euangelion, the Greek word the New Testament uses, was not a religious word when the church took it. It was a word from the herald and the battlefield, the announcement of a victory or the birth of an emperor. An inscription carved in the marketplace of Priene around the year 9 before Christ called the birthday of Caesar Augustus good news, euangelion, for the whole world, the arrival of a savior who would end war and order the earth (Wright 2015). The first Christians knew exactly what they were doing when they took that word. They walked into the empire's own vocabulary and said the real good news, the actual turning point of history, is not the birth of the emperor. It is the death and resurrection of a crucified Galilean. The gospel was a counter-announcement before it was anything else. It was news, and it was treason.

We have turned it back into advice.

Take the strongest version of the first way we do that, because it is the sincere one. The gospel, many good people will tell you, is the call to follow the example of Jesus, to love your neighbor, to live the Sermon on the Mount, to be a decent and compassionate human being. This instinct is guarding something real. It will not let faith collapse into a private feeling that changes nothing about how a person treats the poor or the enemy. It remembers that Jesus said depart from me to people who called him Lord and did nothing. A gospel that produces no life is a corpse, and the moralist is right to refuse it.

But follow the instinct to its end. If the gospel is fundamentally advice about how to live, then it is not news, and it is not good. It is a ladder, and you already know how the ladder ends, because you have been climbing some version of it your whole life and you are tired, and you are not at the top, and the rung you are standing on will not hold your weight much longer. Advice assumes the war can still be won by the listener. The whole problem is that it cannot.

Now the other way, the gentler one. The gospel, a great many will tell you, is simply that God loves you exactly as you are, full stop, no conditions, no demands. This too guards something precious. It refuses to let grace become a transaction, refuses the cruelty of a God you must satisfy before he will have you. It remembers that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, that the love came first and uninvited. The sociologist Christian Smith, studying what American teenagers actually believe, found that this had become the real religion of the country, a creed he named moralistic therapeutic deism, in which God exists mainly to make people feel good about themselves and to be available when needed (Smith 2005). It is gentle. It is not nothing. It is half of something true.

But severed from the cross, that love becomes mere sentiment, a warmth that asks for nothing and therefore changes nothing and therefore cost nothing. Dietrich Bonhoeffer named it in 1937 and the name has never been bettered. Cheap grace is the grace we bestow on ourselves, the preaching of forgiveness without requiring repentance, grace without the cross, grace without Jesus Christ (Bonhoeffer 1937). A love that cost the lover nothing is not the love the New Testament is talking about. The love the New Testament is talking about has a body and the body has wounds.

Both ways make the gospel something about you, your effort or your worth. Paul refused both. When he set down what he meant by the gospel, in the fifteenth chapter of his first letter to Corinth, he did not give an ethic and he did not give a reassurance. He gave a report. I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received, that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared, to Peter, to the twelve, to more than five hundred at once, most of whom are still alive (1 Corinthians 15:3-6 ESV). It is a list of events with a list of witnesses, datable, public, the kind of claim that can be checked and therefore the kind of claim that can be false. J. Gresham Machen, watching the faith dissolve into ethical idealism in 1923, put it as plainly as it can be put. Christianity depends, he wrote, not upon a complex of ideas but upon the narration of an event (Machen 1923). From the beginning the gospel was news.

And the news has a center, and the center is the cross, and the cross is doing the work, not decorating the end of it. Christ died for our sins. The little word for is the engine. It means the death was in our place, that the war we could not win was won by someone else taking the loss that was ours to take. You cannot hear this as good news until the bad news has landed, until you have understood that you are not the neutral civilian in this story but the losing side, that the thing the cross addresses is not your low self-esteem but your guilt. The order matters more than almost anything in the Christian life. Grace offered before the law has done its work is cheap, and grace withheld after the law has done its work is cruelty. Tim Keller spent his ministry on one sentence about this. The gospel is neither religion nor irreligion, neither the moralist's ladder nor the libertine's shrug, but a third thing the world keeps failing to imagine, that we are more sinful than we ever dared believe and more loved than we ever dared hope, at the same time, in the same act, on the same cross.

Here is the reversal the comfortable reader never sees coming. This is more demanding than any moral program, not less. The ladder asks only for improvement, a better version of the self you already are. The gospel asks for that self's death. It does not want your behavior tidied. It wants the whole man handed over, the will, the record, the future, exchanged for a life you did not earn and cannot manage and will spend the rest of your days learning to receive. Grace is not the absence of demand. It is the most total demand there is, because it claims everything, and it gives everything, and there is nothing left over that is still yours to control. Cheap grace is easy because it leaves you on the throne. The real thing costs you the throne.

I have preached the advice and called it the gospel. I have stood up on a Sunday and sent people home to try harder, to be kinder, to do better this week, and called that the good news of Jesus Christ, and it was the moralist's sermon wearing a worship band's clothes. I have done it because advice is safe and news is dangerous. Advice keeps me useful, the helpful expert with the steps. News makes me a beggar telling other beggars where the bread is, with nothing to offer but the announcement and no way to improve on it. The pull toward advice is the pull away from the cross, and I feel it every week.

The herald does not ask you to win the war. He tells you it has already been won, somewhere outside the city, on a hill, by someone else, and the telling is either the best thing you have ever heard or an offense, depending entirely on whether you still wanted to fight it yourself. Good news to the soldier who is exhausted and out of ammunition and ready to lay it down. Treason to the one who was sure he was winning. The gospel has always been both, and which one it is to you tells you exactly where you are standing.

### Works Cited

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1937. The Cost of Discipleship. Translated by R. H. Fuller. New York: Macmillan.

Keller, Timothy. 2008. The Reason for God. New York: Dutton.

Machen, J. Gresham. 1923. Christianity and Liberalism. New York: Macmillan.

Smith, Christian, with Melinda Lundquist Denton. 2005. Soul Searching: The Religious and Spiritual Lives of American Teenagers. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Wright, N. T. 2015. Simply Good News. New York: HarperOne.

title: The Trinity Is Not Optional
excerpt: We treat the Trinity as the church's embarrassing arithmetic. It is the most practical claim Christianity makes, and the ground everyone is standing on.
body:
A child asks how God can be three and also one, and the adults at the table change the subject. We have made the Trinity the church's embarrassing arithmetic, the doctrine we recite in the creed on Sunday and never once use on Monday, the freight we haul because the councils told us to. We can explain why the cross matters and why grace matters and why prayer matters. Ask most believers why it matters that God is triune and you will get a long pause and a diagram involving water or an egg.

This is exactly backward. The doctrine no one uses is the ground everyone is standing on.

Give the skeptic the full force of the objection first, because it is a serious one. The word Trinity is not in the Bible. The fully developed doctrine was hammered out over three centuries and finalized at councils that emperors convened, beginning with Nicaea in the year 325, summoned by Constantine, who cared at least as much about imperial unity as about theology. The fights were political and often ugly. Athanasius, the doctrine's great defender, was driven into exile five times. And on its face the claim looks like incoherence, one equals three, or like later Greek philosophy bolted onto the plain monotheism of a Jewish prophet who only ever told people to worship the God of Israel. Stated that way, the suspicion is understandable. A reasonable person could conclude the church invented a riddle and then demanded everyone affirm it.

Grant the mess. The councils were human and the politics were real. But the doctrine was not an imposition laid on top of the New Testament. It was a synthesis forced out from underneath it, the church's refusal to drop any of the things the text would not let it drop.

The first Christians were Jews. They said the Shema every day, hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one, and they meant it with their lives, and they died rather than grant that Caesar was a god. And these same fierce monotheists prayed to Jesus, sang to him as Lord, baptized in the threefold name, and described the Spirit as God present and personal among them. They did not arrive at the Trinity by speculation. They were driven to it by the refusal to let go of four things all at once. The Father is God. Jesus is worshipped as God. The Spirit is God. There is one God. Arius, in the fourth century, offered a clean way out. Make the Son a high and glorious creature, the first and best thing God made, but a creature, not God himself. It solved the math. The church looked at the solution and saw that it dissolved the gospel, because a creature cannot save, and a Savior you worship who is less than God is an idol however exalted. At Nicaea the church answered Arius with a single word that is not elegant and was never meant to be, homoousios, of the same being as the Father. Athanasius spent his whole hunted life on that one word because he saw what it was protecting (Athanasius 2011).

What it was protecting is most visible not in a creed but in a prayer. On the night before he died, in the seventeenth chapter of John, Jesus prays aloud, and the prayer opens a window into the inside of God. He speaks to the Father of a glory the two of them shared before the world existed. He speaks of being loved by the Father before the foundation of the world. And he prays that his people would be brought inside that very love, that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you (John 17:21-24 ESV). The doctrine of the Trinity is, in the end, only the church learning to say what that prayer takes for granted. Before there was a universe to love, there was love. The Father loved the Son. The love did not begin when creatures arrived to receive it.

This is the thing the doctrine secures, and everything turns on it. Love is not something God started doing when he made a world. Love is what God is, eternally, in himself, three persons giving and receiving without beginning and without end. The Greek fathers had a word for the way the persons make room for one another in this endless mutual life, perichoresis, a kind of eternal indwelling. Augustine spent fifteen books circling it, finally finding its trace in the structure of love itself, which always requires a lover, a beloved, and the love that passes between them (Augustine 1991). C. S. Lewis, trying to get ordinary readers to feel it, said that God is not a static thing but a dynamic, pulsating activity, a life, almost a kind of dance (Lewis 1952).

Now the reversal, the thing the bored Sunday believer never expects. This is the most practical claim Christianity makes. Imagine the alternative were true, that God is a single solitary power, a lonely monad on the throne of the universe. Then God needed the world in order to have anything to love, which means love is something God takes up, a later activity, and the most basic thing about ultimate reality is not love but sheer undifferentiated power and will. A universe with a unitarian god at the top is a universe in which force is more fundamental than love, and the self that images that god will believe, all the way down, that power is what finally matters and relationship is what you do once power is secured. But if God is triune, then the deepest fact about all that exists is not force and not the lonely will. It is self-giving love between persons, older than time. Catherine LaCugna argued that this is the entire point, that the doctrine is not abstract at all but tells us reality itself is personal and relational at its root (LaCugna 1991).

That detonates the central myth of the modern self. Charles Taylor describes the self the Enlightenment built as buffered and sovereign, the individual who imagines he is most free when he owes nothing to anyone and answers to no one he did not choose (Taylor 2007). The Trinity says the opposite is the truth of things. You were made in the image of a God who is community, whose very being is gift, and so you become most yourself not by self-possession but by self-donation, not by guarding your life but by giving it away. The lonely autonomous self is not the height of freedom. It is a small imitation of the lonely god who does not exist.

And the cross is the Trinity made visible in time. On Golgotha the Son gives himself, the Father gives the Son, the Spirit holds them across the dark. Strip out the Trinity and the cross becomes a horror, one being punishing another being to satisfy his anger, which is the caricature the critics rightly despise. Hold the Trinity and the cross is God giving himself, the eternal self-gift of Father, Son, and Spirit reaching into history and going all the way down into death and out the other side. Karl Barth insisted that God's very being is this act, that God is the one who loves in freedom, and that what happened on the cross was not foreign to God but the truest revelation of who God has always been (Barth 1957).

I will confess that I have treated this doctrine as a museum piece, something to defend against heretics rather than something to live inside. I have preached a God of love on Sunday and then spent the week ordering my life as though the basic structure of reality were competition and self-protection, getting mine, securing my position, keeping score. That is functional unitarianism. It is the practical worship of a single solitary power, whatever I say in the creed. The way a man guards his own life gives away the god he actually believes in, and mine has too often been the lonely one.

The child's question was the right question, and changing the subject was the failure. How can God be three and one. The answer is that God is love, and love has never been able to exist alone, because love requires one who loves and one who is loved and the love itself that binds them, and so the God who is love has never once been solitary, and was never going to make us to be solitary either. He made us to be brought inside the oldest love there is. The doctrine you thought was useless is the reason you exist and the home you are being called into. That is not arithmetic. That is the whole thing.

### Works Cited

Athanasius. 2011. On the Incarnation. Translated by John Behr. Yonkers, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press.

Augustine. 1991. The Trinity. Translated by Edmund Hill. Brooklyn: New City Press.

Barth, Karl. 1957. Church Dogmatics II.1. Edinburgh: T and T Clark.

LaCugna, Catherine Mowry. 1991. God for Us: The Trinity and Christian Life. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco.

Lewis, C. S. 1952. Mere Christianity. London: Geoffrey Bles.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

title: Inerrancy, Infallibility, and the Word You Can Trust
excerpt: Most fights about whether the Bible has errors are really fights about fear and control. The deeper question is whether it can do what God sent it to do.
body:
Every argument about biblical inerrancy that I have ever watched turn bitter was not, underneath, an argument about the Bible. It was an argument about fear.

On one side stands the person terrified that if a single sentence of Scripture is allowed to be wrong, the whole structure collapses, and there is no solid ground left, no word from God that can be trusted, only a buffet of human opinion from which each reader takes what flatters him. On the other side stands the person terrified of the opposite, that a Bible declared flawless in every detail becomes a weapon, a closed fist, a way of ending every conversation by insisting the text says exactly what the powerful have always claimed it says. Both fears are pointing at something real. Neither is yet describing what the Bible says about itself.

Begin with the strong case for the high view, because it guards the center. The person who insists on a fully trustworthy Bible is protecting the conviction that God does not lie, that he has actually spoken, and that his word stands over us rather than waiting for our approval. Benjamin Warfield, at Princeton in the late nineteenth century, gave this conviction its rigorous modern form, arguing that inspiration reaches down to the words themselves, so that what Scripture says, God says (Warfield 1948). Without something like that, the worry runs, the believer simply edits God down to his own preferences, keeping the verses he likes and discarding the rest, and a Bible you can edit is a Bible that can no longer command you.

Grant the worry its full weight. Then notice the assumption buried inside the modern form of the doctrine. Warfield was answering the Enlightenment, and he answered it on its own terms, the terms of certainty and factual precision, the text as a flawless database. And here the fundamentalist and the village atheist turn out to be twins. Both assume that truth means encyclopedic accuracy, that if the Gospel writers order events thematically rather than by the clock, or round a number, or report a speech in their own words, the Bible has failed a test. But that is Descartes's test. It is not Isaiah's.

The Bible's own word for the reliability of God's word is not precision. It is faithfulness, the Hebrew emet, the steadiness of a God who keeps covenant. And the claim Scripture makes for itself is a claim about purpose, not about chemistry. All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16-17 ESV). Read what the verse promises and what it does not. It promises that the Scripture is God-breathed and that it equips you for a transformed life. It does not promise a manual of geology or a chronicle that would satisfy a modern newsroom. Its authority is the authority of a word that accomplishes its purpose.

Isaiah heard God say that his word would not return to him empty but would accomplish that which he purposed (Isaiah 55:11 ESV). That is the kind of authority Scripture claims, the authority of efficacy, a word that does the thing it was sent to do, which is to make dead people new. Kevin Vanhoozer presses that Scripture is God's speech-act, not bare information but God doing things with words, promising and commanding and forgiving (Vanhoozer 1998). N. T. Wright argues that the authority of Scripture is shorthand for the authority of God exercised through Scripture (Wright 2005). The Bible is not authoritative the way a textbook is authoritative. It is authoritative the way a king's word is authoritative, because of who speaks it and what it does.

John Calvin saw four centuries ago how God speaks to creatures like us. He accommodates. Like a nurse leaning down to lisp at an infant, God lowers himself to our small capacity, speaking in the language and the categories of the people who first received the word (Calvin 1960). This is not a concession that weakens Scripture. It is the same logic as the incarnation. The Word became flesh, fully God and fully embedded in one human body, one century, one tongue. Scripture is that same Word in human words, wholly from God and wholly clothed in the culture of its writers. To demand that it float free of all that, that it read like a timeless proof dropped from the sky, is to demand a revelation that never actually condescended to become flesh.

So the deepest threat to trusting the Bible was never the discovery that two Gospel writers arrange the temptations in a different order. The deepest threat is the modern demand that God satisfy our standard of certainty before we will let him have us. I have stood on both sides of this. I have used the high doctrine as a club to end conversations I did not want to have, and I have used the low one as an escape hatch from sentences I did not want to obey, and both moves were ways of keeping myself in charge of a book whose whole purpose is to take charge of me.

You can hold a flawless Bible in a closed fist and never once be changed by it. You can also pick the Bible apart for its seams until there is nothing left that can tell you what to do. Both are strategies of control. The word that is actually trustworthy is the one you cannot finally master, the one that reads you while you are reading it, and returns to God having accomplished the thing it was sent to do, which was never to win an argument about certainty. It was to raise the dead.

### Works Cited

Calvin, John. 1960. Institutes of the Christian Religion. Edited by John T. McNeill. Philadelphia: Westminster Press.

Vanhoozer, Kevin J. 1998. Is There a Meaning in This Text? Grand Rapids: Zondervan.

Warfield, Benjamin B. 1948. The Inspiration and Authority of the Bible. Philadelphia: Presbyterian and Reformed.

Wright, N. T. 2005. The Last Word. New York: HarperOne.

title: Grace Is Not a Feeling
excerpt: We turned grace into a warm mood that asks nothing and changes no one. Real grace costs the giver everything, and that is why it is not soft.
body:
We have made grace into a mood. A soft light, a warm acceptance, a general sense that everything is fine and no one should feel bad about anything. And we have called that the heart of Christianity, when it is closer to its anesthetic.

Grace, in the New Testament, is not a feeling and not a temperament. It is charis, a gift, and specifically a gift handed to people who have not earned it and cannot repay it and may not even want it. It has a price, and the price is never paid by the one who receives it. That is the whole scandal of the word, and we have sanded the scandal down until grace means little more than being easygoing about things.

The clearest picture Jesus ever drew of it is not gentle. A younger son demands his inheritance early, which in that world was a way of telling his father he wished him dead, and he takes the money and burns it on a far country, and he comes home only because he is starving and out of options. And the father, who has been watching the road, does the thing no patriarch with any standing would ever do. He runs. An old man gathers up his robe and runs down the road in front of the whole village to reach a son who shamed him, and he cuts off the boy's rehearsed apology before he can finish it, and he calls for the robe and the ring and the fattened calf for a son who deserves, at the very best, a servant's cot in the barn (Luke 15:11-24). That is grace. Notice that it costs the father his dignity, his wealth, and his right to be angry, and notice that the son does nothing to earn it except come home with empty hands. Robert Farrar Capon read the parables of grace as deliberately scandalous on exactly this point, insisting that grace operates with no regard for the recipient's merit and that any accounting of deserving has already missed what the story is doing (Capon 1985).

Take the soft view at its strongest, because it is guarding something true. The view that grace means God receives you exactly as you are, with no conditions, protects the gospel from the elder brother, the man who stayed home and kept every rule and despised his father's mercy. A great many people were raised on shame and need to hear, with no asterisk, that the love came first and uninvited, before they ever cleaned themselves up. That is not a distortion. It is in the parable. The father runs before the son says a word.

But the soft view quietly forgets the cost, and a grace that costs nothing changes nothing. Dietrich Bonhoeffer gave the failure its permanent name. Cheap grace is the deadly enemy of the church. It is the grace we bestow on ourselves, the preaching of forgiveness without requiring repentance, communion without confession, grace without discipleship, grace without the cross (Bonhoeffer 1937). The father's welcome was not the absence of a reckoning. It ran straight through the death of his own honor in front of his neighbors. Costly grace, Bonhoeffer said, is the treasure hidden in the field, the pearl worth selling everything to buy, the call that sends a man from his nets.

Steel-man the opposite fear too, because the legalist is not imagining things. He worries that free grace becomes a license, that if forgiveness is unearned people will sin all the more freely. Paul raises the very objection himself. Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound. His answer is not a lecture but an astonishment. By no means. How can we who died to sin still live in it (Romans 6:1-2 ESV). The worry mistakes what grace is. Grace is not permission. It is power. It never says your sin did not matter. It says your sin has been paid for at a price that, the moment you actually see it, makes you never want to return to it.

Here is the reversal the soft view never sees coming. The grace that asks nothing of you is not kinder than the grace that asks everything. It is crueler, because it leaves you precisely where it found you. A love that requires no change is a love that has quietly given up on you, that has decided you are not worth the trouble of being made new. Timothy Keller, reading this parable, points out that there are two lost sons in it, and the dutiful elder brother seething outside the feast is the one the story leaves standing in the dark, because he wanted the father's things and not the father, and his rule-keeping was only a more respectable way of running from him (Keller 2008). Cheap grace produces elder brothers. Costly grace produces sons.

I preach grace for a living, and I am most tempted to cheapen it precisely because it is the loveliest word I know. It is easy to stand up and tell people God loves them as they are and send them home unchanged and feeling fine, and to call that a gospel of grace, when it is closer to a sedative. The grace that actually saved me was never the one that told me I was fine. It was the one that told me the truth about what I had done and ran down the road to take hold of me in the middle of the telling.

Grace is not a feeling. It is a father on a road in front of a village, his robe in his hands and his dignity on the ground, reaching a son who deserved none of it. It cost him everything and asked the son for nothing but the long walk home. That is not soft. It is the hardest and most total thing in the world, a love you cannot earn and cannot repay and cannot survive unchanged. Anything gentler than that is not grace. It is the word grace, with the cross removed.

### Works Cited

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1937. The Cost of Discipleship. Translated by R. H. Fuller. New York: Macmillan.

Capon, Robert Farrar. 1985. The Parables of Grace. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Keller, Timothy. 2008. The Prodigal God. New York: Dutton.

title: The Council of Nicaea: What Was Actually Decided in 325
excerpt: Nicaea did not invent the divinity of Jesus or pick the books of the Bible. What it actually did still decides what you believe about your own salvation.
body:
Most of what people think they know about the Council of Nicaea, they learned from a novel. The story, repeated until it feels like common knowledge, is that in the year 325 the emperor Constantine gathered the bishops, held a vote, and invented the divinity of Jesus, and that the same council decided which books would go in the Bible, the whole thing a political maneuver to consolidate imperial power. Almost every piece of that is false. What actually happened is harder, and more interesting, and it still decides things you believe about your own salvation.

Nicaea did not settle the canon of Scripture. No book was added or burned there. The legend that the council fixed the New Testament and suppressed the rejected gospels appears in no record of the proceedings, and even skeptical historians of early Christianity grant that the canon was simply not the council's business (Ehrman 2003). And Nicaea did not invent the divinity of Christ. Christians had been worshipping Jesus as Lord, singing to him as God, baptizing in his name, and dying rather than burn incense to Caesar for nearly three centuries before any emperor convened anything. You do not need a council to command you to worship someone you are already willing to be executed for refusing to deny.

So what was the actual fight. A presbyter in Alexandria named Arius taught that the Son, though the first and highest of all beings, was a creature, made by the Father out of nothing before time began, so that, in his famous slogan, there was when the Son was not. The bishop Alexander and his young deacon Athanasius answered that the Son is eternally begotten, not made, of the same being as the Father. The entire conflict turned on one question. Is Jesus God in the full sense, or the greatest of God's creatures. The combatants fought over the same texts, John's claim that in the beginning the Word was with God and the Word was God (John 1:1 ESV), and Paul's that the Son is the firstborn of all creation, which Arius read as created and Athanasius read as heir and head over creation.

Steel-man the skeptic, because the surface facts give him plenty to work with. Constantine did convene the council and did want unity in his fracturing empire. The politics were real and often sordid. The decisive term the council chose, homoousios, of the same being, was not found in the Bible, and its absence troubled even some who were no friends of Arius. And the controversy did not end at Nicaea. It raged for the rest of the century, and Athanasius was driven into exile five separate times, once under an emperor who had swung to the Arian side. A person looking only at the imperial machinery could be forgiven for mistaking the whole thing for politics.

But the substance was not invented, and the vote was not close. Of roughly three hundred bishops present, all but two signed the creed, and many of them carried in their own bodies the scars of the persecutions that had ended barely a decade earlier. These were not imperial functionaries. They were survivors of torture being asked by a brand-new and not-yet-baptized Christian emperor to settle a question the church had raised itself. They drew the line at of one being with the Father because they saw what Arius's tidy solution destroyed. Athanasius made the stakes plain. Only God can save. If the one on the cross is a creature, then a creature is our savior, and we are worshipping someone less than God, which is idolatry, and worse, a creature cannot join us to a God he is not (Athanasius 2011).

The modern historians have shown how far the old cynical story falls short. Lewis Ayres argues that Nicaea was a genuine stage in theological development, the church slowly working out the grammar of what it had always done in worship, not a foreign idea stamped onto simple faith by an emperor (Ayres 2004). Jaroslav Pelikan traced the same long development and showed that the creed did not break with the worship of the earlier church but defended it, naming in formal language the divine Christ the church had confessed from the beginning (Pelikan 1971). That is the reframe the novel misses entirely. The creed did not impose philosophy on a Galilean carpenter. It protected the carpenter, the plain confession that Jesus is Lord, from a sophisticated philosophical attempt to shrink him into a demigod.

And it still matters, because a Christ who is merely the highest creature is a Christ who cannot save, and a Christianity built on him is a religion of admiring a fine example, which is to say a religion of works, you straining to follow a hero who cannot reach back. The entire weight of grace hangs on the one word the bishops fought for. If the one bleeding on the cross is God himself bearing what we owed, that is salvation. If he is a creature God dispatched to bear it, that is cosmic injustice with a halo. Everything you actually believe about whether you can be rescued is hiding inside that word.

The bishops at Nicaea were not defending their power. Most of them had just finished losing everything for refusing to deny the very thing the council affirmed. They handed the church one word it could not read straight off the surface of the Bible but could not live without, and they were right to bleed for it. The novel got the drama right and the facts wrong. The truth was less of a conspiracy and more of a confession, signed by men who had already proven what their confession was worth.

### Works Cited

Athanasius. 2011. On the Incarnation. Translated by John Behr. Yonkers, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press.

Ayres, Lewis. 2004. Nicaea and Its Legacy. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Ehrman, Bart D. 2003. Lost Christianities. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Pelikan, Jaroslav. 1971. The Christian Tradition, Volume 1. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.

title: How the Reformation Started and Why It Still Matters
excerpt: The Reformation was not mainly about corruption. It was about one question: how is a person made right with God. That question is still keeping you awake.
body:
Ask why the Reformation happened and you will usually hear about corruption. A monk named Martin Luther got angry that the church was selling indulgences, slips of paper promising to shorten a dead relative's time in purgatory, and he nailed his protest to a church door in Wittenberg in 1517, and the church split in two. That is true as far as it goes, and it does not go nearly far enough to explain why anyone was willing to die. People do not burn at the stake over administrative corruption. They burn over a question, and the question underneath the Reformation is the same one still keeping you awake at night.

The question is this. How is a person made right with God. Not how is the church funded, not who answers to whom, but the older and more personal terror. When I stand before God, on what basis am I accepted. Luther was an Augustinian monk doing everything the system prescribed, confessing for hours until he wore out his confessor, punishing his body, climbing the holy stairs in Rome on his knees, and he could find no peace, because he knew the standard was perfection and he knew he was not perfect, and a holy God could only condemn what was not.

Then he read Romans, and one sentence broke him open. The righteousness of God is revealed, Paul wrote, from faith for faith, as it is written, the righteous shall live by faith (Romans 1:17 ESV). Luther had always read the phrase the righteousness of God as a threat, the perfect standard that damned him. Now he saw it the other way. The righteousness in the verse is not the standard God demands but the gift God gives, a righteousness from outside us, the very righteousness of Christ credited to everyone who trusts him. He called that discovery the gate to paradise. Alister McGrath, tracing the long history of how the church has understood justification, locates Luther's breakthrough precisely in this turn, the moment the righteousness of God was heard as a righteousness God gives rather than one he merely demands (McGrath 2005). The Latin tag the Reformers used, sola fide, by faith alone, is just the name for the relief of a man who has finally stopped climbing.

Steel-man the Catholic objection, because it is serious and the Reformers were not simply right about everything. The split fractured the visible church that Christ prayed would be one. Sola scriptura, the Bible as final authority, did not produce one pure church but thousands of competing ones, each certain it had the plain reading. The Council of Trent's worry, that faith spoken of apart from transformation curdles into a license to sin, was not foolish. The Catholic historian Brad Gregory argues that the Reformation unintentionally fathered the fragmented, secularized, hyper-individual modern world, the world in which, once the final authority has been relocated into each believer's own reading, every person becomes in effect his own interpreter with no court above him (Gregory 2012). Give all of that its full weight. The downstream costs were real, and the Reformers did not foresee them.

And steel-man the secular reduction too, the account that says it was never really about theology. Yes, the printing press spread Luther's tracts faster than Rome could answer them. Yes, German princes had political and financial reasons to shield him from the emperor. Yes, nationalism and money were in the mix. The material factors were genuine. But they explain the speed of the fire, not the fire itself. Erasmus mocked the church's corruption more wittily than Luther ever did and started no reformation, because mockery of corruption is not a gospel. Luther had a gospel.

Now the reversal, the thing the modern reader assumes is behind us. People treat the Reformation as a five-hundred-year-old institutional quarrel the secular world has happily outgrown. It is the reverse. The question it raised is more alive now than it has ever been, because the modern self simply relocated the courtroom. You may no longer fear standing before God, but you stand every single day before some other tribunal, the market, the feed, the mirror, the endless audit of whether you are successful enough, attractive enough, productive enough, enough. Luther's anguish was not a medieval relic. It was the human condition, and the secular age did not cure it. It only removed the one verdict that could ever have silenced it. The performance treadmill is works-righteousness with God deleted, all of the judgment and none of the grace.

I am a Protestant pastor. I preach justification by faith, and I still live half my life on that treadmill, auditing my worth by the size of the crowd and the warmth of the reviews, which means I have heard Luther's discovery and not yet believed it all the way to the floor. The Reformation is not a date I celebrate once a year. It is a deliverance I need again every week.

Luther stood before the emperor at Worms in 1521 and was ordered to take it all back, and he answered that he could not, because his conscience was captive to the word of God. We remember the courage and forget the relief underneath it. He was not mainly being brave. He was being free, free the way only a man can be who has stopped trying to earn what he has finally learned is given. That freedom is still on offer, and the question that drove him to it is still the only question that finally matters about your life. Not whether you are enough. Whether you will receive the righteousness you could never manufacture. The Reformation was the rediscovery that the answer is yes, and that it costs you nothing, because it already cost God everything.

### Works Cited

Gregory, Brad S. 2012. The Unintended Reformation. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

McGrath, Alister E. 2005. Iustitia Dei: A History of the Christian Doctrine of Justification. 3rd ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

title: The Great Awakenings and the Making of American Faith
excerpt: American Christianity was born in revival. That fire gave it a faith of the heart, and it also taught it to trust feeling over the church. We live in both.
body:
American Christianity was born in fire, and the fire left a mark that is both its genius and its wound.

Twice the country was swept by mass revival, and both times it changed not only how many Americans believed but what believing was. The First Great Awakening broke out in the 1730s and 1740s, when Jonathan Edwards preached and a young Anglican named George Whitefield crossed the colonies drawing crowds of thousands in open fields, and people wept and collapsed and were converted where they stood. The Second came around the turn of the next century, the camp meetings on the frontier, Cane Ridge in Kentucky in 1801 where thousands gathered for days, and the revivalism of Charles Finney, who taught that a revival was not a miracle to be awaited but a result a preacher could produce with the right methods. Out of these two fires came the recognizable shape of American faith. Personal. Emotional. Built on a datable conversion, a moment you were born again.

Take the strongest case for the revivals, because there is a real one. The conversions were often genuine and lasting, and the awakened faith poured itself into reform. The Second Great Awakening fueled the abolitionist movement, the founding of colleges, the care of the poor, the missionary surge that carried the gospel around the world. A faith of the heart rather than a merely inherited and formal religion is exactly what Edwards was defending, and Scripture is on his side, since the first commandment is to love God with all your heart. Pentecost itself, in the second chapter of Acts, was a public outpouring that looked like drunken chaos to the onlookers before it looked like God.

But Edwards, the greatest mind the awakenings produced, spent his best book warning that not every flame is the Spirit. In his treatise on the religious affections, in 1746, he set himself the hardest question a revival raises, how to tell true religious feeling from false, and his answer was unflinching. The test of a genuine work of God is not the intensity of the emotion. Tears and trembling and ecstasy can all be counterfeited or self-produced. The test is the fruit, a changed life and a new and lasting love for God and neighbor that remains after the meeting ends (Edwards 1959). Heat is not light. A strong feeling is not the Holy Spirit.

And here the wound shows itself. Nathan Hatch has shown how the awakenings democratized American religion, stripping authority from the educated clergy and the old institutions and handing it to the individual, the itinerant, the common person and his experience (Hatch 1989). This was liberating, and it was corrosive. Finney's new measures treated conversion as a technique to be engineered. The line from there runs straight to revivalism as manipulation, to a deep anti-intellectualism, and to the believer who trusts the warmth in his chest over the creed, the Scripture, and the church. Mark Noll's verdict on the long result is severe, that American evangelicalism, for all its energy, became a movement that never learned to love God with its mind (Noll 1994).

Here is the reversal. The thing that looks like America's most distinctive religious genius, the personal experience, the unmediated encounter, the faith you can feel, is also the taproot of its deepest distortion. The buffered modern believer who needs no church and no tradition because he has his own experience of Jesus did not come from secular culture. He came from the revival tent. The awakening that freed the believer from dead formalism also cut him loose from the one community that could ever test whether his feeling was the Spirit or only himself.

I preach for conversions, and I want the room to feel something, and I know exactly how to manufacture the feeling, the music under the appeal, the pause, the story, the lowered voice. I have at times mistaken the warmth I produced for the work only God can do. Edwards's question is the one I have to keep asking of my own ministry, and it does not flatter me. Is this fruit, or is it only heat.

The awakenings gave America a faith that could be personally and urgently real, and in a world full of dead religion that is no small gift. They also taught it to trust the fire over the hearth, the moment over the long obedience, the feeling over the body of Christ. We are still living in both halves of that inheritance, and the test Edwards left is still the only way to tell them apart. Not how hot it burned. What it grew.

### Works Cited

Edwards, Jonathan. 1959. A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections. Edited by John E. Smith. New Haven: Yale University Press.

Hatch, Nathan O. 1989. The Democratization of American Christianity. New Haven: Yale University Press.

Noll, Mark A. 1994. The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

title: Why There Are So Many Christian Denominations
excerpt: The thirty-thousand-denominations number is a misused statistic. The real and stubborn fact is how much wildly divided Christians still confess in common.
body:
Someone always brings up the number. There are thirty thousand Protestant denominations, the line goes, so how could anyone possibly know which one is right, and does the chaos not prove the whole thing is just people making it up as they go.

Start by being honest about the wound, because it is real and the New Testament treats it as a scandal. The night before he died, Jesus prayed that his people would be one as he and the Father are one, so that the world would believe (John 17:21). And the first generation was already failing him. In Corinth they were splitting into rival fan clubs, I follow Paul, I follow Apollos, I follow Cephas, and Paul turned on them with a question that should still sting. Is Christ divided (1 Corinthians 1:13 ESV). A fractured church is not a neutral fact. It is a contradiction of the gospel it preaches, and every honest Christian should feel the shame of it.

Steel-man the Catholic and Orthodox critique, which is the serious one. Protestantism cut the authority of the church loose and put a Bible in every hand, and the predictable result was fragmentation without end, because once every believer is his own final interpreter there is no one left to settle the disputes, and so the body keeps dividing. The visible oneness Christ prayed for is precisely the thing Protestantism seems unable to deliver. That argument has real force, and a Protestant who does not feel its weight is not paying attention.

But the famous number is a misuse, and the kind of misuse matters. The thirty thousand figure traces to a particular reference work that counts denominations nation by nation, so that one global communion present in a hundred countries gets counted a hundred times, and that folds in every small independent congregation that ever registered its own name. The source was measuring something other than what the slogan claims. Count actual distinct traditions, the real families of Christian conviction, and the figure is in the dozens, not the tens of thousands. The statistic is not evidence. It is a number stripped of its method and waved like a flag.

Now the reversal, the thing the division cannot hide. Take a Pentecostal in Lagos, a Greek Orthodox in Thessaloniki, a Catholic in Manila, and a Baptist in Alabama, traditions that have argued bitterly for centuries, and put them in one room, and watch how much they still hold in common. They confess the same creed, that God is Father, Son, and Spirit, that Christ was crucified and raised. They baptize. They break bread. They read the same Scriptures and pray to the same Lord. The remarkable thing is not that Christians have disagreed about church government and the mode of baptism. The remarkable thing is that, across two thousand years and every culture on earth and all the blood they have shed, they have kept the same center. Kevin Vanhoozer argues that the Bible in every hand was never bound to fracture the church without end, that a shared reading of the gospel's core can hold a real catholicity together underneath the genuine differences, so that the divisions are not the last word the principle was destined to speak (Vanhoozer 2016). Lesslie Newbigin, who gave his life to Christian unity, insisted that the church is meant to be a sign of the reconciliation God intends for the whole human race, and that its divisions are a wound to be healed, not a reason to abandon the body (Newbigin 1989).

The denominations, then, are scar tissue. They mark real injuries, genuine disagreements about baptism and authority and the supper, things that mattered enough to fight over because they touched the truth. Pretending the disagreements do not matter is not unity. It is indifference, and indifference is not what Jesus prayed for. He prayed for oneness in the truth, which is harder and costlier than a vague agreement to stop arguing.

I am a pastor of one particular tradition, and I have at times worn its distinctives like a team jersey, defined more by what I am against than by the Lord I am for, which is the Corinthian disease exactly. The slogan I follow Paul is alive and well. It has only changed names.

A divided church is a scandal, and the answer is neither to deny it nor to despair of it. It is to grieve it, to refuse both the cheap unity that pretends truth does not matter and the cheap cynicism that pretends the divisions are the whole story, and to live toward the day Christ prayed for. The number was always a distraction. The real and stubborn fact, the one the skeptic should have to explain, is not that Christians divided. It is that after everything, underneath all of it, they are still confessing the same crucified and risen Lord.

### Works Cited

Newbigin, Lesslie. 1989. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Vanhoozer, Kevin J. 2016. Biblical Authority after Babel. Grand Rapids: Brazos Press.

title: The Crusades: What Actually Happened
excerpt: The Crusades are the favorite club used against the faith. The honest history is worse than the cliche, and its deepest critique is Christian, not secular.
body:
The Crusades are the club. Raise the violence of religion in any argument and they arrive within a sentence, offered as the proof that faith makes people kill. The honest history is worse than the cliche and also more complicated than it, and a Christianity that cannot tell the truth about its own worst chapters has no business asking anyone to trust it about anything.

So tell the truth. The First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, and the soldiers massacred the city, Muslims and Jews together, in a slaughter the chroniclers describe with horror and pride in the same sentence. On the way there, in 1096, crusaders in the Rhineland turned on the Jewish communities and murdered thousands, among the first great pogroms of European history, carried out by men wearing the cross. And the Fourth Crusade, in 1204, never reached a Muslim army at all. It sacked Constantinople, the greatest Christian city in the world, and Christians looted and desecrated the churches of other Christians. None of this can be explained away, and the attempt to explain it away is itself a second offense.

Steel-man the critic fully. The argument made by Christopher Hitchens and Sam Harris is that here is religion doing exactly what religion does, sanctifying slaughter with the name of God, and that the Crusades are not an aberration but a revelation of what belief licenses (Hitchens 2007). Give it its weight. The atrocities were real, they were vast, and they were done explicitly in the name of Christ with the promise of heaven attached. A believer who shrugs that off has not reckoned with it.

Now the other correction, because the cartoon is false in the opposite direction. The popular picture of the Crusades as unprovoked Western colonial aggression against a peaceful East is bad history. The historians, Thomas Madden and Christopher Tyerman among them, point out that the Crusades came after four centuries of conquest that had taken three-quarters of the formerly Christian world, including the Holy Land itself, and that the First Crusade was called in answer to an appeal from the Christian East against advancing armies (Madden 2005). The medieval crusader was not a modern colonialist. Most went bankrupt going, and many went believing they were defending their brothers and reclaiming stolen ground. The history is a tangle of real grievance and real horror, and both are true at once.

But here is the reversal that neither the atheist nor the defensive apologist wants to hear. The Crusades do not indict Christianity by being too Christian. They indict it by being a betrayal of Christianity, the photographic negative of its own Lord. On the night he was arrested, Peter drew a sword to defend him, the one moment in the Gospels a disciple takes up arms for Jesus, and Jesus stopped him cold. Put your sword back into its place, he said, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52 ESV). Standing before Pilate he said that his kingdom was not of this world, and that if it were, his servants would fight (John 18:36). The whole logic of the cross is a king who conquers by dying rather than by killing, who refuses the legions he could have called down. Measure the Crusades against that and they are not the fruit of the faith. They are its inversion.

Which means the most devastating critique of the Crusades is not the atheist's. It is the Christian one. The atheist says religion made them violent. The gospel says they abandoned the religion the moment they raised a sword in its name, because the founder of it went unarmed to his own execution and told his followers the world would know them by their love and not by their conquests. You cannot use the Crusades to refute a faith whose Lord and whose earliest martyrs died precisely by refusing to do what the crusaders did.

It is easy to condemn men dead a thousand years. The harder thing is to notice that the crusading impulse, the certainty that God's cause can be advanced by force and that our enemies are therefore his, did not die in the Middle Ages. It only traded the sword for other weapons, the culture war waged as though it were a holy war, the opponent to be crushed rather than the neighbor to be loved. We did this. Some version of we keeps doing it.

The church should not flinch from the Crusades, and it should not excuse them. It should own them, and then it should say the one thing that is both true and damning. They were done in the name of a Lord who would have stopped them, who did stop Peter, who chose the cross over the sword and asked his people to do the same. The kingdom of God has never once advanced by killing for him. It has only ever advanced by people willing to die for him. The crusaders forgot which one they were called to. So, often, do we.

### Works Cited

Hitchens, Christopher. 2007. God Is Not Great. New York: Twelve.

Madden, Thomas F. 2005. The New Concise History of the Crusades. Lanham, MD: Rowman and Littlefield.

Tyerman, Christopher. 2006. God's War: A New History of the Crusades. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

title: What Is the Kingdom of God
excerpt: The kingdom of God is not a place you go when you die and not a program you build with your own hands, and once you see what it actually is, you cannot read the rest of the Bible the same way.
body:
A man walks out of the wilderness in a backwater province of the Roman Empire, and the first thing out of his mouth is a sentence that does not sound like good news to anyone listening. 'The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand. Repent and believe in the gospel' (Mark 1:14-15 ESV). Mark gives us no childhood, no genealogy, no slow build. He drops us into motion. And the first word Jesus preaches is not love, not grace, not even God. The first word is kingdom.

We have spent two thousand years making that word smaller than it is. Ask the average person in the pew what the kingdom of God means and you will get one of three answers, and each of them is a ruin of the original. Some will say it means heaven, the place your soul travels to after death. Some will say it means a better society, the cause you organize for, the politics you bless. Some will say it means a feeling, an inner peace, the territory of the private heart. Each of these contains a fragment of the truth. None of them is the thing. And the gap between the fragment and the thing is where most of our discipleship quietly dies.

Start with the word itself, because the word has been mistranslated in our imaginations. The Greek is basileia. Behind it stands the Hebrew malkuth. Neither word primarily means a territory. They mean reign, rule, the active exercise of kingship. George Eldon Ladd spent his career pressing this single point against a church that kept hearing real estate where the text said sovereignty (Ladd 1959). The kingdom of God is not first a where. It is a happening. It is God stepping into the world to be king of it again. When Jesus says the kingdom is at hand, he is not announcing the address of the afterlife. He is announcing an invasion.

The word also carries a history older than Jesus, and the history matters, because his hearers did not come to that sermon with empty ears. For centuries Israel had sung the malkuth of God in its worship. The Lord reigns, the psalms declared, let the earth rejoice (Psalm 97:1 ESV). But to sing that God reigns while Babylon burned your temple and Rome posted soldiers in your streets was to sing against the visible evidence. The kingship of God had become a contested claim, a hope held in the teeth of an occupation. So when a Galilean stood up and said the reign of God was now at hand, he was not introducing a novel idea. He was lighting a fuse that had been laid centuries before, and everyone within earshot knew what was supposed to happen when that reign finally arrived. The enemies of God would be judged. The exile would end. The world would be set right. That expectation is the pressure behind every page of the Gospels, and we cannot feel the scandal of Jesus until we feel what his hearers were braced for and did not get.

That changes the grammar of the whole Gospel. If the kingdom were a place, the only question would be how to get in. But if the kingdom is God's active reign breaking into history, then the question becomes something far more disturbing. It becomes whether you will surrender to a king who has arrived without your permission. This is why the announcement comes wrapped in a command. Repent. The word is not religious throat-clearing. It is what you do when a true king turns up and you have been living as though the throne were empty.

Consider the strongest version of the objection, because it deserves to be met at full strength. The skeptic, and many honest Christians with him, looks at the world and says the kingdom plainly did not come. Jesus announced God's reign, and then Rome went on ruling, the poor stayed poor, the cross happened, and the centuries since have been a long catalog of war and famine and the church itself often on the wrong side of both. Albert Schweitzer made this case with brutal honesty over a century ago, arguing that Jesus expected the immediate, cataclysmic arrival of the kingdom and was simply wrong, that the wheel of history did not turn and instead crushed him (Schweitzer 1906). This is not a cheap objection. It is the most serious one. If the kingdom came, why does the world look like this.

What the objection gets right is that the kingdom was supposed to be visible. The Hebrew prophets did not dream of a private spirituality. They dreamed of swords beaten into plowshares, of the wolf lying down with the lamb, of a king on David's throne whose government had no end (Isaiah 9:7 ESV). Walter Brueggemann calls this the prophetic imagination, the refusal to accept the present arrangement as final, the insistence that the world owes God an account it has not yet paid (Brueggemann 1978). The skeptic and the prophet agree on one thing the comfortable Christian forgets. If the kingdom is real, it must touch the ground. It must show up in bodies and bread and the actual structures of power. A kingdom that changes nothing visible is not a kingdom. It is a mood.

So we cannot answer Schweitzer by retreating into the inner life. That retreat is exactly the first misreading, the kingdom shrunk to a feeling, and it is a betrayal of everything the prophets meant. Jesus himself blocks that exit. When the Pharisees ask when the kingdom will come, he says the kingdom of God is not coming with signs to be observed, and then, 'the kingdom of God is in the midst of you' (Luke 17:21 ESV). That phrase has been domesticated into 'within you,' as though Jesus were pointing at the human heart. He was not. He was standing in front of them. The kingdom was in their midst because the king was in their midst, eating with them, touching lepers, telling them stories that turned their world inside out. The kingdom is not in your interior. It is in the room, and it has a face.

This is where Ladd's great contribution does its work, and where the false either-or finally breaks. The kingdom has both come and not yet come. Already and not yet. Ladd argued that the New Testament holds two truths in a single grip that we keep trying to pry apart (Ladd 1974). The kingdom is genuinely present. In Jesus the future has invaded the present. When he casts out demons, he says, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (Matthew 12:28 ESV). The reign of God is here, in his person, in his acts, like the first light before dawn that is genuinely day even though the sun has not cleared the horizon. And yet the kingdom is also future. We still pray, 'your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven' (Matthew 6:10 ESV). We would not pray for what we already fully possess. The kingdom has come in the king. The kingdom has not yet come in its fullness. We live in the overlap, in the strange and uncomfortable middle, where the decisive battle is won and the war is not over.

This was not the church's settled instinct, and the history of how we lost it is instructive. The earliest believers lived in the tension naturally, expecting the King's return and ordering their common life around it. But across the centuries the two halves of the truth kept tearing apart. By the fourth century, when Constantine made the faith respectable and the empire baptized itself, a powerful temptation arrived to read the kingdom as already arrived in Christendom itself, the church and the state fused into the visible reign of God on earth.
