Augustine wrote The City of God against exactly that confusion, refusing to identify the kingdom of God with any earthly order, Roman or ecclesial, insisting that the two cities grow up intermingled until the end and are not to be sorted by human hands (Augustine, City of God). He saw what happens when the church mistakes itself for the finished kingdom. It stops praying come and starts policing the borders of a kingdom it imagines it already runs. Augustine's correction held for a time and then was forgotten, and forgotten again, in every age that has tried to build the kingdom by force or announce that we have already arrived.

This is not a clever dodge invented to save Jesus from Schweitzer. It is written into the parables, which are the kingdom's native language. Think of the parables Jesus uses, all of them straining toward this double truth. The kingdom is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, that becomes a tree (Matthew 13:31-32 ESV). It is here, small, easy to miss, and it is going to become enormous, and both things are true at once. The kingdom is like leaven a woman hides in three measures of flour until it is all leavened (Matthew 13:33 ESV). Present, hidden, working, not yet finished. The kingdom is like a man who sows good seed, and then his enemy sows weeds among the wheat, and the master says let them grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:24-30 ESV). The kingdom has come, and the weeds are still standing, and the day of sorting is not yet. Jesus answered Schweitzer's objection before Schweitzer was born. The kingdom did come. It came like a seed, not like an army. The visible fullness is held back, on purpose, to leave room for repentance.

This is the reversal, and it is the heart of the matter. The objection, that the kingdom did not arrive in power, is not a refutation of the gospel. It is a description of the mercy of God. The reason the world is not yet swept clean, the reason the wheat and the weeds still grow in the same field, is that the king is patient, not wanting any to perish but all to reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9 ESV). The delay the skeptic counts as evidence against the kingdom is the very space in which the skeptic is being given time to repent. The gap between already and not yet is not a flaw in the system. It is grace, stretched out in time, holding the door open. If the kingdom had come in full the day Jesus announced it, the door would have shut on every one of us. The slowness is the love.

But we have not yet reached the bottom of the announcement, and the bottom is where the cross stands. Because how does this king establish his reign. Not the way Schweitzer expected and not the way the crowd wanted. The crowd wanted a kingdom that would throw out Rome. They wanted the second misreading, the kingdom as political program, the cause that names its enemies and crushes them. Jesus refused it so completely that when they tried to make him king by force, he withdrew (John 6:15 ESV). And then he marched toward Jerusalem and let himself be killed by the very empire everyone wanted him to overthrow.

N.T. Wright has spent decades insisting that we cannot understand the kingdom apart from the cross, that the crucifixion is not a detour from the kingdom project but the means by which the kingdom comes (Wright 1996). On the cross the king does battle with the real enemy, which was never Rome. The real enemy is the sin and death that hold every human being, Roman and Jew, skeptic and saint, in the same grip. The kingdom comes through a throne that is a gallows. The crown is made of thorns. This is the law before the grace, and we have to feel the law first. The reason the kingdom could not simply arrive and fix everything is that the problem was not out there in the structures. The problem was in us. I am the weed in the field. The empire I most need overthrown is the one I administer in my own chest. Until that is dealt with, no rearrangement of the world's furniture will save it. And it could only be dealt with by a king willing to die for his rebels.

Watch how the placard over his head completes the argument. Pilate had it nailed to the cross, written in three languages so no passerby could miss it, the King of the Jews (John 19:19 ESV). It was meant as mockery, a joke at the expense of a beaten man and the nation he failed to deliver. But the Gospels report it because the mockery told the truth Pilate did not understand. This is in fact how this King reigns. The title is accurate. The throne is the cross. The crowd wanted a Messiah who would do to Rome what Rome did to its enemies, and they got instead a King who absorbed the violence rather than dealing it, who let the empire spend its full force on him and exhausted it there. Brueggemann's prophetic imagination reaches its limit and its fulfillment at this point, because the prophets imagined a reign that would overturn the arrangements of power, and here the reign arrives by submitting to the worst those arrangements could do, and breaking them from the inside (Brueggemann 1978). The kingdom does not defeat the violence of the world by out-violencing it. It defeats it by refusing to play, and dying, and rising anyway.

That is why the announcement begins with repent. Not because God is petty about rules, but because the kingdom is the reign of God, and you cannot have the reign of God in a heart that insists on reigning itself. The cross is where the false king in me is dethroned, and the true king takes the throne by the most unlikely conquest in history, by being conquered. The grave could not hold him, and his rising is the first square foot of the new creation, the not-yet breaking decisively into the already, the guarantee that the harvest will come.

Lesslie Newbigin saw what this means for the church with a clarity born of watching the gospel land in cultures that had never heard it. The church, he wrote, is not the kingdom. The church is the sign, the foretaste, the instrument of the kingdom, a community that lives now by the rules of a reign that is not yet visible everywhere, so that the world can see what is coming (Newbigin 1989). When the church forgets this, it makes both of the old mistakes at once. It either becomes a waiting room for heaven, a society of people killing time until they die, which is the kingdom-as-place error. Or it becomes one more political faction baptizing its preferred power, which is the kingdom-as-program error. The true church is stranger than both. It is a colony of the future, planted in the present, that does not match either the despair of the world or the pretensions of the world. It feeds the hungry not to build utopia but because the king it serves does, and it does not despair when the weeds keep growing because it knows whose hand controls the harvest.

Newbigin had earned this by watching it happen. He spent decades in India, where the gospel arrived in a culture that owed it nothing and shared none of its assumptions, and he saw that the kingdom could not be argued into people as an idea. It had to be visible in a community, or it was not credible at all. The only hermeneutic of the gospel, he wrote, the only interpretation the watching world will finally trust, is a congregation that believes it (Newbigin 1989). That is a heavy word for the church, and it should land as conviction before it lands as comfort. If the reign of God is real and present, then the question the world is entitled to ask is not whether our doctrine is coherent. It is whether anything in our common life looks like a place where God is actually king. I have to ask it of my own congregation, and of myself, and the honest answer is rarely the whole answer I would like to give. We are a sign that is often smudged. We are a foretaste that frequently tastes of nothing. And yet the kingdom does not depend on the quality of the sign for its coming, which is the only reason a smudged church can preach it at all.

So what is the kingdom of God. It is the reign of God breaking into history in the person of Jesus, decisively begun and not yet complete, announced in a sermon, demonstrated in healings, parabled in seeds and leaven, won on a cross, sealed in an empty tomb, entrusted to a people, and aimed at a day when the prayer is finally answered and the will of God is done on earth as it is in heaven. It is not where you go. It is who is reigning. And the only question the announcement leaves you is the one it asked from the beginning, standing there in Galilee with the dust still on his feet. The king has come. The throne is no longer empty. What will you do with the fact that it was never yours.

### Works Cited

Augustine of Hippo. The City of God. c. 426.

Brueggemann, Walter. The Prophetic Imagination. Philadelphia: Fortress Press, 1978.

Ladd, George Eldon. The Gospel of the Kingdom. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1959.

Ladd, George Eldon. A Theology of the New Testament. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1974.

Newbigin, Lesslie. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1989.

Schweitzer, Albert. The Quest of the Historical Jesus. London: A. and C. Black, 1906.

Wright, N.T. Jesus and the Victory of God. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1996.

title: Exodus: The Story Underneath the Whole Bible
excerpt: Every act of rescue in Scripture is told in the grammar of one ancient escape from Egypt, and until you learn that grammar you will keep mistaking the gospel for something smaller than freedom.
body:
Israel did not begin its national memory with a creed. It began with a rescue. When a later generation asked what it meant to belong to this God, the answer was not a definition. It was a story. 'I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery' (Exodus 20:2 ESV). That sentence stands at the head of the Ten Commandments. Before God gives a single command, he names himself by what he did. He is the God who got his people out.

We tend to read Exodus as one episode among many, a dramatic chapter with plagues and a parted sea, useful for children's films. That is a failure of attention. Exodus is not an episode. It is the template. It is the shape every later rescue in Scripture is poured into, the deep grammar of how God saves. Christopher Wright argues that the exodus functions as the paradigm of redemption for the entire Hebrew Bible, the event Israel reached for whenever it needed to understand what salvation was (Wright 2006). When the prophets imagine a future deliverance, they describe a new exodus. When the psalmist needs to praise, he rehearses the sea. The story underneath the whole Bible is the story of a God who hears slaves and comes down.

Look at how it actually begins, because the beginning is the part we rush past. It does not begin with a plan. It begins with a sound. 'The people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. And their cry for help came up to God. And God heard their groaning' (Exodus 2:23-24 ESV). Before there is a Moses, before there is a bush, there is a groan that reaches heaven. This is the first thing Exodus wants us to know about God, and it is the thing we least believe when we are the ones groaning. He hears. The text is almost monotonous about it. God heard, God remembered, God saw, God knew. Four verbs, and salvation has not yet visibly moved, but the whole outcome is already certain, because God has turned his face toward the noise of suffering.

Now consider the strongest objection, the one a thoughtful skeptic raises and a grieving believer feels in the night. If this God hears groaning and comes down to rescue, where is he. The slaves in Egypt cried for four centuries before the sea opened. The objection is not that God never acts. It is that he is unbearably slow, and that the gap between the groan and the rescue is filled with real children who died still enslaved. Walter Brueggemann does not flinch from this. He notes that the exodus is precisely a story told by people who knew exile, who knew what it was to wait on a God whose timing they could not control or excuse (Brueggemann 1997). The honest reading of Exodus does not promise that rescue is prompt. It promises that rescue is real, and that the waiting is not the same as abandonment.

What the objection gets right is the cost of the delay. Scripture never sanitizes it. But the shape of the story answers the objection in a way no argument could. The exodus tells us that God's silence is not God's absence, because the same God who waited four centuries was, the whole time, hearing. The groan was already filed in heaven. The rescue was already coming before the rescuer was born. The slowness we read as neglect, the story reads as a God working below the surface of a history that looks God-forsaken.

Then comes the night that names everything. Because here is the part of the exodus we sentimentalize most and understand least. The final plague does not pass over Israel because Israel was innocent. The destroyer comes for every firstborn in the land, and the only difference between a saved house and a bereaved one is blood on a doorframe. 'The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you' (Exodus 12:13 ESV). A lamb dies so that a household lives. This is the diagnosis before the deliverance, the law before the grace. Israel is not rescued because Israel deserved it more than Egypt. Israel is rescued because a substitute bled in the doorway. The exodus is not a story about good people escaping bad people. It is a story about death passing over a people who had done nothing to earn the lamb.

That is the spine that runs to the cross. The Gospels are not subtle about it. Jesus goes to Jerusalem to die at Passover, the very feast that remembers the lamb. John the Baptist sees him coming and says, 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world' (John 1:29 ESV). Paul writes flatly that Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7 ESV). The New Testament reads the cross through Exodus on purpose, because the cross is the exodus the first one was always pointing toward. Egypt was never the real captor. The real captor was the sin and death that hold every human being, Egyptian and Israelite, in the same chains. And the rescue from that captivity costs the same currency it always cost. A lamb in the doorway. A firstborn who dies so the household lives. Only this time the lamb is the firstborn, and the doorway is a Roman cross, and the blood is the blood of God's own Son.

Now watch the reversal turn. The skeptic's question, where is the God who rescues, is answered not by a God who stays safely above the suffering and pulls his favorites out of it. It is answered by a God who climbs down into the slavery himself. The cross is the exodus where the deliverer does not stand on the far shore waving the slaves across. He becomes the lamb. He takes the place in the doorway. The question, why is God so slow to come down, meets the answer that he came all the way down, lower than Egypt, into the grave itself, and came out the other side leading captives free. The delay you held against him was the long road he was walking toward you the whole time.

And notice what the rescued are rescued for, because this is where most of our gospel goes thin. Israel is not brought out of Egypt to wander free in a vague liberty. They are brought out to Sinai, and from Sinai to a land, and at the center of the land a tabernacle, so that God can dwell among them. The exodus ends not with an escape but with a presence. 'Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst' (Exodus 25:8 ESV). Freedom in the Bible is never merely freedom from. It is freedom for. Out of slavery, into the presence of God. The whole arc bends toward the last pages of Scripture, where the new exodus is complete and the voice from the throne says the dwelling place of God is with man, and he will dwell with them (Revelation 21:3 ESV). The exodus was always heading home.

So we read our own bondage by this light, and we should be careful here, because the exodus refuses both the lie that says we are not enslaved and the lie that says we can free ourselves. Egypt is not only a place in the past. It is the name for whatever holds a human being against the purpose of God, the habit you cannot break, the fear you organize your life around, the resentment you nurse, the self you cannot put down. We do not march out of those by trying harder. No slave ever escaped Egypt by improving his attitude toward Pharaoh. The exodus comes from outside. It comes from a God who hears the groan we are often too defeated even to pray.

That is the story underneath the whole Bible. Not advice. Rescue. A God who hears slaves, comes down into their misery, provides the lamb, leads them through the water, and brings them home to himself. We did not begin with a creed, and neither did Israel. We began in a doorway, in the dark, with the destroyer abroad in the land, listening to the breathing of a household that should have died and did not, because something else died in its place. Whoever understands that night understands everything that comes after it.

### Works Cited

Brueggemann, Walter. Theology of the Old Testament. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1997.

Wright, Christopher J.H. The Mission of God. Downers Grove: IVP Academic, 2006.

title: Why the Bible Is One Story, Not Sixty-Six Books
excerpt: The library on your shelf was written across a thousand years by dozens of hands, and it tells a single story so coherent that the only honest explanation is that one Author was writing through all of them.
body:
Open most Bibles and the table of contents tells you it is a collection. Sixty-six books, two testaments, written across more than a thousand years by farmers and kings and fishermen and a tax collector, in three languages, on three continents. Every honest reader has to begin where the skeptic begins. This looks like an anthology, not a book. It looks like a shelf, not a story. And the question is whether the unity anyone claims to find in it is really there, or whether it is read in afterward by people who needed it to cohere.

That objection deserves its full weight, because it is largely true on the surface. The Bible was not handed down whole. It was assembled. The Hebrew Scriptures took their shape over centuries, and the Christian canon was not formally settled until councils late in the fourth century, Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397, ratifying a consensus the churches had already lived by for generations. A modern critic like James Barr pressed exactly this point, warning against imposing a false theological unity on documents that were diverse and often in tension (Barr 1983). If you flatten the Bible into a single bland message, you have not honored it. You have erased it. The differences are real. Job argues with the easy answers. Ecclesiastes refuses the cheerful ones. The four Gospels do not even narrate the resurrection morning in identical order.

What the objection gets right is that unity imposed by force is a lie. A genuine unity cannot mean uniformity. It cannot mean pretending Leviticus and the Sermon on the Mount sound the same or want the same thing. So if there is a story holding these sixty-six books together, it has to be the kind of unity that survives real diversity, the way a symphony survives the difference between a cello and a trumpet, the way one story survives many chapters that feel nothing alike. The test is whether the parts, left in their full strangeness, still move toward something.

They do, and the something has a name. The whole library is bent toward a single figure. On the road to Emmaus, after the resurrection, a stranger falls in with two devastated disciples, and the text says, 'beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself' (Luke 24:27 ESV). That is the claim the Bible makes about itself. Not that it contains scattered predictions, but that the entire arc, Moses and the Prophets and the Writings, was about him the whole time, and that the disciples had been reading the right books with the wrong eyes. The risen Jesus does not give them new information. He gives them the key to the books they already had.

This is the discipline biblical theology recovers, and it changes how you read every page. Geerhardus Vos, who taught a century ago at Princeton, argued that revelation is not a heap of timeless truths but a history, an unfolding, where God reveals himself progressively across the centuries until the whole reaches its meaning in Christ (Vos 1948). The Bible is not a flat field of equally bright verses. It is a story moving from promise to fulfillment, from shadow to substance, from a garden lost to a city gained. Read this way the differences stop being problems and become the necessary chapters of a plot. Leviticus and Hebrews do not contradict. Hebrews is what the sacrifices were straining toward. The blood of bulls and goats was never the point. It was the promissory note. The cross is where it gets paid.

Trace the single thread and watch it hold. The story opens in a garden where God dwells with human beings, and almost immediately the dwelling is broken, and the rest of the Bible is the long account of how God gets back to dwelling with us. He makes a covenant with Abraham, promising that through one family all the families of the earth will be blessed (Genesis 12:3 ESV). The promise narrows to a nation, then to a king, then to a remnant, then to a single man dying outside a city wall, and then it explodes outward again to every nation, which is exactly where Abraham was always aimed. The story that begins with a garden ends with a city in which God dwells with his people and wipes every tear from their eyes (Revelation 21:3-4 ESV). The first pages and the last pages are answering each other across a thousand years of writing. The breach in Eden and the healing in the new Jerusalem are the same story's opening and close.

Now the reversal. The very feature the skeptic counts against the Bible, its scattered authorship across a millennium, is the strongest evidence for the unity once you see it. If one author wrote a coherent story, that is unremarkable. Any novelist does it. But here are dozens of writers separated by centuries, most of whom never met, most of whom had no way of knowing what the others wrote, and the thing they produce is not a contradiction but a convergence, a single plot moving with intent toward a single climax none of them lived to see completed. The diversity is not the problem for the claim of unity. The diversity is the proof of it. Coherence across a committee that never met is the signature of an author behind the authors.

This is what the church confessed early, before there was a settled canon to confess it about. Irenaeus, writing around 180 against the Gnostics who wanted to sever the Old Testament from the New and invent a different God for each, insisted that there is one God and one story, that the same God who made the world in Genesis is the God who redeems it in Christ, and that to break the Bible in two is to lose the gospel itself (Irenaeus, Against Heresies). The heretics of the second century did exactly what the modern critic fears, they imposed a scheme from outside, and the result was not a more honest Bible but a smaller God. The church's answer was not to flatten the Scriptures into uniformity. It was to read them as one drama with one divine playwright and many human players.

And the cross is where the whole drama turns and proves itself, because this is not a story that resolves by getting nicer. It resolves by going through death. Every thread of the Old Testament that seemed broken, the failed kings, the exile, the silence, the sacrifices that never quite cleansed the conscience, all of it gathers at Golgotha and is answered there. The law diagnosed a wound the law could not heal. It named the sin and named the price and then could not pay it. The whole sacrificial system was a finger pointing at a debt, century after century, and the finger could not settle the account. Then one death settles it. This is why the Bible is one story and not sixty-six books. Sixty-six books with no center would be a library. Sixty-six books that all turn out to be about one death and one rising are a single story that simply took a thousand years to tell.

So we read it differently now, or we should. Not as a grab bag of verses to be lifted out and pasted onto our preferences, which is how most of us were taught to read it and how most of us still do. The single verse torn from the story becomes a slogan, and the slogan usually serves us rather than judges us. The Bible read as one story will not be domesticated like that. It keeps insisting that we are not the main character. There is one protagonist, and he is not me, and the plot does not bend toward my comfort. It bends toward a cross, and then toward a city, and it asks whether I will lose the small story I was telling about myself in order to be written into the true one.

That is the difference between a shelf and a book. A shelf you browse. A book reads you back. The Bible is not a collection you consult for the verse you wanted. It is one story, told by many hands across many centuries, all of them writing toward a man they had not met, and the only adequate explanation for how a thousand years of strangers wrote one coherent story is the explanation the story itself gives. Someone was writing through all of them. The library was always a book.

### Works Cited

Barr, James. Holy Scripture: Canon, Authority, Criticism. Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1983.

Irenaeus of Lyons. Against Heresies. c. 180.

Vos, Geerhardus. Biblical Theology: Old and New Testaments. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1948.

title: What It Means to Bear the Image of God
excerpt: The oldest sentence about human dignity is not that we are smart or useful or productive but that we carry the likeness of God, and everything humane in our civilization is a borrowed inheritance from that one claim.
body:
The first thing the Bible says about a human being is the most radical thing ever said about one. 'So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them' (Genesis 1:27 ESV). Six chapters of cosmos, light and water and stars and beasts, and then God pauses over one creature and stamps it with his own likeness. The Latin phrase the church has carried for centuries is imago dei, the image of God. It is the foundation under every claim your civilization makes about human worth, and most people who depend on it have no idea it is there.

We should begin by feeling the strangeness of it, because the ancient world found it strange. In the cultures surrounding Israel, the image of a god was a statue housed in a temple, and the only human who bore the divine image was the king. Pharaoh was the image of the god. The peasant in the field was not. Then Genesis arrives and does something seismic. It takes the language reserved for the king and the temple statue and hands it to every human being without exception. Male and female. Slave and free. The dying infant and the failing elder. Gerhard von Rad, reading Genesis with care, saw that the image was not first about an internal quality but about a representative function, the human being placed in creation as God's regent, standing in for the king before the world (von Rad 1972). You are not a statue in a temple. You are a living likeness, set in the world to bear the face of the One who made it.

Now the objection, and it is a serious one, perhaps the most serious one a modern person can raise. The skeptic says human beings are not the image of anything. We are evolved primates, remarkable but not sacred, a temporary arrangement of matter that will dissolve. To call us images of God is a comforting fiction, and the honest view is that our worth is a story we tell ourselves to keep from despair. This objection is not crude. Its sharpest exponents, from Nietzsche forward, pressed it with terrible consistency. If God is dead, Nietzsche understood, then the dignity that was borrowed from God dies too, and we will have to invent our worth or admit we have none.

What the objection gets right is the dependency. It is correct that human dignity is borrowed, that it does not float free, that if you saw off the branch you are sitting on you will fall. The atheist philosopher who insists on universal human rights while denying any ground for them is living on inherited capital. Jurgen Habermas, no friend of the church, admitted that the idea of the equal worth of every person is a direct inheritance from the biblical doctrine of the image of God, and that secular reason has not produced a replacement, only continued to spend down the account (Habermas 2006). The skeptic is right that our dignity has a root. He is only wrong about whether the root is real. Cut the root, and you do not get a freestanding humanism. You get a managed humanity, sorted by usefulness, and the twentieth century showed us in detail what that sorting looks like.

Here is where the doctrine does its hardest work, because the image of God is not a flattering thing to be told. It is a weight before it is a comfort. If I bear the image of God, then so does the person I despise, and that is intolerable to the way I actually live. The doctrine indicts me before it dignifies my neighbor. James, the brother of Jesus, drives this exact point. With the tongue, he writes, 'we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God' (James 3:9 ESV). The same mouth. The contradiction James names is the contradiction in every one of us. We affirm human dignity in the abstract and assault it in the particular, in the driver who cut us off, in the relative we have written off, in the stranger whose politics we have decided makes him less. The image of God is not a doctrine that makes me feel good about humanity. It is a doctrine that convicts me of how casually I deface the likeness of God in the people I find inconvenient.

And this is where the story darkens before it heals, where the law comes before the grace. Because Genesis does not stop at chapter one. The image is given, and then the image is defaced. By chapter three the likeness is fractured, and by chapter four one image-bearer is murdering another in a field, and the rest of human history is the long record of the image of God lifting its hand against itself. We are not innocent statues. We are damaged ones, and the damage is not only out there in the violent. Augustine saw this with unflinching honesty, that the image in us is not erased but distorted, bent inward, curved away from the God it was made to reflect, so that we use the very faculties of likeness to grasp for ourselves (Augustine, On the Trinity). The image remains, which is why every human is sacred. The image is broken, which is why no human is safe.

Now the cross, and the cross is where the doctrine of the image is rescued from being merely a sentiment. The New Testament makes a claim that lands like a hammer. Jesus, it says, is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15 ESV). Not an image. The image. The likeness we were made to bear and shattered, he carries undamaged. And then he does the thing that turns the whole doctrine inside out. The true image of God is nailed to a cross by the defaced images of God, by us, and instead of destroying the ones defacing him, he dies to restore them. The image we ruined is repaired by the Image we killed. This is the grace, and it only makes sense after the law has done its diagnosis, after we have admitted that we are not merely image-bearers in need of affirmation but image-defacers in need of mercy.

Watch the reversal complete itself. The skeptic said our dignity is borrowed and therefore unreal. The gospel agrees that it is borrowed and insists that the lender came in person to make the loan good. We did not generate our worth and we cannot. It is given, and not only given at creation but given again at Calvary, where the cost of one defaced image is measured by what it took to restore it. The blood of the Son of God. That is the price tag the cross hangs on a human being. Whatever you think you are worth, the cross says you are worth the death of God to redeem. The skeptic worried our dignity was too cheap to be real. The gospel answers that it is too expensive to be anything but real.

So we go back into a world full of image-bearers, and the doctrine will not let us live the way we did. It abolishes the categories we use to rank people. There is no human being who is merely a means, merely a vote, merely a demographic, merely an obstacle. There is no one beneath your contempt because there is no one beneath God's likeness. James K.A. Smith reminds us that what we love and how we treat others is not first a matter of what we believe but of what we have been formed to desire, and that learning to see the image of God in the people we have been trained to overlook is a slow reformation of the heart, not a single decision (Smith 2009). You will not wake up tomorrow seeing every face as the face of a king's representative. But the cross has set the standard, and the standard does not bend.

This is what it means to bear the image of God. It means you are not an accident and you are not a product and you are not the sum of your usefulness. It means the dignity you hope is real is real, anchored not in your achievements but in your origin and bought back at your Maker's expense. And it means the person you most want to discount is carrying the same likeness, untouchable, redeemed at the same price. The doctrine that lifts you also strips you of the right to look down on anyone. You bear the image of God. So does everyone you were about to dismiss. Now go and treat them like it.

### Works Cited

Augustine of Hippo. On the Trinity. c. 416.

Habermas, Jurgen. Time of Transitions. Cambridge: Polity Press, 2006.

Smith, James K.A. Desiring the Kingdom: Worship, Worldview, and Cultural Formation. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2009.

von Rad, Gerhard. Genesis: A Commentary. Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1972.

title: Already and Not Yet: Living Between Two Worlds
excerpt: The reason your faith so often feels like victory and defeat at the same time is not that you are doing it wrong but that you are living in the exact overlap the New Testament said you would.
body:
Every honest believer eventually runs into the same wall. The promises sound total. The new life, the freedom from sin, the peace that surpasses understanding, the defeat of death. And then you wake up the next morning and you are still anxious, still fighting the same old habit, still standing at gravesides. So which is it. Either the promises are exaggerated, or you are failing to claim them. Most of us oscillate between those two conclusions, blaming the Bible one week and ourselves the next. There is a third possibility, and it is the truest thing the New Testament ever taught about the present moment.

The third possibility has a name. Already and not yet. The phrase belongs to George Eldon Ladd, who spent his career arguing that the New Testament holds two truths together that we keep trying to separate, that the kingdom of God has genuinely arrived in Jesus and has not yet arrived in fullness, and that the entire Christian life is lived in the overlap between those two facts (Ladd 1974). You are not crazy. You are not uniquely failing. You are living in the overlap of the ages, where the new creation has begun and the old order has not finished dying, and both are true at the same time, in the same body, on the same Tuesday.

Let the strongest objection have its say, because it is the objection of every clear-eyed person who has watched Christians make excuses. The skeptic says this already-and-not-yet business is just theology covering its own failures. Whatever the gospel promised but did not deliver gets filed under not yet, and whatever it managed to produce gets filed under already, and the scheme is unfalsifiable, a way of always being right by never being checkable. This is a fair charge, and it would be devastating if the structure were invented after the fact to explain disappointment. The question is whether already and not yet is a patch applied to a leaking theory, or whether it was built into the gospel from the start.

It was built in from the start, and the proof is that the New Testament writers describe the tension as the normal condition before anyone needed an excuse for it. Paul does not stumble into already-and-not-yet when his churches disappoint him. He builds his whole understanding of the present on it. 'If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away, behold, the new has come' (2 Corinthians 5:17 ESV). That is the already, stated without hedging. The old is gone. The new is here. And the same Paul, in the same body of letters, writes that the whole creation groans, and we ourselves groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption, the redemption of our bodies (Romans 8:23 ESV). We have been adopted, and we are waiting to be adopted. We are new, and we are groaning. He says both without embarrassment because both are true, and he knew it before any church gave him a reason to need it.

Here is the text I want to carry through, because it holds the whole tension in a single sentence and refuses to release it. Paul writes that God 'raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus' (Ephesians 2:6 ESV). Read that slowly. Seated. Past tense. Already. In the mind of God your future is so certain that he speaks of it as finished. You are already seated with Christ in glory. And then turn a few pages and the same letter tells you to put on the whole armor of God, because you are in a war that is very much still being fought (Ephesians 6:11 ESV). Seated in glory. Armed for battle. The same person, in the same letter, at the same moment. This is not contradiction. This is the shape of the overlap, and once you see it you stop trying to choose between the two halves of your own experience.

The history of the church is largely a history of refusing the overlap, collapsing it toward one side or the other. Some collapse it toward the already. The triumphalist insists you can have it all now, perfect health, unbroken victory, sin behind you forever, and when reality contradicts him he blames the sufferer for lacking faith. This is cruelty dressed as confidence, and it has broken people I have sat with, who were told their cancer was a failure of belief. Others collapse it toward the not yet. The defeatist concludes nothing really changes until heaven, so the present is just grim endurance, and the new creation language is spiritualized into a someday with no purchase on now. Augustine, writing as Rome fell around him, refused both errors. He described two cities intermingled in this present age, the city of God and the city of man, growing up together, not to be separated until the end, so that the Christian lives as a citizen of one city while residing in the other, neither already home nor entirely in exile (Augustine, City of God). He would not let the believer pretend the kingdom had fully come, and he would not let him pretend it had not come at all.

Now the cross, because the overlap is not an abstract scheme. It is carved into the gospel events themselves. At the cross the decisive battle was won. The text says Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15 ESV). The victory is real, and it is past, and it is total. And yet the defeated powers still thrash. This is why the New Testament so often uses the language of an enemy already beaten who has not yet surrendered. Oscar Cullmann gave the picture that has never been improved, the difference between the decisive battle and the final armistice, between D-Day and V-Day (Cullmann 1951). The war was decided on a single day. The fighting continued after, real fighting, real casualties, but the outcome was no longer in doubt. That is exactly where we live. The cross was the day the war was decided. We are in the mopping-up, where the bullets are real and the result is certain.

Watch the reversal. The skeptic said the not-yet was an excuse for the gospel's failures. But the not-yet is not the gospel's weakness, it is the gospel's mercy, the same mercy we met in the kingdom delayed. If the already were complete, if the final reckoning had come the moment Christ rose, then the door would have shut, and it would have shut on you and on me before we ever heard the news. The reason the new creation has begun but not finished is that the King is holding the field open, leaving time for the war's stragglers to come over to the winning side. The very gap the skeptic counts against the gospel is the room in which the skeptic is still being invited in. The not-yet is not a failure to deliver. It is a refusal to slam the door.

So how do we live in the overlap, between the two worlds, seated and armed at once. We live without the two lies the collapse always produces. We refuse the lie of the triumphalist, that says if you suffer you have failed, because the not-yet is real and your groaning is not unbelief, it is honesty. And we refuse the lie of the defeatist, that says nothing changes until you die, because the already is real and the new creation has genuinely begun in you, and the habit you are fighting is a defeated enemy, not an undefeated one. The overlap is not a comfortable place. It was never meant to be. It is a war you fight as a soldier whose victory is already certified, grieving real losses with real hope, refusing both the false peace and the false despair.

That is the verdict, and it does not resolve, because the overlap by definition does not resolve, not yet. You will feel like a new creation and a groaning captive on the same morning, and both readings will be accurate, and the gospel does not ask you to pick one. It asks you to hold them the way Paul did, seated in glory with the armor still on. The war is won. The fighting is real. And the only people who lose their footing in this strange middle country are the ones who insist on living in only one of the two worlds the gospel says we now inhabit together.

### Works Cited

Augustine of Hippo. The City of God. c. 426.

Cullmann, Oscar. Christ and Time: The Primitive Christian Conception of Time and History. London: SCM Press, 1951.

Ladd, George Eldon. A Theology of the New Testament. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1974.

title: What Christian Nationalism Is and What It Is Not
excerpt: The phrase has become a weapon thrown in both directions, and almost nobody using it has stopped to ask what it actually names.
body:
A man left my office last spring with his jaw set, certain I had insulted his grandfather. He had heard me use the phrase Christian nationalism in a sermon, and what he heard was an accusation against everyone who had ever stood for a flag with their hand over their heart, everyone who had wept at a military funeral, everyone who believed this country was given something by God worth keeping. His grandfather had landed at Normandy. He was not going to sit still while his pastor called that idolatry.

I did not call it idolatry. But I understood why he heard it that way, and the reason I understood is that the phrase has been ruined in both directions. To the man in my office it is a slur, a way for elites to sneer at ordinary patriotic faith. To the people who use it most loudly on the other side it is a catchall for everything they fear about conservative Christians, a word that means little more than people I disagree with who pray. Between those two distortions the actual thing the term was coined to describe has nearly disappeared. And the actual thing is real, and it is dangerous, and we cannot resist it until we can define it without slandering the man whose grandfather landed at Normandy.

So I want to do something slow. I want to say what Christian nationalism is not, at length and in good faith, before I say what it is. Because the first faith handed to me, after I came up out of atheism, was already fused with the flag. Nobody sat me down and taught me the fusion. It was in the air of the building, in the placement of the colors on the platform, in the assumption that to love Jesus and to love America were one undivided loyalty. I did not question it for years. I am not standing outside this. I am standing inside it, writing toward myself.

Let me make the strongest case for the man who fears the phrase, because that case has real weight. He says that loving your country is not a sin. He is right. Scripture does not command us to despise the place we were born or the people we live among. Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of the city where God had sent them, to build houses and plant gardens and pray for Babylon, because in its welfare they would find their own (Jeremiah 29:7 ESV). That is a kind of patriotism, a settled care for a particular place and its people. The man who fears the phrase says that gratitude for a country, its laws, its soldiers, its harvests, is a form of honoring the gifts of God, and he is right about that too. He says that the people who throw the phrase at him have often never set foot in his church, do not know that his congregation feeds the hungry and buries the poor and visits the prisoner, and use Christian nationalism as a way to dismiss faithful people without listening to them. He is frequently right about that, and the carelessness of his accusers is its own sin. I will not defend it.

Here is what he gets right that I most want to honor. He senses that the people warning about Christian nationalism are often selectively alarmed, that they fear religion in public only when it is the wrong religion, that a faith driven entirely out of public life is not neutrality but a different establishment wearing the mask of neutrality. Lesslie Newbigin spent forty years as a missionary in India and came home to a Western culture that imagined itself secular and neutral, and he saw through it (Newbigin 1989). There is no neutral public square. The question is never whether faith shapes public life but which faith and how. The man who fears the phrase has felt this in his bones, and he is not wrong to resent being told that only his convictions must be left at the door.

Now I will answer the strongest version of his case, not the weak one. Because everything he has said so far describes patriotism, and patriotism is not what the phrase names. The scholars who coined the term in its careful sociological sense were not describing love of country. Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry, in their 2020 study Taking America Back for God, drew on years of survey data to define Christian nationalism as a cultural framework, a set of beliefs that fuses American civic identity with a particular Christian identity, that holds the nation has a covenant with God, that its laws should privilege that faith, and that its decline is a story of fall from a Christian founding that must be reclaimed (Whitehead and Perry 2020). The key word is fuses. Patriotism loves a country. Christian nationalism marries the country to God and then refuses to let anyone file for divorce.

The distinction is not mine. Reinhold Niebuhr saw it, watching the Cold War sanctify American power. The love of country, he wrote, is a high form of natural devotion, but it becomes demonic the moment it claims the unconditioned loyalty that belongs to God alone (Niebuhr 1952). That is the line. Patriotism is a love with limits, a love that can be criticized, corrected, repented. Nationalism is a love that has become ultimate, that cannot be questioned, because to question the nation has become the same as questioning God. The grandfather who landed at Normandy was a patriot. The grandfather who came home and believed America could do no wrong because God was on its side had crossed over, and most of us cross over without noticing the line at our feet.

Robert Bellah gave us the older name for the milder version of this in 1967. He called it civil religion, the set of shared beliefs and rituals through which a nation understands itself in relation to the transcendent, the appeals to God in inaugural addresses, the sacred status of founding documents, the liturgy of national holidays (Bellah 1967). Bellah did not think civil religion was simply evil. He thought it could call a nation to judgment as easily as it could flatter it, that Lincoln at Gettysburg used it to indict the country he led. But civil religion is a loaded instrument. It can humble a nation before a God who stands above it, or it can hand the nation a God who exists to bless it. Christian nationalism is what civil religion becomes when the second wins.

So here is the distinction at its sharpest. Not the love of country. The worship of it. Patriotism can stand under judgment. Nationalism cannot, because it has made the nation the thing that judges. The test is not whether you sing the anthem or honor the dead or feel your throat tighten at the sight of the colors. I do all of that. The test is what happens when your country and your Christ command different things. The patriot grieves and obeys Christ. The nationalist has arranged his theology so the conflict can never arise, because he has quietly decided his country and his Christ want the same thing, always, by definition.

The history of how we got here is specific, and the specifics matter, because the man in my office is right that the phrase is often thrown without history. Mark Noll, the finest historian of American evangelicalism, has shown that the colonists did not arrive with a unified Christian nation in mind, that the founders were a theological mixture from devout Calvinists to skeptical deists, that the Constitution names no God and establishes no church on purpose (Noll 2002). The story of a Christian founding lost and needing reclaiming is itself a later construction, built in the nineteenth century and rebuilt in the twentieth. George Marsden has traced how fundamentalism in the 1920s came to see itself as the last defender of a Christian civilization under siege, how the loss at the Scopes trial in 1925 drove that conviction underground where it hardened (Marsden 2006). The sense of a stolen country is not ancient. It is roughly a hundred years old, and it was manufactured.

The figures matter because the dates do. The phrase one nation under God was not in the Pledge of Allegiance when the Pledge was written in 1892. Congress inserted it in 1954, at the height of the Cold War, to mark the difference between a godly America and a godless Soviet enemy. In God we trust became the official national motto in 1956, displacing the older and more modest e pluribus unum. These were not the recovery of a Christian founding. They were the manufacture of one, in living memory, under the pressure of a particular fear. The covenant so many believers now assume to be ancient was legislated within the lifetime of people still in my pews. A covenant you can date to an act of Congress is not a covenant with God. It is a national mood that learned to talk like one.

Kristin Kobes Du Mez carried the story forward in 2020, and she did it carefully, with the sources in front of her. She showed how across the twentieth century a particular vision of Christian manhood, rugged, militant, protective, took on the features of John Wayne, and how the defense of the nation and the defense of that manhood became a single project in much of white evangelicalism (Du Mez 2020). I know some readers will distrust her because of where her conclusions land. Read the footnotes anyway. The pattern she documents is not invented. It is the air I breathed in the first church that taught me to follow Jesus, and I did not know the air had a history until someone showed me.

The sociology of the present moment is more precise than either side's slogans. Whitehead and Perry did not simply assert that Christian nationalism exists. They measured it, sorting Americans along a spectrum from those who reject the fusion entirely to those who embrace it fully, and they found that where a person falls on that spectrum predicts a startling range of other things, attitudes toward immigrants, toward gun control, toward who counts as a real American, with more force than denomination or even church attendance (Whitehead and Perry 2020). That last finding is the one that should stop a believer cold. The strongest expressions of Christian nationalism are often found among people who do not attend church much at all. It is less a deep faith than an identity, a way of marking the boundary of the nation with the language of religion. Which means it can flourish in a heart that has very little of Christ in it, because it was never really about Christ. It was about the nation, dressed in his name.

Now carry the one text that should govern all of this. When Jesus stood before Pilate, the man who held Rome's power in that province, he said something that should have ended Christian nationalism before it was born. My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36 ESV). The kingdom Jesus announced does not arrive by capturing a nation. It does not advance by seizing the levers of the state. The moment a movement believes the gospel needs a country to enforce it, the moment it believes Christ requires Caesar's sword to finish his work, it has confessed that it does not believe what Jesus told Pilate. And that confession is the engine room of Christian nationalism. It does not trust the kingdom that is not of this world, so it builds a kingdom that is.

This is where the law does its work before grace can speak. The man who fears the phrase wanted me to absolve patriotic faith, and I can absolve patriotism. But I cannot absolve the deeper thing, because the deeper thing is in me. I have wanted my country to be the kingdom. I have wanted to win by the means Jesus refused. I have stood at the line Niebuhr drew and stepped across it, loving my nation with a loyalty that left no room for the nation to be wrong. That is not the grandfather's sin alone. It is mine, and naming it as sin is the only door to the grace that can heal it. You cannot repent of a thing you are still calling virtue.

Stanley Hauerwas spent a career insisting that the first task of the church is to be the church, not to run the country, that the church is itself a polity, a people gathered around a crucified Lord whose only weapon is the truth (Hauerwas 1991). When the church forgets this, it does not lose its faith all at once. It trades it slowly, a little theology for a little power, until the cross has become a flagpole and nobody remembers the exchange.

The deepest theological objection to Christian nationalism is not that it loves the wrong country. It is that it tells the wrong story about how God saves. The fusion always carries a quiet account of salvation along with it, an account in which the nation is the vehicle of God's purpose in history, its founding a kind of new covenant, its decline a fall, its restoration a redemption that faithful citizens are called to bring about by reclaiming what was lost. That is a complete account of sin and salvation, and Jesus is not at the center of it. The nation is. Mark Noll, surveying how American Christians have read their own history, warned against exactly this habit of reading providence directly off the events of national life, of assuming that we can know that God favored this army or blessed that founding, when Scripture is far more reticent about such certainties than we are (Noll 2002). The God who works through nations does not thereby endorse them. He used Assyria as a rod and then broke the rod. A nation can be an instrument in God's hand and still stand under his judgment, and the believer who cannot hold both has confused the instrument with the hand. Augustine saw the same trade sixteen centuries earlier, watching Rome fall and watching Christians panic as though the city of God could fall with it. Two cities, he said, built by two loves, the earthly city by the love of self reaching the contempt of God, the city of God by the love of God reaching the contempt of self (Augustine 426). Every generation is asked which city it serves. We answer not with our slogans but with what we will do for power.

There is a further danger that the man in my office did not see, and it cuts toward him rather than away from him. Christian nationalism does not finally serve the nation either. It corrupts both halves of what it fuses. It gives the believer a faith too small to judge his country and gives the country a god too tame to correct it, and the result is a Christianity that cannot speak prophetically to power because it has married power, and a patriotism that cannot be honest about its own history because honesty has become blasphemy. Newbigin saw that a gospel which simply blesses a culture has lost the very thing that makes it gospel, its capacity to call that culture to repentance (Newbigin 1989). A faith that can only affirm the nation has nothing left to say to it. It has become the chaplaincy of the status quo, and the status quo has never once been saved by its chaplains.

So what is Christian nationalism. It is not loving your country. It is not gratitude for a soldier's sacrifice or a settled care for the welfare of your city. It is the fusion of the nation and the faith into one loyalty that cannot be questioned, the belief that God has a covenant with this particular country that requires its laws to privilege this particular faith, and the conviction that the kingdom of Christ can be advanced by the capture of the state. It is patriotism that has stopped being able to repent.

The man left my office certain I had insulted his grandfather. I had not. I had described a fork in the road that his grandfather and mine both stood at, the same fork I stand at every time I am tempted to want the country more than the cross. The phrase is not a slur against patriotic faith. It is the name for what patriotic faith becomes the moment it forgets the kingdom is not of this world. Most of us forgot. I forgot. The question is whether we will remember before the flag finishes covering the cross.

### Works Cited

Augustine. The City of God. Circa 426.

Bellah, Robert N. Civil Religion in America. Daedalus, 1967.

Du Mez, Kristin Kobes. Jesus and John Wayne: How White Evangelicals Corrupted a Faith and Fractured a Nation. Liveright, 2020.

Hauerwas, Stanley. After Christendom. Abingdon Press, 1991.

Marsden, George M. Fundamentalism and American Culture. Oxford University Press, 2006.

Newbigin, Lesslie. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Eerdmans, 1989.

Niebuhr, Reinhold. The Irony of American History. Scribner, 1952.

Noll, Mark A. America's God: From Jonathan Edwards to Abraham Lincoln. Oxford University Press, 2002.

Whitehead, Andrew L., and Samuel L. Perry. Taking America Back for God: Christian Nationalism in the United States. Oxford University Press, 2020.

title: The Difference Between Loving and Worshiping Your Country
excerpt: Love can be corrected, and worship cannot, and that single difference is the whole line between honoring your country and serving it as a god.
body:
My oldest son asked me once, after a parade, why we put our hands over our hearts. I gave him the easy answer about respect and the people who died. Then I drove home turning the question over, because it was a better question than my answer. We put our hands over our hearts in two settings. One is in front of the flag. The other is when we pray. A child notices the rhyme that an adult has stopped hearing.

The question underneath my son's question is the oldest one a believer faces. What may I love, and how much, before love becomes worship. Because love and worship are not opposites. Worship is what love becomes when it stops admitting any limit. And a country is one of the easiest things in the world to love past its limit, because a country asks for that love openly, with music and graves and the names of the fallen, and to withhold it feels like betrayal of the dead.

I want to defend the love before I warn against the worship, because the warning is dishonest without the defense. A Christian may love his country, truly and without apology. The same Scripture that exiled Israel to Babylon told them to love Babylon, to seek its welfare, to pray for it, to plant gardens in it (Jeremiah 29:7 ESV). That is not grudging tolerance. That is a command to care for a place that was not even their own. How much more may a person care for the country that raised him, fed him, schooled his children, buried his father. The instinct that tightens a man's throat at a military funeral is not a sin. It is a love, and love is a good thing, and the people who sneer at it have usually never loved a place enough to be embarrassed by their own tears.

The strongest objection to everything I am about to say comes from the believer who hears warnings against nationalism as warnings against love itself. He says the warnings always cut one direction, that nobody scolds the cosmopolitan who feels nothing for any place, that the suspicion of patriotism is itself a kind of contempt for ordinary people and their ordinary loyalties. He is right that the contempt is real and common. He is right that a man who loves nowhere is not more holy than a man who loves somewhere. Rootlessness is not a virtue. So I am not arguing for the cold heart that the warnings sometimes smuggle in. I am arguing for the difference between a warm heart and an enthroned one.

Here is the line, and I will draw it as plainly as I can. Love can be corrected. Worship cannot. You can love your wife and still tell her she is wrong, still grieve when she sins, still refuse to follow her into something evil, and the love survives the correction, even deepens through it. But the thing you worship cannot be corrected, because correction assumes a standard above the thing, and worship has put the thing at the top where no standard reaches it. The test of whether you love your country or worship it is not how you feel at the parade. It is what you do when your country is wrong. The lover says my country, and grieves, and resists. The worshiper says my country, and defends it, because the alternative would mean his god has failed.

Reinhold Niebuhr named this near the end of his life, watching the United States sanctify its own power in the Cold War. Patriotism, he wrote, is a high form of devotion, but it becomes demonic when it claims an unconditioned loyalty, the loyalty that belongs to God alone (Niebuhr 1952). The word he chose was demonic, and he did not choose it for effect. He meant that a good thing loved past its limit does not stay good and shrink. It becomes a power that demands sacrifice, that silences conscience, that turns the love of a place into the willingness to do evil for it. That is the mechanism of every idol. The idol is rarely a bad thing. It is usually a good thing that has been asked to be God.

Augustine saw the same mechanism a millennium and a half earlier, and he gave it the cleanest definition we have. Sin, he taught, is disordered love, love poured out in the wrong proportion, the lesser good loved as though it were the greatest (Augustine 397). The drunk does not love wine too much in some simple sense. He loves it out of order, above his health, above his family, above God. The nationalist does not love his country too much. He loves it out of order, above the kingdom, above the stranger his country fears, above the Christ who told him the stranger bears the image of God. The problem was never the size of the love. It was the place the love was put.

Carry one text as the spine of this. When the people demanded a king so they could be like the nations around them, God told Samuel something that should unsettle every patriot who has ever wanted his country to be great. They have not rejected you, he said. They have rejected me from being king over them (1 Samuel 8:7 ESV). Israel wanted a nation that could stand tall among the nations, a king they could see, a strength they could point to. God read that desire correctly. It was not a political preference. It was a transfer of trust, away from the God they could not see and toward the nation they could. He gave them the king they asked for, and the king taxed them and conscripted their sons and led them into the very ruin they had been warned about. The desire to be like the nations is never merely political. It is always, underneath, a quiet abdication of the throne.

This is where I have to stop pointing and step into the indictment, because the line I have drawn runs through me. I have loved my country out of order. There have been seasons when I would have been more upset to hear my nation criticized than to hear my Lord ignored, and that ratio is the whole diagnosis. The thing you defend most fiercely is the thing you actually worship, whatever your mouth confesses on Sunday. I have watched myself grow hot at an insult to the flag and cool at an insult to the cross, and the temperature gauge does not lie. The law has to land here before any grace can. You cannot be forgiven for an idol you are still defending as devotion.

The cross does the actual work at exactly this point. Because the cross is what God does with disordered love. Christ does not come to scold us into reordering our affections by willpower. He comes to die, and in dying he exposes every false king for what it is, the nation that crucified him no less than the temple that handed him over. The empire put him on a Roman cross under a sign that named him a political threat, and he let it, and in letting it he broke the spell that says power saves. Caesar killed God and God rose anyway. After that morning no nation can credibly claim to be the thing that saves, because the strongest nation that ever lived already killed the one who saves and could not keep him dead. The resurrection is the permanent demotion of every empire.

So what do I tell my son now, when he asks again why we put our hands over our hearts. I tell him we love this place, and loving it is good, and he should love it too. Then I tell him that the same hand goes over the heart in two rooms, and the order of the two rooms is the whole of the Christian life. In one room we honor a country that can be wrong. In the other we worship a Lord who cannot. The day we forget which room is which, we will still be putting our hands over our hearts, and we will have no idea that the gesture has changed its god.

Love your country. Refuse to worship it. The difference is whether you can still tell it the truth.

### Works Cited

Augustine. Confessions. Circa 397.

Augustine. On Christian Doctrine. Circa 397.

Niebuhr, Reinhold. The Irony of American History. Scribner, 1952.

title: Flags in the Sanctuary: A Theology of the Nation
excerpt: The flag stands on most American platforms because nobody put it there on purpose, and that is precisely the problem.
body:
There are two flags on the platform of the church where I learned to preach. I did not put them there. Neither did the pastor before me, or the one before him. They have stood beside the pulpit longer than anyone alive in the congregation can remember, which means no one ever decided to place them there. They simply appeared, sometime in the middle of the last century, and they have been guarding the Word ever since with a quiet authority that no business meeting ever granted them.

That is the strange thing about the flag in the sanctuary. Almost nobody chose it. It arrived the way the air in a room arrives, without a vote, and now to move it would feel like an act of aggression, while to have placed it would have felt like nothing at all. The asymmetry is the whole subject of this essay. We will defend to the point of fury an arrangement that we never once chose to make. And a thing you will fight to keep but would never have thought to install is worth examining, because it has more power over you than the things you actually decided.

Let me make the honest case for the flag before I question it, because the case is real and the people who make it are not fools. They say the flag in the sanctuary is simple gratitude, a way of honoring the country that protects the freedom to gather and worship at all. They say it honors the men and women of the congregation who served, some of whom did not come home, and that to remove it would wound the families of the dead for the sake of a theological abstraction. They say the church does not live in heaven yet but in a particular country, under particular laws, and that pretending otherwise is its own dishonesty. Every one of those points has weight. The freedom to gather is a real gift. The dead are owed real honor. The church is in a real place. I will not wave any of that away.

The strongest version of the case goes further, and I want to state it at full strength. It says that removing the flag is not neutrality but a statement of its own, a signal that the church is ashamed of its country, that it has joined the cultured despisers who look down on ordinary patriotic believers. And that is sometimes exactly what removal means and exactly how it is meant. I have seen the flag taken down as a sneer, not a confession, by people more eager to perform their sophistication than to worship. So the question is not settled by simply removing the cloth. A bare platform can serve pride as easily as a draped one can serve idolatry. The object is not the disease. The disease is in what the object is permitted to mean.

Now I will answer the strongest case, and I will answer it with a question about geography. Where does the flag stand. Not in the lobby, where we might thank God for the gift of a free country and the service of its soldiers. On the platform. Beside the pulpit. Inside the space the architecture reserves for the most sacred things, the Word and the table and the waters of baptism. The placement is a sermon, and it preaches every week whether or not anyone notices, because the eye learns from arrangement faster than the ear learns from speech. A symbol that stands beside the cross will eventually be read as the cross's equal, and a child raised in that room will absorb the equality long before he could put words to it. My own children have.

Robert Bellah taught us to see this as liturgy and not decoration. Civil religion, he wrote in 1967, is a real religion with its own sacred objects, its own holy days, its own scriptures in the founding documents, and its own saints among the founders and the war dead (Bellah 1967). The flag is not a neutral piece of fabric. It is a sacred object in a functioning religion, and when you carry a sacred object from one religion into the holy space of another, you do not get nothing. You get fusion. You get a worshiper who can no longer feel the seam between the two faiths, who experiences his patriotism and his Christianity as one undivided devotion, which is the precise definition of the thing the careful scholars call Christian nationalism (Whitehead and Perry 2020).

Carry the governing text. When Solomon finished the temple, the glory of the Lord filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister, because the glory filled it (1 Kings 8:11 ESV). The sanctuary in Scripture is the place where one glory dwells, and it tolerates no rival in its space. The whole architecture of Israel's worship was a long lesson in the danger of bringing the symbols of the nations into the holy place. When the kings of Judah set up the altars of other gods beside the altar of the Lord, the prophets did not call it diversity. They called it the thing that brought the house down. The sanctuary is jealous space. It was built to be jealous. To bring a second glory into it is not addition. It is competition, and the second glory always wins eventually, because it asks for less and flatters more.

I cannot write this from a safe distance. The flags on my platform have outlasted my objections to them. I have stood beside them Sunday after Sunday and preached the kingdom that is not of this world while the kingdom of this world stood at my right hand, and I have not moved it, because I know what moving it would cost and I have not been willing to pay it. That is the confession underneath this essay. I am not the prophet clearing the temple. I am the priest who has grown used to the second altar and tells himself it is only cloth. The law lands on me first. I have let the symbol stand because the symbol is easier to keep than to explain.

Here is where the cross does its work in the room itself. The cross is the one symbol in that sanctuary that refuses to share. It is not a symbol of strength but of a state execution, the empire's own instrument turned into the throne of God. When you stand the flag of any nation beside the cross, you have placed the sword of empire beside the thing the empire used to kill God, and you have asked them to mean the same devotion. They cannot. The cross is the permanent judgment on every nation, including the one whose colors stand beside it, because every nation would have done to Christ exactly what Rome did, and most of them have done it to his people since. The cross does not bless the flag. The cross indicts the flag, gently, and waits to see whether the church will hear.

So what is the theology of the nation that the sanctuary should teach. Not contempt for the country. Honor it, in its place, in the lobby of gratitude, in the prayers of the people, in the genuine thanks we owe for freedom and for the dead. But not on the platform, not beside the Word, not in the jealous space where one glory dwells. The nation is a real thing that God uses and judges, owed honor and owed truth, and the church serves it best by refusing to worship it. A church that cannot tell its country the truth has already handed the country the throne, and the arrangement of its furniture confessed the surrender before the preacher said a word.

I have not moved the flags yet. Writing this is the beginning of moving them, or it is one more way of not. The reader will know which when he visits, and so will my sons, who are watching where their father puts the second glory. The sanctuary teaches whether or not we mean it to. The only question is what we are willing to let it teach.

### Works Cited

Bellah, Robert N. Civil Religion in America. Daedalus, 1967.

Whitehead, Andrew L., and Samuel L. Perry. Taking America Back for God: Christian Nationalism in the United States. Oxford University Press, 2020.

title: Whose Kingdom? Jesus and Political Power
excerpt: Jesus was offered every kingdom of the world by someone who actually had them to give, and what he did with the offer settles the question we keep reopening.
body:
Before Jesus preached a sermon or healed a single body, he was taken to a high place and shown every kingdom of the world. The one showing him had the authority to make the offer. All these I will give you, he said, if you will fall down and worship me (Matthew 4:9 ESV). It was not a hollow temptation. The kingdoms were really on the table. And the price was a single act of worship aimed in the wrong direction. Jesus refused, and the refusal is the founding decision of his entire ministry. He would not take the kingdoms of the world on the terms by which the kingdoms of the world are taken.

We reopen this question every election cycle as though Jesus never settled it. We ask how the church should hold political power, what it should do with influence, how it should bend the levers of the state toward righteousness. These are not foolish questions. But they are downstream of a prior question that the wilderness already answered, and we keep skipping the answer because we do not like it. The prior question is whether the kingdom of God advances by the means the world uses to advance its kingdoms. Jesus said no in the desert, said it again to Pilate, and said it most loudly on a cross. We have spent two thousand years pretending we did not hear.

The strongest objection to a hands-off reading deserves a full hearing, because it is not the objection of cowards. It comes from believers who say the church cannot retreat from public life and call the retreat holiness. They point out that the prophets confronted kings, that John the Baptist lost his head for telling Herod his marriage was unlawful, that William Wilberforce used political power to end the British slave trade, that Bonhoeffer joined a plot against Hitler. They say that to abandon the public square in the name of a kingdom not of this world is to leave the vulnerable at the mercy of whoever does not abandon it. That is a serious charge, and it is largely true. A church that washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people that power crushes.

I want to grant the whole of it, because the half-grant is a cheat. The prophets did confront kings. Christians did and should engage the machinery of justice. A faith that has nothing to say to Pharaoh is not the faith of the Exodus. The error I am warning against is not engagement. It is the belief that engagement means seizing the throne, that the kingdom of God is the kind of kingdom you install by winning, that Christ needs to govern through Caesar because he cannot govern any other way. Wilberforce did not try to make Britain the kingdom of God. He pressed a particular evil with the tools at hand and trusted a Lord who reigns whether or not the vote goes his way. The difference between that and Christian nationalism is the difference between salt and a coup.

So carry the governing text to its end. When Jesus stood before Pilate, the only man in the room with the power to kill him, Pilate asked if he was a king. Jesus answered with the sentence that should have ended the argument forever. My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over (John 18:36 ESV). Read what he is saying. He is not saying his kingdom has no bearing on this world. He is saying it does not come from this world's source and does not advance by this world's method. The proof he offers is the absence of fighting. A kingdom that fights to install its king is a kingdom of this world by definition. The kingdom of God is recognizable precisely by its refusal to take up the sword that every earthly kingdom requires.

This is the reversal that the nationalist reading cannot survive. The crowd on Palm Sunday wanted exactly the king the tempter offered, a king who would ride into Jerusalem and throw out Rome and restore the throne of David by force. They spread their cloaks and shouted hosanna, which means save us, and they meant save us from the empire. Jesus rode in on a donkey, the animal of peace, not a warhorse, and within the week the same crowd was screaming for his blood, because he would not be the king they wanted. They wanted power that conquers. He gave them power that dies.
