Augustine wrote that in the fourth century about his own youth, a brilliant, sensual, exhausted young man who had tried philosophy, ambition, sex, and prestige, and found every one of them a door that opened onto another empty room. He is the original case study for what is happening now. Not a man argued into faith by evidence alone, but a man worn out by the failure of every immanent thing to hold the weight he kept placing on it. Gen Z has been handed the most complete buffet of immanent satisfactions in human history, every pleasure and distraction available on a device in their pocket, and a measurable share of them have eaten the whole buffet by twenty and found themselves still hungry. The restlessness Augustine named is not a bug in the secular age. It is the secular age failing to deliver on its only promise.

Trace the root and the irony sharpens. The generation that is stirring was raised by the most thoroughly secular parenting in Western history, the children of the children of the sixties, formed by a culture that told them the self was sovereign and meaning was self-authored and no story was truer than any other. And it did not make them free. It made them anxious. The mental health data on this generation is grim and not in dispute, and a self handed total authorship of its own meaning turns out to be a self crushed under a weight it was never built to carry. Newbigin saw the shape of this coming, that a culture which severs fact from value and locks faith out of the realm of public truth leaves its young with private feelings and no public ground to stand on (Newbigin 1989, 16). We built them a world with no floor and called it liberation. Some of them have stopped falling long enough to ask whether there was ever a floor.

Here is the reversal the church most needs to hear, and it cuts against our instinct. The young are not coming back because we became more like them. They are coming back, where they are coming back, because the world became exactly like them and it was unbearable. The seeker-sensitive instinct of the last forty years was to strip the church of everything strange, to make the service feel like the culture so the culture would feel at home. And the culture did feel at home, which is precisely the problem, because a generation drowning in the culture does not want one more building that feels like it. They want the smell of something older than their anxiety. Reverence. Mystery. A word spoken with authority by someone who did not invent it. Eugene Peterson warned us for decades that the pastor's job was never to entertain but to pay attention to the holy and refuse the role of religious salesman (Peterson 1993, 18). The churches reaching the young are, strikingly, often the ones that never apologized for being churches.

And here the law has to come before the grace, or we will flatter them to death. The law says this generation has been lied to, and some of us did the lying. We told them the gospel was mainly therapeutic, a tool for their flourishing, Christ as life coach, and they tried it and found it thin, because a gospel that exists to serve the self cannot save the self from itself. The hard word the young are actually responding to is the word we have been too cowardly to preach. That they are sinners, that the cross was necessary and not merely nice, that following Christ will cost them the very autonomy their whole culture told them to defend. The law indicts me here. I have softened the cross to keep a room comfortable. I have preached the resurrection and skipped the death it required. And the young can smell that evasion from across the sanctuary. They have been marketed to their entire lives, and they recognize a sales pitch faster than any generation before them.

Which is why the grace, when it comes clean, lands so hard on them. A generation exhausted by performing, by curating, by the relentless labor of authoring its own worth, hears that righteousness is a gift it cannot earn and weeps. The young man at the coffee shop did not come to faith because I made it easy. He came because I told him the truth, that he could not save himself, that Christ already had, and that the only thing left for him to do was to stop running and receive it. He was baptized in the fall. He still asks hard questions. I hope he never stops.

The church that wins this generation by flattering it will lose it again within a decade, because flattery is exactly what they are fleeing. The church that tells them the truth, the whole weight of it, law and cross and grave and empty tomb, will find them more ready to hear it than we have any right to expect. They have tried the world we built for them. They are restless. We know what that means. We were restless too.

Do not give them comfort. Give them Christ.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 2008. Confessions. Translated by Henry Chadwick. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Bible Society. 2025. The Quiet Revival. London: Bible Society and YouGov.

Newbigin, Lesslie. 1989. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1993. The Contemplative Pastor: Returning to the Art of Spiritual Direction. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Pew Research Center. 2024. Religious Landscape Study. Washington: Pew Research Center.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge: Harvard University Press.

title: Replanting: When a Church Has to Start Over
excerpt: Replanting asks a congregation to do the one thing flesh resists most, to lay down its own life so that something it will not control can rise in its place.
body:
The vote was twenty-three to nine. Twenty-three older members of a congregation that had run six hundred strong in 1978 agreed to dissolve as they were and hand their building, their name, their endowment, and their Sunday morning to a replant they would not lead and could barely recognize. I was in the room as an outside voice, and I watched a woman in her eighties raise her hand for yes with tears running down her face. Afterward I asked her how she could vote to end the church she had given her life to. She said it was the only way to keep it from ending. Then she said something I have not been able to shake. We are not voting to die. We are voting to be buried, which is different, because you only bury what you expect to see again.

Replanting is the hardest word in this whole vocabulary, harder than revitalization, because revitalization still lets a church believe it is fundamentally the same body getting healthier. Replanting does not. Replanting says this body, as it is, cannot continue, and that the most faithful thing it can do is hand its life to a new work that will keep very little of what it was. The real question in a replant is not strategic. It is spiritual to the bone. Can a congregation love Christ and His mission more than it loves its own continuation. Almost everything else is logistics. That one question is the whole war.

Let me steel-man the people who say no, because they are not villains and the easy caricature of them is a lie. The members who resist a replant are usually accused of selfishness, of clinging to the carpet and the casseroles. But the strongest version of their position is not selfish at all. They will say that a church is not an interchangeable franchise, that it is a particular people with a particular history, that the saints buried in its memory and the prayers prayed in its walls are not disposable, and that to wipe it all away and call the result the same church is a kind of forgery. There is real theological weight here. The communion of saints is not a brand to be relaunched. Tim Keller, who spent his career thinking about how churches start and renew, warned against treating congregations as mere delivery systems for programs, insisting that a church is a body with a history and a culture that cannot be engineered from a manual (Keller 2012, 19). So the honest version of the objection is this. Replanting risks treating a living tradition as scrap. And the answer to that objection is not to deny it but to go through it, because Scripture has a category for a death that honors what died precisely by refusing to embalm it.

The spine here is the same hard saying of Jesus that haunts every page of this subject. Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24 ESV). Notice what the seed keeps and what it loses. It does not keep its shape. The husk is destroyed, dissolved in the dark, unrecognizable. But the seed keeps its life, its very specific genetic identity, and what rises is not a different plant but the same life in a form the seed could never have produced by staying intact. This is the exact answer to the objection. Replanting done faithfully is not the erasure of a tradition. It is the burial of a husk so that the life inside it can rise. The woman in her eighties understood the verse better than the consultants. You only bury what you expect to see again.

The history of this is older and more Protestant than we admit. We talk about replanting as a new movement of the last fifteen years, and the practical models are recent, but the underlying conviction runs back to the Reformation itself, which was at bottom a massive replant. The reformers did not believe they were inventing a new church. They believed they were recovering a buried one, that the institution had so encrusted the gospel that the only faithful move was to tear down structures and start the visible church again on the recovered foundation. Mark Noll has shown how the renewal movements that shaped Protestant vitality across the centuries came again and again through disruption rather than maintenance, through people willing to lose the existing form to recover the buried center (Noll 1992, 4). Replanting is not a betrayal of the inherited church. It is the inherited church doing the very thing it was born doing.

Now the reversal, and it is the one that converts a strategy into a death worth dying. We assume the replant is for the sake of the new people, the unreached neighborhood, the young families who will fill the rebuilt sanctuary. That is true but it is not the deepest truth. The replant is also, and maybe first, for the sake of the people voting yes. Because the act of laying down your own church for a future you will not control is itself the most Christlike thing many of those saints will ever do, and it forms them in the image of their Lord more than another decade of survival ever could. I have watched older believers come spiritually alive in the very act of agreeing to their congregation's death, freed at last from the exhausting work of keeping a dying thing propped up, released into the joy of pure gift. The replant did not just serve the new. It saved the old from the slow corrosion of self-preservation. Eugene Peterson said the pastoral task is to keep insisting that the most important things are the things we cannot make happen, only receive (Peterson 1987, 6). The yes vote is exactly that, a refusal to make survival happen, an opening of the hands.

The law has to be preached here without flinching, and it cuts the leader first. The law says that much of our resistance to replanting is idolatry wearing the mask of faithfulness. We say we are protecting the legacy, and sometimes we are protecting our own importance, our own grief, our own fear of admitting that what we built could not last. I have felt this in myself. I have wanted a thing I led to outlive me more than I have wanted Christ to be honored in its ending, and that wanting is not love, it is the same self-preservation the gospel came to kill. The law strips the noble language off the fear and shows it for what it is. A church that will not die for the mission has already started worshiping itself, and the slow death that follows is not tragedy. It is judgment.

And then grace, which is the only thing that makes the burial bearable. The grace is that the God who asks the seed to fall into the earth is the same God who went into the earth first. Christ did not ask of any congregation a death He had not already died, alone, in the dark, with no guarantee visible to flesh that anything would rise. And because He rose, the burial of a faithful church is not a leap into nothing. It is a leap into the pattern of the only One who has ever come back from where He went. The endowment becomes seed. The building becomes soil. The saints who voted yes become, in their final ministry, the very wheat their Lord described, and what rises in that place will carry their life in a form they could not have imagined and will, I believe, one day recognize.

Not every church should be replanted. Some have the health to be revitalized and should be. Some are too far gone for either and should be buried with honor and no pretense of resurrection in this age. Discernment is the whole art, and it cannot be reduced to a flowchart. But where a replant is the faithful road, the church that takes it is not surrendering. It is doing the most ancient Christian thing there is. It is following its Lord into the ground, in the stubborn confidence that the ground is not the end of the story but the one place the story has always begun.

You only bury what you expect to see again. The saints knew that before the consultants did.

### Works Cited

Keller, Timothy. 2012. Center Church: Doing Balanced, Gospel-Centered Ministry in Your City. Grand Rapids: Zondervan.

Noll, Mark A. 1992. A History of Christianity in the United States and Canada. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1987. Working the Angles: The Shape of Pastoral Integrity. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

title: Leading a Church When Trust Is Gone
excerpt: Trust cannot be restored by competence or charisma but only by the slow, costly work of a leader who tells the truth when the truth indicts him.
body:
I followed a man who had lied to the congregation for years. Not about money, which would have been simpler, but about who he was, a pattern of deception that came apart all at once and left a church of good people unable to believe anything said from the pulpit, including the things that were true. I arrived eight months after he left. The wound was not in the budget. It was in the eyes. People listened to me preach with their arms folded, not because they disliked me but because the last man had stood in the same spot and sounded sincere, and look what that was worth. You cannot lead people who have learned that listening is dangerous. And they had learned it from a master.

The instinct in that situation is to rebuild trust by being trustworthy, by being competent and consistent and clearly not the last guy, and that instinct is not wrong but it is not nearly enough. The real question when trust is gone is not how the leader proves himself. The real question is whether the leader understands that broken trust is not primarily a problem to be solved but a wound to be grieved, and that the people are not being difficult, they are being faithful to an injury they did not ask for. A pastor who treats lost trust as an obstacle to his leadership has already revealed that he does not understand it. The lost trust is not in his way. It is the thing he is there to serve.

Here is the strongest case against my whole approach, and it comes from sharp people who have watched too many churches paper over real harm. They will say that talk of rebuilding trust is often a tool of institutional self-protection, that when leaders call for unity and healing they usually mean be quiet and let us move on, and that the demand for renewed trust frequently falls hardest on the very people who were hurt, asking the wounded to extend something to the institution that wounded them. This is not cynicism. It is observation, and it is frequently correct. The history of the church's handling of abuse and deception is a history of premature calls for reconciliation that served the powerful and silenced the harmed. I have to grant this in full, because to wave it away would be to commit the exact sin it names. So the honest version of the objection is this. Trust language is often a weapon against the wounded. And the only answer that is not itself a dodge is to insist that real trust can never be rebuilt by asking the hurt to pretend. It can only be rebuilt by leaders willing to stand inside the indictment rather than above it.

The text I carry into these churches is the most uncomfortable restoration scene in the New Testament. Peter had denied Christ three times, publicly, by a fire, when it cost something to be loyal. And the risen Jesus does not restore him with a warm word and a clean slate. By a charcoal fire, the same kind of fire Peter stood at when he lied, Jesus asks him three times, once for each denial, do you love me (John 21:15 ESV). It is not gentle. The text says Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time (John 21:17 ESV). Jesus rebuilds trust by walking Peter straight back into the smell of his own failure and refusing to let him skip past it. This is the pattern, and it is the opposite of how we usually do it. We rebuild trust by changing the subject. Christ rebuilds it by returning to the wound, naming it fully, and only then speaking the future. Feed my sheep. The commission comes after the fire, never instead of it.

The history of this in the church is long and not flattering, and naming it is part of the repair. The crises of trust that have hollowed out congregations across the last several decades, the financial scandals, the abuse coverups, the celebrity pastors whose private lives contradicted every public word, did not erode trust by accident. They eroded it through a consistent institutional reflex to protect the name over the truth, exactly the Sardis reflex, reputation kept alive after integrity had died. Gallup has measured public confidence in American institutions since the early nineteen seventies, and the long line for nearly every institution, the church among them, bends downward across the decades that follow, and the church accelerated its own fall every time it chose the cover story over confession (Gallup 2022). We were not merely victims of a cynical age. We taught a watching world to distrust us, one cover-up at a time, and the young especially have learned the lesson well.

Now the reversal, the thing that took me three years in that wounded church to learn. The leader cannot rebuild trust by being trusted. He rebuilds it by being trustworthy in a way that does not depend on whether anyone trusts him yet, and that means his faithfulness has to be aimed past the congregation's approval entirely. The moment I needed their trust in order to lead, I made my leadership a transaction, and they could smell the need, and the need is exactly what the last man had. He needed their belief and so he managed his image to secure it. The only way I could be different was to stop needing their trust and start simply telling the truth, including the truths that cost me, including the times I was wrong in front of them, with no anxious eye on whether it was working. Trust, it turns out, is never built by the man who is trying to build it. It is the slow accidental fruit of a man who has stopped trying and started confessing. Eugene Peterson said that the pastor's integrity is in the unseen disciplines, the angles no congregation watches, and that a ministry built for the visible approval rots at the unseen root (Peterson 1987, 2).

So the law comes, and it comes for the leader before it comes for the people who broke trust. The law says that a pastor inheriting a wounded church will be tempted to use the wound, to position himself as the trustworthy rescuer against the villain who left, and that this self-positioning is its own quiet lie. I have done it. I have let a congregation's relief at my arrival become a thing I enjoyed too much, have let myself be the hero of a story whose real hero is Christ and whose real victims deserved more lament than I gave them. The law indicts the rescuer fantasy. It says that the man who rebuilds trust by being the not-villain is still making the church about himself, just in a more flattering pose. I cannot stand outside this. I am exactly the kind of leader who would rather be admired for honesty than actually pay its cost.

And then grace, which is the only ground a wounded church can finally stand on. The grace is that the trust the congregation most needs to recover is not trust in their leaders, who will fail them again because all leaders are men, but trust in the Christ who restored Peter at the fire and did not flinch from the wound. A church whose trust in its pastors has been destroyed has, painfully, been freed from an idol it should never have had. It was never safe to put ultimate trust in a man. The collapse of that trust, brutal as it is, can become the doorway to a deeper and unbreakable trust in the only One who has never once managed His image, who told the truth about us at the cost of His life, and who returns to our fires not to shame us but to commission us. Feed my sheep is spoken to a man who failed and was not pretended past it. That is the only kind of leader a broken church can follow. One who knows the fire.

Trust does not come back when the leader proves he is worthy. It comes back, slowly, when the leader stops needing it and starts telling the truth, especially the truth that costs him. There is no shortcut. There was none for Peter. There is none for me.

The fire is where it starts. We would rather it started anywhere else.

### Works Cited

Gallup. 2022. Confidence in U.S. Institutions Down to a New Low Average. Washington, DC: Gallup.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1987. Working the Angles: The Shape of Pastoral Integrity. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

title: How Individualism Changed the Way We Read the Bible
excerpt: We did not stop believing the Bible, we quietly rewrote who it was talking to, and the someone it now addresses is me alone.
body:
A man stands in my office and tells me God has a plan for his life. He means his life. Singular. The job, the move, the woman he is unsure about. I believe God is at work in all of it. But I notice what he does not notice, which is that the sentence he reached for to describe the will of God landed entirely inside the borders of one person, and that person is himself. He did not learn that sentence from Scripture. He learned it from the air he breathes.

The question is not whether God cares about individuals. He does, down to the hairs of the head. The question is whether the individual has become the only unit we can see, the lens so close to the eye that we no longer recognize it as a lens. We think we are reading the Bible. We are often reading ourselves into it, and calling the echo revelation.

Let me give the strongest version of the other side, because it is strong. The defender of the personal Bible will say that the gospel really is personal, that Jesus left the ninety nine for the one, that Paul writes I have been crucified with Christ, that conversion is not a committee vote, that every believer stands before God without a mediator but Christ, and that the Reformation itself fought and bled for the conscience of the single soul against the machinery of the institution. All of that is true. I would die on that ground. The recovery of the individual conscience before God is one of the great gifts of the church to the world, and the skeptic who values his own freedom of conscience is living, whether he knows it or not, on borrowed Christian capital.

But here is what that argument gets right and then takes too far. It is true that I am saved as a person. It is not true that I am saved as an isolate. The same Paul who says I have been crucified with Christ spends most of his ink writing to churches, in the plural, about a body with many members, and almost every you that English readers hear as singular is in the Greek a you that means all of you together. We read a letter written to a congregation as if it were a note left on my pillow.

Carry one text through this. When Jeremiah delivers the most quoted promise in the American devotional, For I know the plans I have for you, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope (Jeremiah 29:11 ESV), he is not whispering to a discouraged individual about a career change. He is writing a letter to a nation in exile in Babylon, a deported people, telling them to build houses, plant gardens, marry, and seek the welfare of the very city that conquered them, because their God has not abandoned the community even in captivity. The you is a people. The plan is corporate, generational, costly, and seventy years long. We took a word spoken over a traumatized nation and shrank it to fit a coffee mug.

How did this happen. Trace it. Robert Bellah and his colleagues, studying American life in the early 1980s, named the thing precisely. They called it expressive individualism, the conviction that each person has a unique core of feeling and intuition that must be unfolded if individuality is to be realized, and they showed how even the most religious Americans had absorbed it so deeply that they described their faith in the language of personal preference (Bellah 1985). One woman in their study named her own religion after herself. Sheilaism. Charles Taylor traced the longer arc, the slow construction across five centuries of what he calls the buffered self, the modern interior shielded from the world, sealed off, the meaning of a life generated from inside rather than received from outside (Taylor 2007). The porous self of the ancient world, open to God and neighbor and the dead, became the buffered self of the mall, open mainly to its own desires.

The church did not resist this. The church baptized it. By the time American revivalism had run its course through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the altar call had made the decision of the individual the hinge of everything, which is half a glory and half a wound. The glory is that no one is saved by belonging to a crowd. The wound is that we began to imagine the crowd did not matter at all, that a Christian is a sovereign consumer of religious goods who attends a church the way he subscribes to a service, retaining at all times the right to cancel.

Now watch the reversal, because Scripture refuses our flattery. The most individual moment in the Bible, a man alone in a garden at night, sweating blood, is the moment Jesus is least alone in purpose, because he is there for a body he is about to gather out of the whole earth. He prays not for himself but for them, and not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one (John 17:20 ESV). The cross is the most personal act in history and the least private. He died, one man, for a people. The pronoun is singular at the nail and plural at the empty tomb.

This is where law has to come before grace, and the law is this. If I read the Bible as a private message to me, I will use it. I will mine it for the verses that serve my plans and skip the ones that bind me to people I did not choose. I will treat the church as a vendor and my neighbor as scenery. And I will do all of this with a Bible open on my lap, sincerely, never once suspecting that I have made the living God into an accessory to a life I was going to live anyway. That is not a small sin. That is the slow theft of the whole counsel of God, one comforting verse at a time. I have done it. I do it on the mornings I am tired and want the text to console me rather than command me.

The grace is that the God of the letter to Babylon does not abandon the captives, even the captives of our own age, even the ones whose captivity is so comfortable they call it freedom. He still writes to a people. He is still building a house with many rooms and many members, and he means to put me in it next to someone I would not have picked, and call that salvation.

So read the next verse you love and ask the question first. Who is the you. If the answer turns out to be all of you together, and it almost always does, then the verse was never the private property you thought it was. It was a word to a people, and you were being invited to stop being an audience of one.

We made the Bible smaller to make ourselves larger. The book will not stay that size.

### Works Cited

Bellah, Robert N., Richard Madsen, William M. Sullivan, Ann Swidler, and Steven M. Tipton. Habits of the Heart: Individualism and Commitment in American Life. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1985.

Taylor, Charles. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2007.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Consumerism Is a Spiritual Formation
excerpt: The mall is not neutral, it is a cathedral, and we have been worshiping in it longer than we have been worshiping anywhere else.
body:
My sons can tell the difference between two phones I cannot see a difference between. They were not taught this in any class. No one sat them down. They absorbed it the way I absorbed my father's absence, which is to say through the body, through repetition, through a thousand small mornings that added up to a shape before anyone named the shape. They have been formed. The question that should keep a pastor awake is not whether they have been formed but by what, and toward what end.

We assume that what makes us who we are is what we believe. State the doctrine, win the mind, and the life follows. This is the great quiet error of the modern church, and I held it for years. We built ministries on the premise that the human being is fundamentally a thinker, a brain on a stick, and that if we could only get the right information into the head the body would fall in line. So we lectured. We informed. And we watched people who could pass a theology exam live indistinguishably from their unbelieving neighbors, and we blamed their willpower, when the problem was never the head.

Here is the strongest case for the way we have done it, and it deserves respect. Truth matters. Doctrine is not optional. The mind is not nothing, and a faith that cannot say what it believes is a feeling waiting to evaporate. The long Christian tradition of catechism, of teaching the faith as content, saved generations from sentimentality and heresy alike. A church that stops caring whether things are true has already begun to die. I will not give an inch on that. The skeptic who prizes evidence and clear thinking is closer to the kingdom than the believer who prizes a warm vague glow.

But here is where that case runs out. You are not primarily what you think. You are what you love, and you do not choose your loves the way you choose your beliefs. James K. A. Smith put it as sharply as anyone has in a generation. He argues that human beings are desiring creatures before we are thinking creatures, that we are shaped most deeply not by ideas we consider but by practices we repeat, by what he calls cultural liturgies, the rituals that aim our love at something before our mind ever weighs in (Smith 2009). And the most powerful liturgy in the modern world is not held in a church. It is held in a mall, and now it is held in your hand.

Walk through what the mall does, because Smith is right that it is a temple and we should say so plainly. It has a clean and beautiful interior set apart from the street. It has icons in the windows, images of the redeemed life, bodies made perfect, the promise of belonging. It has an order of service. You enter, you wander, you are met by ministers who help you find your size, you make your sacrifice at the register, and you leave carrying a small sacrament in a bag, briefly fuller, soon empty, certain to return. No one believes a doctrine here. Everyone is being formed here. The mall does not care what you think about the mall. It only needs you to keep coming, and you do.

Carry one text. Jesus does not say where your treasure is, there your thinking will be correct. He says, For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21 ESV). Notice the order. He does not say fix your heart and your spending will follow. He says follow the money and you will find the heart, because the heart goes where the treasure has already gone. Spending is not the symptom. Spending is the formation. Every purchase is a small act of worship that trains the desires a little more, and after ten thousand of them you are a certain kind of person, and you never decided to be.

Trace the history, because this captivity has a date. The American economy of the early twentieth century faced a crisis the founders of advertising named openly. Production had outrun need. The factories could make more than people wanted. The solution, pioneered by men like Edward Bernays in the 1920s, was to manufacture wants, to attach products to desires that had nothing to do with the product. Bernays famously staged a group of women lighting cigarettes in a public parade, an image his circle framed as torches of freedom, and the method he helped pioneer taught a generation of admakers to bind a product to status or identity rather than to mere use. The point, in his hands and theirs, was to sell the cigarette as emancipation and, later, the car as a self, to graft the product onto a hunger it could never actually satisfy. Jacques Ellul saw the deeper machinery. He argued that modern technique and the propaganda that serves it do not merely persuade us of things, they integrate us into a system, forming the individual to fit the apparatus, so that the person comes to want exactly what the system needs him to want and calls it his own free choice (Ellul 1964). The genius of consumer formation is that it never feels like formation. It feels like me being myself. That is what makes it a liturgy and not an argument.

Now the reversal. We think the danger of consumerism is that it makes us want bad things. The deeper danger is what it does to wanting itself. It trains us to be people who are constituted by acquisition, who resolve every ache by purchasing, who cannot sit in an unsatisfied moment for ninety seconds without reaching for the phone to buy our way out of it. It does not corrupt our desires so much as it corrupts our capacity to desire God, who cannot be acquired, who will not fit in the bag, who asks not to be consumed but to be loved. A people trained for sixty years to fill every emptiness will not know what to do with a God who sometimes leaves the emptiness in order to fill it himself.

Law before grace, and the law is heavy. I am formed by this. I do not stand above it as a diagnostician. I reach for my phone in the silence. I have measured my worth by what I could afford and felt the lift of a purchase and called that lift joy. I have preached against the mall on Sunday and shopped my way through Monday's anxiety, and the gap between those two days is the size of my actual discipleship. The honest word is that the liturgies of the market have catechized me more hours than the church ever has, and it is not close.

The grace is that formation answers formation. If we are shaped by repeated practice and not by single decisions, then the worn old disciplines of the church are not quaint, they are counter formation, deliberate liturgies aimed at retraining a heart the market has trained against itself. The Lord's table is the anti mall, a meal you cannot buy, a sacrifice already made, a belonging you did not shop for. The Sabbath is a refusal to produce or to purchase for one day in seven, a weekly act of treason against an economy that needs you restless. These are not tips. They are the slow reconstruction of a person, and like all formation they work only by repetition, only by years, only by showing up to the table on the mornings you would rather be at the store.

We became what we bought while we were busy guarding what we believed.

The heart went where the treasure went. It always does.

### Works Cited

Smith, James K. A. Desiring the Kingdom: Worship, Worldview, and Cultural Formation. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2009.

Ellul, Jacques. The Technological Society. Translated by John Wilkinson. New York: Vintage Books, 1964.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: The Church Held Captive to the Culture War
excerpt: We were promised the culture war would defend the faith, and instead it quietly rewrote the faith to fit the war.
body:
A man left my church a few years ago not over a doctrine but over a vote. He could not understand how I could shepherd people who voted the other way. He said it as a matter of faithfulness, and he meant it. What unsettled me was not that he was political. We are all political, and the gospel has public weight or it has none. What unsettled me was that he could no longer locate his deepest loyalty. When I asked him gently what he believed about the cross, he answered me with a position on a policy. The grammar had shifted underneath him, and he had not noticed, and I am not sure I would have noticed in his place.

The real question is not whether Christians should care about justice and law and the shape of the common life. We must. The question is what happens to a church when the framework through which it sees everything is no longer the kingdom of God but the war between two tribes, when the categories that organize the Christian mind are imported wholesale from a politics that was not built to carry the weight of the soul.

Here is the strongest defense of Christian engagement in the culture war, and it is not weak. The faith makes claims about reality. It says the unborn child is a person, that marriage has a given shape, that there is such a thing as truth, that the powerful will answer for the vulnerable. These are not private opinions to be kept behind the church door. They are public truths, and a church that retreats into a spiritual interior while the world burns has abandoned the prophets, who stood in the gates of the city and named the sins of the nation by name. The believer who fights for the weak in the public square is doing something the Bible commands. To call that captivity would be a slander. I hold these convictions. I have not softened them.

But here is what that defense cannot account for. There is a difference between the church speaking prophetically to the powers and the church being captured by one of the powers. The prophet stands outside the kingdoms and judges them all by a higher throne. The captive stands inside one kingdom and judges the other in its terms, and calls his captivity courage. The test is simple and brutal. When your political tribe does the very thing you condemned in the other tribe, do you say so. If the answer is no, if the sin becomes acceptable the moment your side commits it, then you are not a prophet. You are a chaplain to a faction, and the faction owns you.

Carry one text, the oldest temptation, told as a true story. The devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him, All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me (Matthew 4:8 ESV). Read it slowly. The offer was the kingdoms. The offer was real power, real influence, the levers of the nations placed in the hand of the Son of God, and it would have skipped the cross entirely. The price was a single act of worship redirected. Not the abandonment of the kingdoms. The reordering of worship to obtain them. That is the precise shape of the church's captivity. We are not offered evil. We are offered influence, and asked only to bow slightly, to make the cause the thing and the cross the instrument, and we tell ourselves we are still worshiping God while we do it.

Trace the history, because this is older and more bipartisan than we admit. In the early 1980s a coalition formed that fused a wing of the American church to a political movement with a discipline neither had known before. It delivered real victories and a real cost, and the cost was that a generation of believers learned to read their Bibles through a partisan lens so total that the parties began to function as denominations. David Wells, watching the church across these decades, named the underlying disease before the politics ever crystallized. He argued that the evangelical church had already hollowed out its theology, had traded the weight of truth for the techniques of relevance and success, so that when the culture war came it found a church with no theological center strong enough to resist being annexed by something with a center of its own (Wells 1993). A church that had stopped being formed by its doctrine was available to be formed by its politics, and it was, and so was the church on the other side, the progressive congregation that discovered its entire moral vocabulary had quietly been issued by the latest social movement, with the cross retained as decoration.

Neil Postman saw the mechanism that made all of this possible and worse. He argued that the move of public life onto the screen does not merely change what we know, it changes the form of knowing itself, dissolving argument into image and conviction into entertainment, so that a culture organized around the television and now the feed comes to experience even its most serious commitments as a kind of show (Postman 1985). The culture war is not primarily a war of ideas. It is a war of feelings staged for an audience, and the church walked onto that stage carrying the gospel and started performing it for applause, and forgot it was holding something that was meant to be died for, not posted.

Now the reversal, and it cuts. We entered the culture war to defend the faith. The war did not destroy the faith from outside. It rewrote it from inside. It taught us to feel our deepest belonging with our tribe and only our nominal belonging with the brother across the aisle who shares our baptism. It made the enemy a category of people rather than the principalities and powers Paul actually names. We came to save the faith and we let the faith be conscripted, and the proof is that for many of us it now costs more to break with our political side than to break with our Lord. We would lose more friends. That sentence should stop us cold.

Law before grace, and I am inside the law. I have felt the warm pull of the applause line, the sermon that lands because it confirms what my people already wanted to hate. I have measured a brother by his vote before I measured him by his cross. I have been quieter about the sins of my own side because quiet was cheaper, and I have called that prudence when it was cowardice. The captivity does not happen to other pastors in other states. It happens at my desk, on the weeks I want my people to love me more than I want them to be free.

The grace runs straight through the temptation in the wilderness, because the one being offered the kingdoms refused them, and went and got them another way, by the cross, by dying, by rising, by a throne no election confers and no defeat removes. He owns the kingdoms now, all of them, the ones my tribe runs and the ones the other tribe runs, and he holds them so lightly and so surely that he can ask me to love my political enemy without fear, because the outcome was never riding on my faction. The kingdom does not need my captivity to advance. It only needs my allegiance, and allegiance has only ever had room for one throne.

The war promised to make us strong. It made us loud, and then it made us its own.

Not a prophet to the nation. A chaplain to a faction. We can still tell the difference, if we are willing to fail the tribe's test on purpose.

### Works Cited

Wells, David F. No Place for Truth: Or Whatever Happened to Evangelical Theology. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1993.

Postman, Neil. Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business. New York: Viking, 1985.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Outrage Is Not a Spiritual Gift
excerpt: We mistook the heat of our anger for the fire of the Spirit, and the machine that sells our attention was happy to let us believe it.
body:
I caught myself last week reaching for my phone before I had finished the prayer. Not after. During. There was a thing happening online, an outrage cycling through the people I follow, and my body wanted to be in it the way a younger man wants to be in a fight. I noticed the hunger and it frightened me, because it was not a hunger for righteousness. It was a hunger for the feeling of righteousness, which is a different and more dangerous thing, and I had been trained to crave it by an instrument I carry in my pocket and call a tool.

The question underneath the noise is whether our public anger is the holy thing we tell ourselves it is. We call it standing for truth. We quote the prophets. We remember that Jesus made a whip and cleared the temple, and we use that one afternoon to justify a permanent disposition of fury at strangers. The question is whether the anger forming us is the anger of God or the anger of the algorithm, and whether we have lost the ability to tell them apart.

Give the strongest case for the anger, because there is one. Some things ought to make us furious. A world without holy anger is a world that has made peace with cruelty. The prophets burned. Jesus wept over a city and overturned tables in a temple. The abolitionist who was not enraged by the slave market had a defective conscience, not a mature one. Anger at genuine evil is not a sin, it is a sign of life, the proof that you still love something enough to be wounded when it is violated. A faith that produces only mild men who are upset by nothing is not Christianity, it is sedation. I will defend righteous anger. Scripture commands it.

But here is where the case collapses under its own weight. The Bible never treats anger as a reliable indicator of righteousness. It treats it as a fire that must be watched every moment it burns. Be angry and do not sin, Paul writes, and then immediately, do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil (Ephesians 4:26 ESV). Read what that assumes. It assumes anger, even permitted anger, even righteous anger, is precisely the doorway through which the enemy enters, that it has a shelf life of hours, that it spoils by nightfall and becomes something the devil can use. The text does not celebrate the anger. It puts a clock on it. It treats holy anger the way you treat a controlled burn, useful, necessary, and one gust of wind from destroying the whole field.

Now here is the part we will not want to hear. The machine that delivers our anger to us was engineered, deliberately, to make sure the sun never goes down on it. Trace the history. In 2009 the major platforms gave us the instruments of measurement, the Facebook like button in February and the Twitter retweet button that November, with the frictionless share spreading across the web in the years on either side, small buttons that turned communication into a tally. Engineers learned quickly what kept people on the screen, and it was not joy and it was not peace. It was moral emotion, and the most engaging moral emotion is outrage at an outgroup. The systems were then tuned, by optimization more than by malice, to surface exactly the content that made us angriest at people not like us, because angry people scroll, angry people share, and angry people return. Jonathan Haidt has assembled the data with care, showing that the years following this redesign tracked with a sharp rise in adolescent anxiety, depression, and self harm beginning around 2012, especially among girls, a generation rewired by the very engines of moral outrage and social comparison they were handed before they could drive (Haidt 2024). We did not stumble into a culture of rage. We were farmed for it.

Marshall McLuhan said the thing decades before the engineers proved him right. The medium is the message. The form of a technology shapes us more than any content we pour through it, and we are constitutionally blind to the form because we are mesmerized by the content (McLuhan 1964). We argue about what to post. The medium has already decided what we are becoming by posting, and what we are becoming is people for whom the resting state of the soul is a low grade fury looking for an object.

Carry the reversal here. We believe we are using the outrage to fight evil. The outrage is using us to feed the machine, and the machine does not care which side we are on. It profits identically from the rage of the right and the rage of the left. It will hand the progressive his daily villain and the conservative hers, and bill them both, and call it engagement. The most sobering fact about Christian outrage online is that it is indistinguishable in form from every other outrage, runs on the same fuel, serves the same masters, and produces the same fruit, which Paul lists plainly as enmity, strife, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, the works of the flesh wearing the costume of conviction.

Law before grace, and I am the chief defendant. I have felt the rush of the righteous post and refreshed the screen to count who agreed. I have been angrier at a stranger on the internet than at my own sin, which is the exact inversion of the gospel order. I have let the sun go down on it, and the next sun, and called the residue zeal. I have modeled this for my five sons, who watch their father reach for the glowing rectangle in the silence, and learn from the reaching what their father actually treasures. The outrage was never a spiritual gift. It was a work of the flesh I had dressed in Scripture so I would not have to repent of it.

The grace is that the Spirit produces something the algorithm cannot manufacture and cannot sell. Against the works of the flesh Paul sets the fruit of the Spirit, and it begins with love and ends with self control, and in the middle, impossibly, it lists peace and patience and gentleness, the precise traits the machine is built to burn out of us (Galatians 5:22 ESV). The Spirit grows slowly and the algorithm rewards instantly, and a person can tell which one is forming him by asking what he is becoming. More peaceful or more reactive. More patient or more triggered. Gentler with his children or quicker to the phone. The fruit does not lie, and it does not trend.

We thought our anger proved we still cared. It proved we had been captured.

Let the sun go down on it. That is not weakness. That is the first free act in a long captivity.

### Works Cited

Haidt, Jonathan. The Anxious Generation: How the Great Rewiring of Childhood Is Causing an Epidemic of Mental Illness. New York: Penguin Press, 2024.

McLuhan, Marshall. Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man. New York: McGraw-Hill, 1964.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Formed by Screens: Technology and the Soul
excerpt: The screen does not only fill our time, it slowly remakes the kind of soul we have time for.
body:
My youngest can find a video faster than I can find my keys. He is not corrupt. He is a boy with a boy's open face, and he loves his mother and asks me hard questions about God at bedtime. But I have watched something happen to his attention over a season, a fraying, a difficulty in staying with one slow thing, and I cannot honestly blame him, because I have watched the same fraying happen to me. I sit down to read Scripture and my hand reaches for the phone before my mind has settled, and the reaching is so automatic that it has stopped feeling like a choice. Something is forming us both, and it is not the Word.

The question is not whether technology is good or evil. That question is too small and too old, and it always ends in a shrug about how anything can be used well or badly. The real question is sharper. What kind of person does a given technology make of you simply by being used as it was designed to be used. Not abused. Used. Because every tool carries inside it a hidden curriculum, a way of forming the one who holds it, and the screen has a curriculum, and we have all enrolled, and most of us never read the syllabus.

Give the strongest case for the screen, and give it honestly. These devices are astonishing gifts. I can carry the whole of Scripture, the Fathers, the Reformers, and a thousand sermons in one hand. A grandmother sees her grandchild's face across an ocean. A man in a remote village hears the gospel he could never have reached in print. The pandemic years would have been unbearable without the screen that kept the lonely connected to the living. To call all of this captivity would be ungrateful and untrue, the grumbling of a man who wishes for a past that was never as holy as he remembers. Technology is a good gift of a creative God to creative creatures. I use it to write the words you are reading. I will not pretend otherwise.

But here is what the grateful case keeps stepping around. A tool is not only what it does for you. It is what it does to you while you use it, and these two are often opposites. Charles Taylor described the modern self as buffered, sealed off from a world that once pressed in on it from every side, and the screen is the final architecture of that buffering, the wall made portable and pleasant (Taylor 2007). It promises to connect us and it insulates us. It puts a pane of glass between me and the man across the table, between me and the slow boredom out of which prayer is born, between me and my own unmanaged thoughts, which are exactly the thoughts in which God has always done his quietest work. The screen does not merely occupy the silence. It abolishes the capacity for silence, and silence is where the soul learns to hear.

Carry one text, and let it be strange enough to wake us. After the wind and the earthquake and the fire, none of which held the Lord, there came a low whisper. And when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out (1 Kings 19:12 ESV). God was not in the spectacle. He was in the whisper, the sound that requires a quiet so deep that a man would have to have built his whole life around the practice of listening to hear it at all. Now ask the honest question. Could the version of me that checks the phone in the silence of his own prayers hear a whisper. The screen is a technology of the wind and the earthquake and the fire, endless spectacle, endless noise, and a God who speaks in a whisper is a God we have engineered ourselves to miss.

Trace the history, because formation by tools is not new, only newly total. Jacques Ellul argued in the middle of the last century that the deepest danger of modern life is not any single machine but technique itself, the relentless drive toward efficiency that subordinates every human end to the question of what works, until the person is reshaped to serve the apparatus rather than the apparatus the person (Ellul 1964). The screen is technique made intimate. Neil Postman, building on this, warned that the move from the printed word to the image does not just change our entertainment, it changes the structure of our thought, training us for fragments and against arguments, for stimulation and against contemplation, until a whole civilization loses the patience that sustained things like reading a long book or sitting with a hard truth or praying without a phone in reach (Postman 1985). They saw the river's direction before most of us felt the current. We are now far downstream.

Here is the reversal, and it is the one that matters most. We believe we are using these devices to save time, and we are, and then we have no idea what the saved time was for, so we give it back to the same devices, and we are formed not by the content we consume but by the ten thousand small acts of consuming, the reach, the scroll, the flick, the refresh, repeated until they are no longer things we do but the shape of who we are. The danger was never that the screen would make us believe something false. The danger is that it would make us into a certain kind of soul, restless, distractible, incapable of the long slow attention that love and prayer and presence require, and that it would do this so gently we would mistake the new self for the only self we ever had.

Law before grace, and the law has my name on it. I have prayed with one ear on the notification. I have been bodily present with my sons and mentally somewhere in a feed, and they know the difference even when I pretend they do not, because children read presence the way the rest of us read words. I have told my congregation that God speaks in the whisper and then lived a life arranged so that no whisper could ever reach me. I am not the doctor here. I am the patient, and the diagnosis is the same one I would write for the man in my office who cannot sit still long enough to be loved by God.

The grace is that we are formed creatures, which means we can be re formed, and the church has known the medicine for two thousand years. The old disciplines of silence and solitude and fasting are not nostalgia. They are deliberate counter formation, structured acts of refusing the wind and the earthquake and the fire so that the whisper has a chance to land. To put the phone in another room and sit in the unbearable quiet until it stops being unbearable is not a productivity hack. It is repentance with a body, the slow undoing of a formation we did not choose, the clearing of enough silence that a God who has been whispering the whole time can finally be heard saying what he said to Elijah, which was not condemnation but a question, gentle and terrible. What are you doing here.

The screen did not steal our time. It quietly stole the kind of soul that has time for God.

Not a tool we are using. A liturgy that is using us. We can still walk out into the silence, wrap our faces, and listen.

### Works Cited

Taylor, Charles. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2007.

Ellul, Jacques. The Technological Society. Translated by John Wilkinson. New York: Vintage Books, 1964.

Postman, Neil. Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business. New York: Viking, 1985.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: What the Bible Actually Says About Money
excerpt: The Bible refuses both the prosperity preacher who blesses your portfolio and the secular reader who reduces it to anti-wealth socialism, and the refusal is the point.
body:
A man once told me, after a funeral, that he had spent thirty years building something he could not take into the ground he was about to fill. He was not confessing greed. He was confessing surprise. He had played by every rule the culture handed him, and the rules had not lied to him about how to acquire, only about what acquiring would do to him. I have stood at enough gravesides to know that money keeps its promises and breaks them in the same motion. It delivers the house. It does not deliver the man who can live in it.

The question of what the Bible says about money is usually asked by someone who already suspects the answer and wants permission to dislike it. So let me name the real question first, because it is not whether wealth is allowed. The real question is whether money is a neutral tool that takes its moral color from the user, or whether money is a power, an active rival, something that wants you. The Bible answers that second question with a clarity that embarrasses most of our preaching. Money is not neutral. It has a name, and the name is mammon.

The spine of this whole matter runs through one passage, and I want to carry it the entire way. Paul writes to Timothy that godliness with contentment is great gain, that we brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out, and then the sentence everyone misquotes. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs (1 Timothy 6:6-10 ESV). Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say money is the root. He says the love of it is a root, one root among others, and that this love is not a vice on the surface of a life but a craving that reorganizes the whole interior around itself. The word he uses for craving describes a reaching, a stretch toward. Money is not the problem. The stretch is the problem. And the stretch is in me before it is in my bank.

Let me steel-man the two answers that want to silence Paul before he finishes.

The first is the prosperity teaching, and I will not caricature it, because at its best it gets something real. It says God is a Father who gives good gifts, that the creation is good, that poverty is not holy, that the dualism which treats matter as dirty and spirit as clean is a Greek lie the church absorbed and never coughed up. All of that is true. Israel's God made a world of vineyards and oil and wine and called it good before any human ruined it. The Scriptures are full of feasting. Abraham was rich. Job was restored. To pretend the Bible romanticizes destitution is to read it through a monk's bad day. The prosperity preacher is right that God blesses, and right that shame about the body and the field has done real damage. So I take the strongest form of it. God wants to bless His people, and He often blesses them with abundance.

The second answer comes from the other direction, the secular reduction that hears all this talk of the poor and concludes the Bible is simply an ancient socialism, a class document in religious dress, useful for guilt and nothing more. This reading also gets something right. It has actually read the prophets, which is more than many churchgoers can say. It has noticed that Amos thunders against those who sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals (Amos 2:6 ESV), that the Jubilee resets debt, that Jesus blesses the poor and warns the rich with a regularity that should unsettle anyone comfortable. The secular reader is right that the Bible is not indifferent to who has and who lacks. It is right that any Christianity which never disturbs the wealthy has not read its own book. So I take the strong form of that too. The Bible is dangerous to the comfortable, and it means to be.

Now watch what Paul's sentence does to both.

The prosperity teaching cannot survive verse nine, where the desire to be rich is itself the trap, where the wanting plunges people into ruin and destruction. Paul is not warning the rich here. He is warning the aspiring, the ones who want to be rich, which is nearly everyone reading this, including the man who writes it. The prosperity gospel takes the legitimate goodness of blessing and bolts a craving onto it, then baptizes the craving. It tells you the stretch is faith. Paul tells you the stretch is a hook. The two cannot both be true.

But the secular reduction cannot survive the passage either, because Paul does not abolish wealth, he disarms it. Three verses later he tells Timothy to command those who are rich, not to stop being rich, but to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, storing up treasure as a foundation for the future (1 Timothy 6:17-18 ESV). That is not socialism, which seizes. That is not capitalism, which absolves. It is something the modern political menu has no item for. The rich remain rich and are commanded to bleed their wealth outward until it stops being theirs in any way that matters. The Bible does not nationalize the vineyard. It haunts the man who owns it.

So the answer to the real question is neither pole. Money is not morally neutral, which refutes the secular reduction, and money is not safely blessed, which refutes the prosperity preacher. Money is a power, and the only question is who serves whom.

Jesus said it without a single hedge. No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money (Matthew 6:24 ESV). Read it slowly. He does not say you should not. He says you cannot. It is not a prohibition. It is a description of a wiring that will not run two currents. And the word He chooses for money is not the ordinary coin. It is mammon, an Aramaic term He personifies as a rival lord. Jesus is not moralizing about budgets. He is naming a god with a small g and telling you it has applicants for your worship and a contract ready.

This is where the history matters, because the church has known this and forgotten it on a long cycle. In the fourth century, when Constantine's peace flooded the church with wealth it had never held, John Chrysostom preached in Antioch and Constantinople with a ferocity we have lost the stomach for. He told congregations of the newly comfortable that the rich man is a kind of thief, not because he stole, but because what he hoards is the bread of the hungry, the cloak of the naked, the coin owed to the poor (Chrysostom, Homilies on Lazarus). Not to share, Chrysostom said, is to rob. Preaching like that, year after year against the comfort of the powerful, was part of what set the imperial court against him and ended in his exile. We have softened it into a stewardship seminar.

The Reformers wrestled the same beast under the question of usury, the lending of money at interest, which the church had forbidden for over a thousand years on the authority of Scripture. By the sixteenth century commerce had outgrown the prohibition, and Calvin allowed interest within limits, not because he had grown lax but because he distinguished the productive loan from the predatory one. The distinction collapsed almost immediately, as such distinctions do, and within two centuries interest was simply the air the economy breathed. Jacques Ellul, the French theologian and sociologist, watched the end of that long erosion and named what we had done. Money, Ellul argued, is not a tool we picked up but a power we serve, and the modern person's pretense that it is neutral is precisely the lie that lets it rule (Ellul 1984). The man who insists his money is just a tool is the man the tool already owns.

Then came the move that finished us. In 1714, Bernard Mandeville published a poem and then a book, The Fable of the Bees, with the subtitle that should have been a warning, Private Vices, Public Benefits. His argument was simple and corrosive. Greed, vanity, the endless reaching, these private sins are the engine of public prosperity, and a society of saints would be a society of beggars. Adam Smith would later refine the insight into something gentler and truer, but the cultural residue was Mandeville's. We came to believe that the love of money, the very craving Paul called a root of evils, was the secret fuel of the common good. We did not reject Paul's diagnosis. We inverted it. We called the disease the cure.

And once a society decides its central vice is actually its engine, it needs a story about what money is for, a story that quiets the old warnings. Charles Taylor traced how the modern order came to imagine itself as a self-running economic mechanism, a great interlocking exchange in which each person pursuing his own gain produces, as if by design, the good of all (Taylor 2007). It is an elegant picture, and it is not entirely false. Markets do coordinate strangers across distances no charity could reach. But notice what the picture quietly accomplishes. It removes the moral question from the center of economic life and reassigns it to the edges, to private conscience, to what a man does with his surplus on a Sunday. The getting becomes neutral, even virtuous, and only the spending carries any weight. Paul will not allow that division. He locates the danger not in the spending but in the wanting, in the very motion the modern story has declared innocent. The love of money is a root, he says, and roots are underground, in the getting, where we have agreed to stop looking.

Wendell Berry has spent a working life refusing that agreement. He has argued that an economy which treats the love of gain as harmless will inevitably treat everything else, the land, the neighbor, the community, the body, as raw material for that gain, because once the central motion is exempted from judgment there is nothing left to limit it (Berry 1987). Berry writes as a farmer, which matters, because he has watched the abstraction do its work on actual ground, watched the family farm consolidated into the holdings of men who will never see it, watched the field Israel was told not to harvest to its edges reaped now to the very fencerow and beyond. He is describing in modern terms what Isaiah saw in the eighth century before Christ, the joining of house to house and field to field until there is no more room. The machinery is new. The hunger is the same hunger Paul named. It does not change across the millennia. Only its instruments grow more efficient.

And here is the reversal, the place where the objection, followed honestly, turns back toward the cross. The secular reader who says the Bible is just a class document has, without meaning to, paid the gospel a compliment. Because the reader is right that money is about power, right that the having and the lacking are never innocent, right that something is deeply wrong in the distance between the man with the vineyard and the man at his gate. The reader has seen the wound. What the reader has not seen is that the Bible saw it first, named it as sin and not merely as inequality, and refused the two cheap cures the world keeps offering. The world says, seize the vineyard, and calls it justice. The world says, bless the owner, and calls it grace. The gospel says something neither side can stomach. The vineyard owner is a debtor before God, and his only hope is the same as the beggar's.

Press the spine one more time before the cross, because Paul has not finished with us. He says the love of money pierced some through with many pangs, and the verb is worth sitting in. Pierced. Not disappointed, not distracted. Pierced, as a man is pierced who reached for something and was run through by it. This is the testimony of nearly every rich man I have buried and a good many I have counseled while they still had breath. The money did not fail to arrive. It arrived, and it kept arriving, and somewhere in the arriving the man discovered he had been hollowed out to make room for it, that the contentment Paul named at the start of the passage had been the one thing the wealth could not deliver and the one thing he had traded for it. We have all heard the sentiment that money cannot buy happiness, and we file it under platitude. Paul says something far worse. Money can buy the appetite for more money, and that appetite, fed, becomes the whole of a person. The hook does not let go. It sets deeper with every catch.

This is why the cross stands in the center of any honest theology of money, and not as a closing decoration. Gary Anderson has shown that in the biblical and later Jewish imagination, sin was understood as a debt, a weight recorded against the sinner, and that almsgiving to the poor was understood as the paying down of that debt, treasure stored in heaven in the most literal economic grammar (Anderson 2009). When Jesus tells the rich to store up treasure in heaven, He is not speaking in metaphor. He is telling them their accounts are in the wrong bank. And then He does the unthinkable. He pays the debt Himself. He who was rich, Paul says, for our sake became poor, so that we by His poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9 ESV). The richest sentence in the economy of God is a bankruptcy. The Son liquidates everything, down to the garment they gambled for at the foot of the wood, and the liquidation is the inheritance.

This is the law before the grace, and it must come in that order or it is sentiment. The law says the love of money has wormed into every one of us, the prosperity preacher and the prophet of equality alike, and that none of us serves the right master cleanly. The law says I have stretched toward security a thousand times in ways I dressed up as prudence. I have a family. I have five sons. The reaching wears the costume of love and is sometimes only fear. The law indicts the man who writes this before it indicts the man who reads it. Only after that indictment lands does grace mean anything, and then it means everything, because the debt I cannot pay has been paid in a currency I could not have minted.

So what does the Bible actually say about money. It says money is real, good, and dangerous, in that order and all at once. It says the goods of creation are gifts and not garbage, which silences the false holiness of poverty. It says the love of those goods is a root that grows in the dark, which silences the false holiness of wealth. It says you will worship something, and money is the most patient idol you will ever meet, because it never asks for worship in words. It only asks for your trust, a little more each year, until the day a man stands at a graveside and realizes he gave it everything and it gave him a house he is about to leave.

The contentment Paul names is not resignation. It is the freedom of a man who has already been bought, and so cannot be bought again. We brought nothing in. We will take nothing out. Between those two empty hands, the only question worth answering is whose we are. Mammon will take you on any terms. Christ has already paid for you in full. You cannot serve both. You were never able to.

### Works Cited

Anderson, Gary A. Sin: A History. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2009.

Berry, Wendell. Home Economics. New York: North Point Press, 1987.

Ellul, Jacques. Money and Power. Translated by LaVonne Neff. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press, 1984.

John Chrysostom. On Wealth and Poverty. Translated by Catharine P. Roth. Crestwood: St. Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1984.

Taylor, Charles. A Secular Age. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2007.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Is Poverty Political? The Bible's Uncomfortable Answer
excerpt: The question assumes poverty is either a private misfortune or a partisan football, and the prophets refuse both with a word our politics has no translation for.
body:
Ask whether poverty is political in most American churches and you will watch faces close. The word political has become a smell, a signal that someone is about to import the news cycle into the sanctuary. So people answer fast. Poverty is a heart issue, they say. It is about generosity, not policy. Keep the government out of the gospel. I understand the instinct, and I have shared it. I have also read Amos, and Amos will not let me keep it.

The real question hiding under the surface one is this. When the Bible commands care for the poor, is it speaking only to my private compassion, or is it also speaking to the systems my compassion operates inside. Is poverty a matter of individual hearts, or a matter of structures, gates, courts, and laws. The honest answer is that the prophets do not let us choose. They indict hearts and systems in the same breath, and they do it with a single Hebrew word.

The spine of this is Amos. Let the words stand as they are. Thus says the Lord, for three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment, because they sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals, those who trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the afflicted (Amos 2:6-7 ESV). Read what Amos attacks. He does not attack a feeling. He attacks a transaction, a courtroom verdict bought with silver, a legal system in which the poor lose because the poor cannot pay. Amos is not preaching against stinginess at the dinner table. He is preaching against a rigged court. That is a political charge in any century.

Let me steel-man the strongest version of the other side, because it is not foolish and I have preached it myself. The conservative instinct says that when you make poverty political, you replace the slow, costly, personal work of love with the cheap satisfaction of voting for a program and feeling absolved. It says government compassion is compassion with someone else's money and someone else's hands, and that it lets the giver off the hook of ever knowing the name of the poor man. It says the early church did not lobby Caesar, it sold its possessions and laid them at the apostles' feet. There is real weight here. A man who marches for the poor and never opens his door to one has learned to love humanity in order to avoid loving a human. Charity that becomes only policy does rot into a transaction between strangers. The strong form of this objection is a warning against substituting the system for the soul, and the warning is true.

Now hear why it cannot be the whole answer. The same prophets who indict individual greed spend most of their breath on what we would call structures. They condemn the merchants who make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances (Amos 8:5 ESV), which is to say, weights and measures, the regulatory architecture of an ancient economy. They condemn those who join house to house and field to field until there is no more room and they are made to dwell alone (Isaiah 5:8 ESV), which is to say, the consolidation of land into fewer hands, a policy outcome before it is a personal sin. The Torah itself legislates. It commands that the harvest not be reaped to the edges so the poor can glean (Leviticus 19:9-10 ESV). That is not a suggestion to be generous. It is a law that structures the field so that provision for the poor is built into the system whether the landowner feels charitable that morning or not.

This is the word our politics cannot translate. The Hebrew is mishpat, usually rendered justice, and Christopher Wright has shown that it does not mean the blind even-handedness of a Western courtroom. Mishpat is the active intervention that puts wrong things right, that takes the side of the one who cannot defend himself, the widow, the orphan, the stranger, the poor (Wright 2004). Paired with it runs tsedaqah, righteousness, which is not private moral cleanness but right relationship lived out in the community's economic life. Tim Keller put it plainly, that mishpat and tsedaqah together describe a life so generous and so structurally fair that the two cannot be pried apart, and that to have tsedaqah without mishpat is to be privately pious and publicly complicit (Keller 2010). The Bible has no category for a righteous person who is content to live inside an unjust arrangement.

Walter Brueggemann traced where the trouble starts, and he started early, in the very founding of the monarchy. He argued that Solomon built what Brueggemann called the royal consciousness, an economy of accumulation, forced labor, and managed abundance for the few, and that the prophets rose precisely as the alternative consciousness that remembered the God of the Exodus, the God who heard the cry of slaves and broke the economy that produced their bricks (Brueggemann 2001). Read that way, the prophetic tradition is born political, born as a critique of a state economy that had forgotten the slaves it was built on. Poverty was political the day Pharaoh raised the quota and withheld the straw.
