I have stood in front of a room and known exactly which idol I was willing to name and which one I would let sleep, and the one I let sleep was always the one my own heart was guarding. The newspaper had gotten into my Bible after all.

There is a test for whether you have preached politics or preached the party, and it is brutal in its simplicity. After the sermon, which half of the room felt comforted. If the same half walks out warmed every single week, the half that already agreed with you on Friday, then you have not been preaching the cross. You have been preaching the platform, and the cross has become the decoration on the platform. The genuinely prophetic word leaves your own side uneasy too, because the kingdom of God does not map onto any ballot, and the man who has heard it rightly goes home unable to feel fully at home in the camp he arrived in. I came to faith out of atheism, which means I have no inherited tribe in the church to protect, and I still catch myself protecting one, the one I drifted into, the one whose approval feels like belonging. The pull is not theological. It is the simple hunger to be on a side that will have me, and that hunger has bent more sermons than bad exegesis ever did.

So preach the issue when the text raises it, and let the text decide which issue and which week, not the news cycle, not the donor, not the half of the room you are afraid of. Brueggemann argued that the prophetic word does its work not by scolding but by offering a counter-world so vivid that the official world loses its grip (Brueggemann 1989). That is the aim. Not to tell people how to vote. To make the kingdom of God so concrete in their imagination that every kingdom of this world, including the one they voted for, looks smaller than it did on Tuesday.

You will lose people either way. Lose them to the gospel, not to the party.

### Works Cited

Barth, Karl. 1963. Barth in Retirement. Interview. Time, May 31, 1963.

Brueggemann, Walter. 1989. Finally Comes the Poet. Minneapolis: Fortress Press.

Stott, John R. W. 1982. Between Two Worlds. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

title: Expository vs. Topical Preaching: Which and When
excerpt: The argument between expository and topical preaching is usually a disguise for a deeper question, which is whether the preacher will submit to a text or use one.
body:
Two preachers prepare for the same Sunday. The first opens his Bible to where he left off last week, the next paragraph of Romans, and his sermon is decided for him before he has had a single idea, because the text decided it. The second begins with a question that has been pressing on his people, anxiety, money, a marriage falling apart, and he goes looking for the passages that speak to it. By Saturday night both will have a sermon. The question the conferences keep arguing about is which of them did it right. The question underneath, the one that actually matters, is which of them let the Word be in charge.

That is the real fault line, and it does not run cleanly between the two methods. There are expositors who march verse by verse through a book and never once let the text correct them, because they have already decided what each verse will say. And there are topical preachers who chase a theme and end up more captive to Scripture than the expositor, because the theme drove them back into six passages they could not control. Method is not the same as submission. We have spent a generation treating it as though it were.

Let me give the case for expository preaching its full strength, because it is strong and I believe most of it. When a preacher commits to working through a book of the Bible, paragraph by paragraph, he surrenders his right to avoid. He cannot skip the verse about money this autumn because the building campaign is on. He cannot dodge the hard saying about divorce because three couples in the room are in the middle of one. The discipline of the next verse drags him into territory he would never have chosen, and that is precisely its gift. Haddon Robinson built his whole case on this, that the expositor lets the biblical idea, not the preacher's idea, govern the sermon, so that the authority in the room is the text and not the man (Robinson 1980). John Stott went further and said that all true Christian preaching is expository in spirit, because all of it exists to open up the meaning of a text and let it speak (Stott 1982). I will not argue against that. The discipline of the consecutive text has saved more sermons from the preacher's vanity than any other practice I know.

But the strongest form of the expository case has a blind spot, and naming it is not an attack on the method. It is this. The Bible itself does not always preach expositorily. When Peter stands up on the day of Pentecost, he does not open a scroll and work through it verse by verse. He has a topic, and the topic is the thing that just happened in the street, and he reaches for Joel and for two Psalms and for the promise to David, pulling texts from across the canon to answer one question the crowd is screaming (Acts 2:14-36 ESV). That is a topical sermon. It is in the Bible. It converted three thousand people. Whatever rule we are about to make against topical preaching, the apostle broke it on the first day of the church, and the Spirit blessed the breaking.

Carry that Pentecost sermon as the spine, because it teaches the actual rule. Peter's sermon is topical in arrangement and ruthlessly expository in submission. He does not bend the texts to his theme. He lets the texts dictate what the theme is allowed to mean. He quotes Joel and then insists that the strange thing in the street is the very pouring out of the Spirit that Joel saw in the last days (Acts 2:17 ESV). He quotes the Psalm and then refuses to let David claim it for himself, because David died and was buried and his tomb is with us to this day, so the incorruption the Psalm promised must belong to another (Acts 2:29-31 ESV). The topic gave Peter his starting point. The text gave Peter his authority. He did not choose between the two. He ordered them rightly.

This is the distinction the whole argument keeps missing. The danger of topical preaching is real, but it is not the topic. The danger is the proof-text, the verse yanked out of its paragraph to nod along with a point the preacher already owned. The danger of expository preaching is also real, and it is not the consecutive text. The danger is the running commentary, the verse-by-verse march that explains everything and lands nowhere, that mistakes coverage for proclamation. I have committed both sins. I have used a Psalm to prove a thing the Psalm was not saying. I have also walked a congregation through fourteen verses of Leviticus and left them more informed and less pierced than when they came in, and called it faithfulness because it was thorough.

Watch how Peter's submission shows itself, because it is the part we cannot fake. When the crowd, cut to the heart, cries out asking what they should do, Peter does not soften the topic to keep them. He has just told them they crucified the Lord of glory, and now that the wound is open he pours grace into it, repent and be baptized, every one of you (Acts 2:38 ESV). The law came first and it came hard, the plain charge that this Jesus, whom you crucified, God has made both Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36 ESV). The topic did not let Peter dodge that sentence. The topic was the resurrection of a man the crowd had killed, and you cannot preach that topic faithfully without the indictment that makes the grace necessary. So the test of a topical sermon is not whether it began with a theme. The test is whether the theme was allowed to wound before it healed, or whether the preacher reached for a comfortable topic precisely so he would never have to.

The history clarifies why we are so anxious about this. The verse-by-verse expository sermon, the kind associated with the consecutive exposition of a whole book, has deep roots, but its modern American dominance owes much to the twentieth-century reaction against the topical sermon's collapse. By the mid-century the liberal pulpit had so often used a verse as a springboard into the preacher's own opinions that conservatives recoiled toward the text and would not let go. The recoil was justified. The springboard sermon deserved to die. But a recoil is not a doctrine. We turned a healthy correction into an absolute, and we began to speak as though Spurgeon, who almost never preached consecutively through a book and took a single text wherever it served the wounded soul in front of him, had somehow been doing it wrong (Spurgeon 1875). Spurgeon was not doing it wrong.

So when each. Preach the consecutive book when your people need to be confronted with the whole counsel of God and cannot be allowed to live on the preacher's favorite forty verses. Preach the consecutive book when you yourself are the danger, when your instinct to avoid the hard text needs a stronger master than your instinct. That is most seasons. But preach topically when a death has torn through the congregation and the next paragraph of your series has nothing to say to it, because to ignore the open grave in the room in order to protect your schedule is to love the method more than the people. Preach topically when the culture has put a question to the church that the church is fumbling, and the answer is scattered across the canon and has to be gathered. Phillips Brooks said the truth must come through a personality that has been changed by it (Brooks 1877). A method cannot be changed by anything. Only a man can.

There is also an honesty the method debate lets us avoid, and it is about why we choose what we choose. I have hidden inside the expository series for reasons that had nothing to do with the whole counsel of God. A long series is a long permission to coast. The decisions are made for the year, the trajectory is set, and a tired man can lean on the structure the way a tired man leans on a wall. I have likewise reached for a topical sermon not because a grave had opened but because the next paragraph of Romans frightened me and a softer subject was available. The method was a costume in both cases. Underneath the costume was the same man making the same choice, which was the choice to spare himself. No method will save you from that choice. The consecutive text can become an alibi as easily as the topic can become an escape. The question is never which method is faithful. The question is which one, this Saturday, you are using to hide.

And in both, the cross has to do its work, and the law has to come before the grace. The expositor can hide from this behind his careful verbs and his Greek, ending the sermon in the lexicon instead of at the foot of the cross. The topical preacher can hide from it behind relevance, scratching the felt need so gently that no one is ever cut. Both evasions leave the room comfortable. Neither method protects you from the one failure that matters, which is preaching about a text instead of letting the text preach to you first and then through you to them.

Do not ask which method is holy. Ask which one, this week, makes you submit.

### Works Cited

Brooks, Phillips. 1877. Lectures on Preaching. New York: E. P. Dutton.

Robinson, Haddon W. 1980. Biblical Preaching. Grand Rapids: Baker.

Spurgeon, Charles H. 1875. Lectures to My Students. London: Passmore and Alabaster.

Stott, John R. W. 1982. Between Two Worlds. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

title: Five Preaching Habits That Empty a Room
excerpt: A room does not usually empty all at once, it leaks, one Sunday at a time, through habits the preacher cannot see because he is the one performing them.
body:
No one walks out in the middle of a sermon. That is not how a room empties. It empties slowly, over months, through a thousand small decisions made in cars on the way home, the decision that next week can wait, that the children have a game, that nothing will be lost by missing it. The preacher rarely sees the leak because the leak is silent and because he is standing at the exact spot where it begins. I have emptied rooms. Not with scandal. With habits I could not see in myself because I was the one doing them.

Before the list, the strongest objection, and it is one I half believe. A faithful preacher should not be managing the room at all. The numbers are the Spirit's business. Noah preached for decades and saved eight. Jeremiah cleared the building every week and was right every week. If you start preaching to keep people, you will stop preaching the truth, because the truth empties rooms on purpose, and the cross was the emptiest room in history, down to a few women and a borrowed tomb. There is real steel here. The preacher who counts heads will eventually trim the gospel to fit the heads he wants to keep, and a trimmed gospel is no gospel. I hold that with both hands.

But the objection proves less than it claims, because there is a difference between a room emptied by the offense of the cross and a room emptied by the offense of the preacher. Jesus said the word would divide households and that men would hate his disciples for his name (Matthew 10:22 ESV). He did not promise they would hate us for being boring. When people leave because the gospel cut them, that is the cost of faithfulness. When they leave because the man in front of them mistook his habits for the gospel, that is not a cross. That is a waste, and we have learned to baptize our waste by calling it persecution. So examine the habits, and be honest about which kind of emptying you are causing.

The self-deception here is comfortable, which is why it lasts. A man whose preaching is dull can read the parable of the sower and decide his hearers are simply the path, the rocky soil, the thorns, and that the seed was fine all along. The parable gives him cover, because it is true that some hearts are hard. But the same parable says the sower scatters, and a sower who has fallen asleep against the fence post is not faithfully losing seed to bad soil. He is just asleep. I have used the doctrine of the hardened heart to explain away rooms that I myself bored into the parking lot. The doctrine is real. My use of it was a lie. Discernment begins with refusing to let a true doctrine cover a false comfort, and the five habits below are five comforts I have hidden behind.

The first habit is preaching to no one. The sermon is built for a congregation that does not exist, the general Christian, the person in general, and so it lands on no actual chest in the room. Haddon Robinson warned that a sermon must aim its single idea at the real lives present, not at humanity in the abstract (Robinson 1980). The abstract sermon is safe, because no one feels named, and that safety is the leak. The woman whose son will not speak to her did not come to hear about reconciliation in general. She came in case God had a word for that, the specific grave she is carrying, and the general sermon tells her, week after gentle week, that he does not.

The second habit is explaining when you should be proclaiming. The preacher becomes a lecturer, accumulating information about the text, the Greek, the historical setting, the cross-references, until the sermon is a seminar with a prayer at each end. The people leave knowing more and feeling nothing, and a person who feels nothing will eventually decide that nothing is at stake. Fred Craddock noticed that the church had trained preachers to explain the gospel so thoroughly that they forgot to announce it (Craddock 1971). Information is not proclamation. You can teach a man the chemistry of bread and leave him starving.

The third habit is the sermon with no spine. It has parts, and the parts are each true, but they are stapled together rather than grown from one root, and the listener cannot carry any of it out because there was no single thing to carry. The mind does not retain a list. It retains a thrust. When a sermon has three good points and no governing idea, the people remember that the preacher was earnest and forget what he was earnest about, and a thing forgotten by Tuesday is a thing that will not bring them back by Sunday.

The fourth habit is the soft landing, and this one I committed most. The sermon builds, the law presses, the text has the listener cornered, and then at the last moment the preacher loses his nerve and lets everyone off easy. A comfortable closing. A reassurance that softens the very thing the text spent its force to say. Walter Brueggemann argued that the prophetic sermon must not resolve the tension it raises but leave the hearer standing in it, because a too-quick comfort robs the word of its power to change anything (Brueggemann 1989). The soft landing is the preacher protecting the room from the text and the text from the room, and the room can feel the protection, and the protection is condescension wearing the mask of grace. People do not return to a place that keeps telling them nothing is wrong.

The fifth habit is the borrowed self. The preacher steps into the pulpit and becomes someone else, a pulpit voice, a pulpit cadence, a borrowed certainty that belongs to no one in his actual life. Phillips Brooks defined the whole enterprise as truth through personality, and he meant that the truth has to pass through a real person who has been changed by it, not through a performance of a person (Brooks 1877). When the self in the pulpit is borrowed, the people sense the gap without naming it. They feel handled. They cannot say why they distrust the man, only that they do, and distrust is a slow exit. The cross was the most personal thing God ever did, a body, named, on a Friday, and we announce it through a mask.

There is a sixth thing under the five, and it is worth naming because it explains why the habits cluster. A man does not usually pick up these habits one at a time, like bad swings in golf. He picks them up together, all at once, the first time the pulpit frightens him. The fear is reasonable. To preach is to stand up and claim that God is speaking, and that claim invites a judgment no other public speech invites. So the frightened man reaches, almost without deciding, for every available shelter. He generalizes so no one is named. He explains so he can hide behind data. He multiplies points so no single one can be wrong. He softens the ending so the room will not turn on him. He puts on a voice so that if they reject the sermon they are only rejecting the voice and not the man. Five habits, one fear, and the fear is the fear of being seen failing at the most exposed task a person can attempt.

Notice what all five share. Each is a way of avoiding contact. The abstract sermon avoids the particular person. The lecture avoids the demand to proclaim. The spineless sermon avoids the one hard thing. The soft landing avoids the wound. The borrowed self avoids the cost of being known. Every emptying habit is the preacher protecting himself, and the room leaves because it can smell the self-protection, even from the back row, even through the music.

So carry one text out of this. Paul tells the Thessalonians that he was ready to share not only the gospel but his own self, because they had become dear to him (1 Thessalonians 2:8 ESV). That is the cure for all five at once. The shared self is particular, so it cannot preach to no one. It proclaims, because it is not hiding behind data. It has a spine, because a person under conviction speaks of one thing. It does not soften the landing, because a man who loves you will tell you the truth that costs. And it is not borrowed, because it is his own self he is handing over. The room does not empty around a preacher who is willing to be known.

The habits that empty a room are all the same habit. Hiding.

### Works Cited

Brooks, Phillips. 1877. Lectures on Preaching. New York: E. P. Dutton.

Brueggemann, Walter. 1989. Finally Comes the Poet. Minneapolis: Fortress Press.

Craddock, Fred B. 1971. As One Without Authority. Nashville: Abingdon Press.

Robinson, Haddon W. 1980. Biblical Preaching. Grand Rapids: Baker.

title: The Difference Between a Sermon and a Talk
excerpt: A talk informs you and lets you go, but a sermon claims you, and the difference is not the subject or the skill but who is doing the speaking through the man.
body:
A man stands up with notes and speaks for thirty minutes about God, and at the end you cannot tell whether what just happened was a sermon or a talk. The room cannot tell either. They clap or they do not, they take notes or they do not, and they go home essentially unchanged, having heard something true and useful and survivable. That last word is the whole problem. A talk is survivable. You can hear a good talk and remain exactly who you were. The question of what makes a good sermon is, at bottom, the question of why a sermon is not supposed to be survivable.

The two can look identical from the back row. Both can have a clear point and a memorable line and an honest delivery. Both can quote Scripture. Both can be moving. The difference is not visible in the technique, which is why so much preaching instruction misses it, drilling the mechanics of a thing whose essence is not mechanical. You can teach a man everything about how to give a talk and have taught him nothing about how to preach, because you have trained the hands and never touched the question of who is speaking.

Let me build the case that there is no real difference, because intelligent people make it and it deserves answering. A sermon, the argument runs, is just a religious talk. It uses a Bible instead of a business case, it ends in prayer instead of applause, but the underlying act is the same, a prepared person communicating ideas to a listening group. The talk that helps a man forgive his father has done more good than a sermon that bored him. Communication is communication, and the spiritual gloss we put on preaching is mostly the profession protecting its mystique. There is a real point buried here, and I will grant it before I answer it. A sermon that is badly communicated is not made holy by being a sermon. Clarity is not optional. Mumbling is not anointing. Many sermons would be improved by learning what a good talk knows.

But take the argument at its strongest, that communication is communication, and it collapses on one verse. Paul reminds the Romans that faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17 ESV), and then he asks how they will hear without someone preaching, and how anyone will preach unless he is sent (Romans 10:14-15 ESV). That word sent is the whole difference. A talk is something a man decides to give. A sermon is something a man is sent to deliver. The speaker of a talk is the source. The preacher of a sermon is a courier, and a courier who edits the message is a thief. The act is not the same, because the authority behind the act is not the same, and the listener, even one who could not explain it, feels the difference between a man offering his opinion and a man under orders.

Carry that sent-ness as the spine, because it changes everything downstream. Augustine, who had been a professional teacher of rhetoric before his conversion, wrestled with exactly this in the fourth book of his treatise on Christian teaching, written near the year 426. He knew every device of the talk, every trick of persuasion the empire could teach. And he concluded that the Christian speaker must subordinate all of it to a higher aim, that he speaks not to be admired but so that the truth may be loved and obeyed, and that his own life must preach alongside his tongue or the tongue is a clanging thing (Augustine 426). The rhetorician gives a talk to win the room. The preacher, Augustine saw, is trying to lose the room to God. Those are not two grades of the same act. They are opposite acts that happen to use the same lungs.

What makes Augustine's argument matter is that he was not a man suspicious of skill. He had eaten his bread by skill. He had taught young men in Milan how to move a crowd toward whatever the crowd needed to be moved toward, and he never once pretended that eloquence was worthless. He kept it. He told preachers to use the whole armory of the rhetoricians, the clear style for teaching, the moderate style for delight, the grand style for bending the will. But he reversed the master. In the schools, the cause served the eloquence, because a paid speaker would defend any cause that paid. In the church, the eloquence serves the cause, and the cause is fixed, and the speaker did not choose it and may not amend it. That single reversal is the whole boundary line between a talk and a sermon. The talker owns his subject and bends it to his gift. The preacher is owned by his subject and bends his gift to it. A man can have the identical skill in both rooms and be doing two different things, because in one room he is the lord of the message and in the other he is its servant.

This is why the cross has to be in a sermon in a way it never has to be in a talk. A talk about generosity can stand on its own legs, can move a man to write a check by the sheer force of the case. A sermon about generosity that does not run, sooner or later, into the one who though he was rich became poor so that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9 ESV), is a talk wearing a stole. The cross is the watershed. A talk persuades you to do better. A sermon announces that you cannot do better, kills the man who thought he could, and raises a new one who gives because he has been given to. The first leaves you with a task. The second leaves you with a grave and a resurrection. Tim Keller pressed this point hard, that preaching to the heart must always show how the text drives to Christ and his work, or it becomes mere moral advice with a religious accent (Keller 2015). Moral advice is a fine talk. It is a failed sermon.

And here is the reversal, the thing that humbles the preacher who thinks he can manufacture the difference. The man cannot make his talk into a sermon by his own effort. He cannot add enough Scripture or enough passion or enough cross to cross the line by technique, because the line is not technical. A sermon happens when God speaks through the speaking, and that is not in the preacher's power to guarantee. He can only prepare the kindling. The fire is given. This should terrify us out of our professionalism and free us from it at the same time, because it means the worst-delivered sermon, given by a sent man who has been broken by his text, may do what the most polished talk can never do, while the preacher who trusts his polish may give a flawless talk every Sunday for thirty years and never once preach.

I know which of those preachers I have most often been, and the confession is not modesty. There were years I gave excellent talks. They were clear, they were warm, they had a line people quoted in the lobby, and they cost me almost nothing, because I had not let the text get its hands on me before I stood up. I had studied the passage the way a lawyer studies a brief, mastering it, standing over it, never once standing under it. A talk is what comes out of a man who has mastered his material. A sermon is what comes out of a man whose material has mastered him, and the difference is felt in the chest before it is understood in the mind. My polished years were my emptiest years. The people were entertained and unchanged, and so was I, and I mistook the lobby compliments for fruit until a season came that broke me open and I learned, late, what it costs to actually be sent.

So what makes a good sermon. Not the skill, though skill serves it. Not the subject, though it must be the right subject. A good sermon is one through which a man who was sent says the thing he was sent to say, having been changed by it first, so that the cross does its killing and its raising work inside the room, and the people leave unable to remain who they were. Phillips Brooks called it truth through personality, and the personality matters, but the truth is the master and the man is the window (Brooks 1877). A talk shows you the man. A sermon shows you through him to the thing that has hold of him.

The test is the morning after. A talk you admired. A sermon admired you back, found you, named you, and would not let you stay. If you remember the speaker, it may have been a fine talk. If you cannot stop thinking about your own life, your father, your money, your unforgiveness, the grave you have been avoiding, it was probably a sermon, and the speaker has already done the one thing a preacher is for. He got out of the way.

A talk you survive. A sermon survives you.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 426. On Christian Teaching. Translated by R. P. H. Green. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Brooks, Phillips. 1877. Lectures on Preaching. New York: E. P. Dutton.

Keller, Timothy. 2015. Preaching. New York: Viking.

title: The Most Segregated Hour: Why Sunday Morning Is Still Divided
excerpt: The hour we call holy is the hour we keep apart, and the building of that wall has a history older than our discomfort with naming it.
body:
Martin Luther King Jr. said it, and we have been quoting him ever since as if quoting him were the same as repenting. Eleven o'clock on Sunday morning, he said, is the most segregated hour in America. We nod. We put the line on a slide behind the worship leader. Then we drive home to the same neighborhood we drove from, to the same church we have always attended, and nothing about Monday morning is different from Saturday night.

The sociologists confirm what King saw. Michael Emerson and Christian Smith, in their 2000 study Divided by Faith, found that a congregation counts as multiracial only when no single group exceeds eighty percent of the membership, and by that low bar fewer than one in ten American churches qualified. The number has crept upward since. It has not moved far. The most segregated hour is still the most segregated hour, and we have grown comfortable enough with the diagnosis that we no longer feel the wound.

There is a serious objection to make here, and I want to make it well before I answer it. Some say the church talks about race too much already, that the constant return to this subject has politicized the pulpit, baptized a partisan agenda, and turned the gospel into a program of social management. They say people of every background already worship freely, that the doors are open, that nobody is turned away, that segregation by preference is not segregation by law and the two should never be confused. They are right about something real. The gospel is not a political platform. A church that preaches a party has lost the cross. And the people who fill our pews on Sunday are not standing at a barred door. No usher checks their skin.

But the open door is not the whole truth, and the people who say it know it is not. Preference did not fall from the sky. Preference was built. The text I want to carry through this is short and it does not flatter us. In Christ, Paul writes, God has broken down the dividing wall of hostility, has made the two groups one, has created in himself one new humanity in place of the two, thus making peace (Ephesians 2:14-15 ESV). Paul is not describing a feeling. He is describing a demolition. There was a wall in the temple, a literal partition past which a Gentile could not go on pain of death, and Paul says the cross tore it down. The question for us is not whether the wall is gone in heaven. The question is who keeps rebuilding it on earth, and the answer includes me.

Trace it back. The dividing wall in American Christianity was not an accident of geography. In 1845 the Baptists split into North and South over whether a slaveholder could be a missionary, and the Southern Baptist Convention was born to defend a man's right to own a man and call himself sent by God. The Methodists had split the year before. The Presbyterians would fracture too. The largest churches in the land organized themselves around the keeping of human beings as property, and they did it with open Bibles. Jemar Tisby calls this the color of compromise, the long record of a church that did not merely fail to resist racism but actively constructed it (Tisby 2019). The wall in our sanctuaries is the same wall. We did not inherit a neutral silence. We inherited a structure.

After slavery came the next layer. Black Christians who had sat in the balconies of white churches walked out and built their own, not from preference but from refusal, the refusal of white congregations to seat them as equals at the same table. The Black church in America is in large part a monument to white Christian rejection. Then came the federal redlining maps of the 1930s, the restrictive housing covenants, the highways routed through Black neighborhoods, the suburbs sold to whites only. By the time King named it, the segregated hour was the natural fruit of a hundred years of deliberate sorting. We did not choose it on a given Sunday. Our grandparents chose it across a century, and we have not chosen against it.

Howard Thurman saw the cost from inside. In Jesus and the Disinherited, written in 1949, he asks what the religion of Jesus has to say to those with their backs against the wall, and he records the searing question his own grandmother, born enslaved, put to the faith she was handed. Why would she keep a book that had been used to keep her down. Thurman's answer is that the religion of the slaveholder and the religion of Jesus are not the same religion, that one blesses the wall and the other breaks it (Thurman 1949). The tragedy is that they wore the same name and met in the same hour, and to the watching world they were indistinguishable.

Here is the reversal. We treat the segregated hour as a problem of comfort, as if the solution were to make worship a little more varied so everyone feels welcome. But Ephesians does not aim at comfort. The wall Paul names is a wall of hostility, and the cross does not redecorate it. The cross kills the hostility (Ephesians 2:16 ESV). That is violent language and it is meant to be. The thing standing between us is not difference. Difference is the gift of God, every tongue and tribe a facet of his glory. The thing standing between us is enmity, and enmity does not yield to a friendlier greeting at the door. It yields to death, the death of the old humanity that needed the wall to feel safe.

So the law comes before the grace, and the law is this. We built the wall. The white church in America, my church, the tradition I serve in, laid every course of brick with Scripture in hand, and the fact that the mortar has dried and we no longer remember mixing it does not make us innocent. To say the door is open while standing in a building our fathers designed to keep certain people in the balcony is to mistake the absence of a new crime for the presence of repentance. We have not torn down the wall. We have stopped noticing it.

And here is the grace, which is harder than the comfort we wanted. The cross has already done the demolition. Paul does not command us to build one new humanity. He announces that God has made it, past tense, finished, in the body of Christ. Our task is not construction. It is to stop maintaining the ruin. To walk into the hour we have kept apart and refuse, with our feet and our budgets and our pulpits and our friendships, to keep it apart any longer. That is not a program. It is obedience to something already true.

King's line was never meant to be a lament we recite. It was meant to be a verdict we answered. We have recited it for sixty years. The hour is still divided. The wall is down in heaven and standing in our sanctuaries, and the hands holding it up are our own.

### Works Cited

Emerson, Michael O., and Christian Smith. Divided by Faith: Evangelical Religion and the Problem of Race in America. New York: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Thurman, Howard. Jesus and the Disinherited. Boston: Beacon Press, 1949.

Tisby, Jemar. The Color of Compromise: The Truth about the American Church's Complicity in Racism. Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 2019.

title: What the Bible Means by Reconciliation
excerpt: We have shrunk a word that once meant the end of a war down to the size of a handshake, and the church is paying for the theft.
body:
A man stands up after the sermon and says he is tired of the word. Reconciliation, he says, has become a code, a Trojan horse, a way to smuggle a politics into the church under the cover of a Bible word. He is not entirely wrong. The word has been used as cover. But the answer to a stolen word is not to abandon it. The answer is to find out what it meant before we got our hands on it.

The Greek is katallage. It does not come from the language of feelings. It comes from the language of war and the language of money, the exchange that ends a hostility, the settling of an account that stood open between two parties who were enemies. When Paul reaches for it, he is not describing two people deciding to get along. He is describing the end of a conflict that one side could not end on its own.

The spine of this is one passage, and I want to press on it the whole way. All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-19 ESV). Read it slowly. God is the actor. We were the enemy. The reconciling happens at the cross, where the trespasses that stood between us and God are not waved away but absorbed, not counted, because they are counted somewhere else, in a body on a tree. Reconciliation in the Bible costs blood. It is never cheap. It is never a feeling.

Now the strongest objection, and it is strong. Some Christians say that this passage is about reconciliation with God and nothing else, that Paul is writing about salvation, about the sinner brought home, and that to extend it to relations between human groups is to bend a vertical text into a horizontal program it was never meant to carry. They say the gospel is reconciliation with God, full stop, and that when we make it about Black and white we have changed the subject from the cross to a cause. I take this seriously because it guards something precious. The vertical is the foundation. A reconciliation between people that is not grounded in reconciliation with God is just diplomacy, and diplomacy does not save.

But read three verses further than we usually stop. The same Paul who wrote 2 Corinthians 5 wrote that Christ is our peace, who has made the two groups one (Ephesians 2:14 ESV), and the two groups he names are not the sinner and God. They are the Jew and the Gentile, two peoples divided by a wall of hostility, made one in the same cross that reconciled them both to God. Paul does not let us choose between the vertical and the horizontal. He fastens them together. The cross that ends the war with God ends the war between us in the same stroke, because the second war was always a symptom of the first. The wall between peoples is held up by the same pride that built the wall between us and heaven.

Willie James Jennings traces how we lost this. In The Christian Imagination he argues that the modern church learned to imagine salvation as the rescue of individual souls from the world, severed from bodies, from land, from peoples, and that this severing was not innocent (Jennings 2010). It happened alongside the colonial enterprise, the very moment European Christians were sorting the peoples of the earth by skin and worth. A faith that could reconcile a soul to God while leaving the slave in the field was a faith that had already cut katallage in half. We kept the vertical and amputated the horizontal, and the amputation was convenient. It let us be saved and stay segregated.

So what does the full word require. First, it requires truth, because you cannot reconcile an account you refuse to read. The reason God could not count our trespasses against us is that he counted them fully, named them, laid them on Christ. There is no reconciliation that skips the naming of the debt. This is where the church most often fails. We want the peace without the ledger. We want the handshake before the truth. John Perkins, who was beaten nearly to death by Mississippi officers in 1970 and gave his life afterward to the work of Christian community development, insisted that reconciliation without justice is a lie, that you cannot bind a wound you will not first clean (Perkins 1976). The cross did not pretend the debt was small. It paid it in full.

Second, the full word requires that we receive a ministry, not announce a feeling. Paul says God entrusted to us the ministry of reconciliation. A ministry is labor. It has hours and costs and failures. It is not the warm glow of a unity service once a year. It is the slow, expensive, often unrewarded work of a people who have decided that the war is over and now have to live as though it is, in budgets and friendships and the seating of a sanctuary. We were made ministers of the thing God did. That is a job, and most of us have not shown up to it.

Here is the reversal we need. We tend to think reconciliation is something we achieve, a goal we work toward, a summit at the end of enough dialogue. But Paul says it is something God already accomplished and then handed to us to announce. We are not negotiating a peace. We are publishing one. The war is over because of the cross, not because of our efforts, and our refusal to live in that peace does not undo it. It only puts us on the wrong side of a verdict already rendered. The reconciled who will not reconcile are a contradiction the watching world can read at a glance.

Lisa Sharon Harper presses the word back to its root in shalom, the Hebrew vision of the world made whole, every relationship set right, between people and God, between people and people, between people and the ground itself (Harper 2016). Reconciliation is not the absence of conflict. It is the presence of that wholeness, the debt settled, the wall down, the enemy seated at the table as kin. That is bigger than getting along, and it is the only thing big enough to be worth the blood it cost.

The man who is tired of the word is tired of a counterfeit, and he should be. The counterfeit is reconciliation without truth, peace without the ledger, a handshake offered to people whose wounds we will not name. But the real word is harder and better than anything we have made of it. It means a war is over because God ended it at terrible cost, and we who were the enemies are now ministers of the peace.

We did not earn this word. We stole it, shrank it, and sold it cheap. The least we can do now is preach it whole.

### Works Cited

Harper, Lisa Sharon. The Very Good Gospel: How Everything Wrong Can Be Made Right. Colorado Springs: WaterBrook, 2016.

Jennings, Willie James. The Christian Imagination: Theology and the Origins of Race. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2010.

Perkins, John M. Let Justice Roll Down. Glendale: Regal Books, 1976.

title: The Image of God and the Lie of Race
excerpt: Race is a recent invention dressed up as an ancient fact, and the church helped sew the costume.
body:
Ask a child where race comes from and she will tell you it has always been here, that people simply are these colors and these kinds, the way the sky is blue. Ask a historian and you get a different answer. Race as we mean it, the sorting of humanity into a ladder of worth by the color of skin, is younger than the printing press. It was made. And the making has a date, a motive, and a set of hands, and some of those hands held a Bible.

The text I want to carry is the oldest claim Scripture makes about a human being. God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them (Genesis 1:27 ESV). The imago dei. Before nation, before tribe, before anything we call race, there is this. Every human being bears the image of God, and that image is not distributed by degree. It is not more present in one people and less in another. It is the floor under all of us, the thing that makes a person a person, and Scripture lays it down in the first chapter before sin has even entered the story.

Here is the strong objection, and I want it stated at full strength. Many thoughtful people say the church should stop talking about race entirely, that the very category is the problem, that to keep naming Black and white is to keep alive a fiction we should let die. Color blindness, they argue, is the Christian position. We are all one in Christ, there is neither Jew nor Greek, so why keep sorting the body by a distinction the gospel abolished. There is something genuinely right in this, and I will not pretend otherwise. The category of race is a lie. It has no basis in biology. The differences we have built a ladder upon are surface deep, and the gospel really does make one new humanity out of the many.

But here is where the color-blind answer fails, and it fails for a reason worth understanding. You cannot heal a wound by refusing to name the weapon. Race is a lie, yes. But it is a lie that built a world, that wrote laws, that drew maps, that decided who got a loan and who got a noose, and you do not undo a four-hundred-year-old structure by closing your eyes to it. Telling a man whose grandfather was redlined out of a neighborhood that you do not see color does not return the house. It only blinds you to why he does not have one. The lie of race must be named precisely because it is a lie that did real damage, and the damage did not vanish when we stopped saying the quiet part out loud.

Trace the invention. Before the European slave trade, people knew themselves by tribe, by city, by faith, by tongue. There were enslaved people of every shade, and slavery, evil as it was, was not yet organized around color. Then came the seventeenth century and a problem the planters needed to solve. African labor was being held for life while European labor was held for years, and that difference needed a justification that could survive a Christian conscience. So the category was built. Willie James Jennings shows how European Christians, in the age of conquest, began to read the peoples of the earth through a new lens, with whiteness placed at the top as the measure of the human and Blackness at the bottom, and how theology lent its weight to the sorting (Jennings 2010). Race was not discovered. It was theologically manufactured to make a sin look like an order of creation.

The church did not merely permit this. It supplied the verses. The so-called curse of Ham, drawn from a misreading of Genesis 9, was preached for centuries as the divine charter for African slavery, the claim that a whole people had been cursed to servitude by the word of God. It was a lie laid on top of the lie of race, Scripture twisted to baptize an economy. Esau McCaulley, reading the Bible from within the Black church tradition, shows how the same texts the slaveholder weaponized were read by the enslaved as a charter of dignity and deliverance, how Reading While Black means refusing both the oppressor's distortion and the despair it was meant to produce (McCaulley 2020). The book that was used to forge the chain was the same book that named the prisoner an image-bearer. Only one of those readings was true.

Here is the reversal, and it is the heart of the matter. We tend to think the problem of race is a problem of difference, that if we could only see past our differences we would be at peace. But Genesis says the opposite. The problem is not that we are different. God made the difference and called the whole creation very good. The problem is that we took a difference God made and built a hierarchy God never authorized. The sin is not color. The sin is the ladder. And the cure for a ladder is not to pretend everyone is on the same rung by ignoring the ranks. The cure is to tear the ladder down and confess we built it.

The imago dei does real work here, and it does it as law before it does it as grace. As law, it indicts. If every human bears the image of God, then every act of the slave trade, every lynching, every redlined map, every sermon that ranked the races was an assault on the image of God, a defacing of his likeness in the person of his neighbor. There is no neutral ground. To diminish a human being by color is to spit on the face of God reflected in that human being, and the church that taught the diminishing taught blasphemy with a Bible open. I am in that church's lineage. So is every white believer in America. The indictment includes us.

And as grace, the imago dei restores. The image cannot be erased by any lie. Four hundred years of teaching that Black bodies were worth less did not make them worth less, because worth was never ours to assign. It was set by God in the first chapter and sealed by God in the incarnation, when the Word took on flesh and dignified the human body forever. Augustine wrote that the image of God in us, defaced by sin, is being renewed in those who turn to Christ, restored to the likeness it was made for (Augustine, The Trinity 14). The lie of race tried to deface the image. The gospel renews it. And a church renewed in the image of God cannot keep the ladder. The renewal and the ladder cannot stand in the same body.

So we do not get color blindness, and we do not get the ladder either. We get something harder than both. We get the call to name the lie for what it is, to confess the hands that made it, and to look at every human face, including the faces our fathers ranked, and see what was always there.

The image of God. Defaced for four centuries. Never once erased.

### Works Cited

Augustine. The Trinity. Translated by Edmund Hill. Brooklyn: New City Press, 1991.

Jennings, Willie James. The Christian Imagination: Theology and the Origins of Race. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2010.

McCaulley, Esau. Reading While Black: African American Biblical Interpretation as an Exercise in Hope. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press, 2020.

title: Lament: The Prayer the Church Forgot
excerpt: We taught ourselves to skip past the prayers of grief, and in skipping them we lost the only language honest enough to carry what race has done.
body:
Open the hymnal of most white churches and try to find a song that does not resolve. Try to find one that ends in the question and not the answer, that leaves the grief standing, that does not hurry to the bridge where everything is fine. You will be looking a long time. We have a thousand songs of triumph and almost none of sorrow, and that absence is not a matter of taste. It is a theology, and it has cost us the ability to speak honestly about race.

A full third of the Psalms are laments, prayers of complaint, grief, and protest addressed to God. They are not polite. How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever (Psalm 13:1 ESV). My God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Psalm 22:1 ESV). These are not the prayers of people whose faith is failing. They are the prayers of the most faithful people in the Bible, and Jesus himself died with one of them on his lips. Lament is not the opposite of faith. It is faith refusing to lie about the state of the world.

Let me carry one psalm as the spine. Psalm 13 moves in three movements, and the church has learned to live only in the last. It opens in complaint, four times the cry how long, the prayer of a man who feels forgotten by the God he still addresses. Then it turns to petition, consider and answer me, light up my eyes. And only at the end does it arrive at trust, I will sing to the Lord because he has dealt bountifully with me (Psalm 13:6 ESV). Three movements. Complaint, petition, trust. We skip the first two and sing only the third, and a third of a prayer is not a prayer. It is a performance of arrival we have not actually made.

Now the strong objection, because there is one. Some will say that lament risks becoming a wallow, that endless grief over race keeps wounds open that grace means to close, that the gospel calls us to rejoice and to forgive and to look forward, not to camp in lamentation as if the resurrection had not happened. They say a faith fixated on sorrow has forgotten the empty tomb. And there is truth here worth holding. The Christian does not grieve as one without hope. Lament that never moves toward trust curdles into despair, and despair is not a Christian word.

But notice what the objection assumes. It assumes that the choice is between grief and hope, when the Psalms refuse that choice entirely. Psalm 13 does not arrive at trust by skipping the complaint. It arrives at trust through the complaint, by way of it, having spoken the grief fully to God first. The hope at the end of the psalm is earned, weighted, real, precisely because the sorrow at the beginning was not censored. A church that cannot lament cannot truly hope either, because its hope has never passed through honesty. It has only passed around it. And a hope that goes around the wound is a denial wearing the mask of faith.

Here is where this touches race directly. The reason the white church struggles to speak about race is, in part, a liturgical failure. We have no language for it. We know how to celebrate and we know how to instruct, but we do not know how to grieve, because we deleted grief from our worship generations ago. So when the history of slavery and lynching and segregation is set before us, we have no vessel to receive it. We reach for explanation, for defense, for the quick turn to reconciliation, because we never learned the prayer that simply sits in the wreckage and says to God, how long. The Black church kept that prayer. The spirituals were lament, the slave singing nobody knows the trouble I have seen straight into the face of God. We who lost lament lost the very language the moment required.

The history is specific and the silence around it is the proof. From 1877 to 1950 the historians at the Equal Justice Initiative have documented more than four thousand racial terror lynchings in the American South, public killings often attended by churchgoing crowds, sometimes on a Sunday, sometimes with the body displayed near a house of worship. The white church of that era did not lament these murders. It largely watched, or looked away, or in some cases supplied the crowd. There is no widely sung hymn of grief for them. The absence of that lament, eighty years on, is itself a sin we have not confessed. We never even learned to cry about it.

Walter Brueggemann argues that the loss of lament is the loss of a whole dimension of faith, that a community which can only praise has surrendered its capacity to hold God accountable and to tell the truth about its own pain (Brueggemann 1986). Without lament, he says, the covenant becomes one-sided, a relationship in which the powerful are never questioned and the suffering are never heard. A church that cannot lament cannot do justice, because justice begins with the truthful naming of what is wrong, and that naming, addressed to God, is exactly what lament is. We traded the prayer for a smile, and we lost the truth in the trade.

Here is the reversal. We have treated lament as a sign of weak faith, a stage to grow out of, a sorrow that mature believers transcend. But the Bible treats lament as a sign of intimacy. You do not complain to a stranger. You complain to a father, to the one you trust enough to be honest with, to the one you believe is listening and able. The freedom to cry how long, O Lord is the freedom of a child who knows the father is there. To refuse lament is not strength. It is distance. It is a politeness that has stopped believing God can take the truth.

The cross does the deepest work here, and it does it before it comforts. On the cross Jesus prayed Psalm 22, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, and in praying it he sanctified lament forever. God himself, in the flesh, lamented. The sinless one took the prayer of grief onto his own lips and made it holy. So there is no spiritual height above lament, because the highest one stooped into it. The law here is plain. A church too proud to grieve is a church that thinks itself above its own Lord.

And the grace is this. Because Christ lamented and was heard, our laments are heard too. The how long is not a cry into an empty sky. It rises to a God who has himself cried it, who knows the weight of the forsaken from the inside, who will not despise the broken prayer because he prayed it first. We are free to grieve all the way down, because the bottom is not despair. The bottom is a man on a cross who got there before us.

We forgot how to lament, and forgetting it, we lost the only honest language we had for what race has done. The first repentance may be smaller and harder than we think. Not a program. A prayer. How long, O Lord. We have not even begun to pray it.

### Works Cited

Brueggemann, Walter. The Costly Loss of Lament. Journal for the Study of the Old Testament 36 (1986): 57-71.

Equal Justice Initiative. Lynching in America: Confronting the Legacy of Racial Terror. Montgomery: Equal Justice Initiative, 2017.

Thurman, Howard. Jesus and the Disinherited. Boston: Beacon Press, 1949.

title: Building the Multiethnic Church Without Faking It
excerpt: A church can put many colors in the room and still leave one culture in charge of everything, and God is not fooled by the photograph.
body:
There is a kind of multiethnic church that exists mostly in the brochure. The faces on the website are varied. The worship band is varied. The greeters at the door were chosen, you suspect, with the camera in mind. And underneath the varied surface, every decision that matters is made by one group, in one cultural key, in the style they have always preferred, and the people of other backgrounds are welcome to attend the church that white leadership has built. This is not the one new humanity of Ephesians. It is assimilation with a diversity filter, and the people being assimilated can feel the difference even when the brochure cannot.

The question this article asks is not whether to build a multiethnic church. The question is how to build one that is real, and the difference between the real and the fake is not the photograph. It is who holds the power.

The spine is a scene from the early church, the first time the gospel had to decide whether it was big enough to hold more than one culture. In Acts 6 the church in Jerusalem is feeding its widows, and a complaint arises. The Hellenists, the Greek-speaking Jews, find that their widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution, while the Hebrew-speaking majority's widows are cared for (Acts 6:1 ESV). A diverse church. A real grievance from the minority culture. And here is what the apostles do not do. They do not tell the Hellenists they are imagining it. They do not call for unity over division. They restructure the leadership. They appoint seven men to oversee the distribution, and every single name on the list is Greek. The minority that was overlooked is given the power to fix the problem. That is how the first multiethnic church handled it, and it should haunt every church that handles it differently.

Now the strong objection. Some will say this whole project is misguided, that churches grow best when they reach a particular people with a particular culture, that the homogeneous unit principle, named by church-growth researchers in the 1970s, is simply realism, that people come to faith most readily among their own kind, and that forcing a multiethnic blend produces awkward, shrinking congregations while letting churches be culturally specific produces thriving ones. There is data behind this, and I will not wave it away. It is often true that the single-culture church grows faster. The multiethnic church is harder, slower, and more prone to conflict. Anyone who tells you otherwise has not tried it.

But here is where the realism fails. The gospel was never a growth strategy. The dividing wall in Ephesians was not torn down because mixed congregations grow better. It was torn down because Christ died to make the two one, and a church that stays segregated for the sake of efficiency has subordinated the cross to the numbers. Paul could have grown the church in Antioch faster by keeping Jews and Gentiles in separate fellowships. Instead he confronted Peter to his face when Peter pulled back from the Gentile table (Galatians 2:11-14 ESV), because the unity of the body across the dividing line was not optional decoration. It was the truth of the gospel itself, visible. A faster church that contradicts the cross is not a success. It is a well-attended denial.

So how is it built without faking it. First, power must move, not just bodies. The Acts 6 pattern is not diversity in the pews. It is diversity in the decisions. A church that wants people of color in the room but keeps every position of real authority in white hands has built a plantation with better music. The test is not the photo on Sunday. The test is who sets the budget, who chooses the preaching, who shapes the worship, whose cultural instincts are treated as normal and whose are treated as additions. Until that power is genuinely shared, the multiethnic church is a costume.

Second, one culture cannot be the default. In the fake version, the dominant culture's way of doing everything is simply the water, invisible, assumed, and every other culture is an accommodation to be tolerated on special Sundays. The real version dies to that. It means the majority gives up the comfort of its own preferences as the unquestioned norm, in music, in length, in volume, in the rhythm of the service, in the very feel of belonging. This is a death, and it is felt as a death by those asked to die. The white believer who has never once worshiped in a style not built for him is being asked to lose something he did not know he had. That losing is the cross at work in the body, and there is no real multiethnic church without it.

John Perkins spent his life on this and refused the cheap version. Reconciliation, he insisted, is not Black and white people smiling in a sanctuary. It is the redistribution of power and resources, the relocation of the comfortable into the hard places, the redistribution that makes the unity more than a feeling (Perkins 1976). His three R's, relocation, reconciliation, redistribution, put the costly word last and meant it. A church that wants the reconciliation without the redistribution wants the photograph without the cost, and Perkins, who bled for this, would not let us have it on those terms.

Here is the reversal. We tend to think the multiethnic church is a goal we build, a thing we assemble by careful planning, the right hires and the right music and the right outreach. But Ephesians says the one new humanity is not something we build. It is something Christ already made, on the cross, finished. Which means our task is not construction but excavation. We are not assembling a unity that does not exist. We are removing the rubble, the structures and habits and power arrangements, that bury a unity Christ already accomplished. The church does not manufacture the new humanity. It stops smothering it.

And this is where law precedes grace one more time. The law: the segregated church and the cosmetically diverse church are both denials of a unity that already exists in Christ, and no amount of good intention changes the denial into obedience. To leave the power where it has always been while claiming the name of reconciliation is to lie with a budget. That is the indictment, and as a white pastor I stand inside it, because the default culture of my tradition is the one I have most often mistaken for the gospel itself.

The grace: because the new humanity is Christ's accomplishment and not ours, we are not condemned to build what we cannot build. The pressure is off our cleverness and onto his finished work. We are freed to do the slow, costly, unglamorous labor of clearing rubble, knowing the thing underneath is real, already there, waiting to be uncovered. The multiethnic church is not a goal we might fail to reach. It is a fact we are called to stop hiding.

So the brochure is the wrong question. The right question is the one the Hellenist widows asked without words. When the minority is overlooked, who gets the power to fix it. Answer that honestly, and you will know whether you have built the one new humanity or only its photograph.

God is not looking at the picture. He is reading the ledger of who decides.

### Works Cited

DeYmaz, Mark. Building a Healthy Multi-Ethnic Church. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 2007.

Jennings, Willie James. The Christian Imagination: Theology and the Origins of Race. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2010.

Perkins, John M. Let Justice Roll Down. Glendale: Regal Books, 1976.

title: What the Sabbath Is and Why You Need It
excerpt: The Sabbath is not a day off and not a religious chore left over from an older world, it is a weekly act of trust that the world will hold together while you stop, and the reason you cannot stop tells you almost everything about who you think God is.
body:
There is a sentence in the first chapter of the Bible that should have stopped me cold the first time I read it as a new convert, and it did not, because I read it the way most people read the opening of Genesis, as a creation account I was supposed to defend or attack. I came to faith from atheism. I came in arguing. So I read those chapters looking for the fight about origins and missed the quietest and most subversive thing on the page. God works for six days. Then God stops. The text does not say God grew tired. It says God rested, and then it does something it does for no other day in the week. It blesses the seventh day and makes it holy (Genesis 2:3 ESV). Holiness, the first time it lands in Scripture, lands not on a mountain, not on a person, not on a place. It lands on a span of time.

Abraham Heschel saw this more clearly than anyone in the last century, and his line has become the one everyone quotes, that the Sabbath is a palace in time (Heschel 1951). But I want to slow down before the phrase gets pretty, because in the original setting it was not pretty, it was a bomb. The peoples around Israel built holiness into space. They built ziggurats and temples and sacred groves, they marked off the ground and said God lives here, come to this place. Israel was handed something stranger. Before they had a temple, before they had a land, before they had anything but a wilderness and a promise, they were given a holy day. You cannot conquer a day. You cannot garrison it or sell it or stand on it with an army. A holy day belongs to no empire. That is the first thing the Sabbath is, and we have nearly lost the ability to feel how radical it was.

Now let me give the objection its full strength, because if I cannot say it better than the skeptic can, I have no business answering it. The honest modern person looks at the Sabbath and says this is a relic. It belonged to an agrarian people with no electricity, no global markets, no children with three activities a night and a mortgage that does not pause for anyone. The command to rest assumes a world where rest was possible, and that world is gone. To impose a stop-day now is either a luxury for the comfortable or a cruelty to the exhausted, one more thing to fail at, one more box the religious will use to measure you. And there is something underneath that objection even sharper. The skeptic suspects that rest is for people who can afford it, and that telling a single mother working two jobs to keep the Sabbath is the kind of thing only a man with a salary and a study would say.

That objection is right about more than the church wants to admit. We have made the Sabbath a performance. We have used it to rank people. And the version of rest sold in the wellness aisle, the self-care weekend, the digital detox you pay for, that version really is a luxury good, and it really does leave the tired more tired and more ashamed. I am not going to defend that. I am going to argue that it is the opposite of what the command was given for, and that the people who most need the Sabbath are precisely the people the modern world has convinced they cannot have it.

To see why, you have to go to the second time the command is given, because the Bible gives the Sabbath command twice and changes the reason. In Exodus the reason is creation. Remember the Sabbath, because God rested on the seventh day (Exodus 20:11 ESV). But in Deuteronomy, forty years later, Moses repeats the law to a new generation and grounds it somewhere else entirely. Observe the Sabbath day, and remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God brought you out (Deuteronomy 5:15 ESV). Read those two reasons together and the whole thing opens. The Sabbath is creation and it is exodus. It is the rhythm of the God who made the world, and it is the protest of the God who breaks slaveries.

Walter Brueggemann built a small and ferocious book on exactly this, and he names the thing the rest of us tiptoe around. Pharaoh, he writes, is the system that cannot rest and will not let you rest, the economy of endless production whose first demand on slaves was always more bricks (Brueggemann 2014). The God of Israel walks into that economy and legislates a stop. One day in seven, the brick count goes to zero, and nothing falls apart, and the slaves discover they are not the ones holding the sky up. That is why the command extends so radically far. It covers your son and your daughter, your servant, the foreigner inside your gates, even the ox and the donkey (Exodus 20:10 ESV). The Sabbath is the one law in the ancient world that gave the slave the same rest as the master. It was never a luxury for the comfortable. It was a weekly emancipation, and the people who needed it most were the ones with the least.

Which means the modern objection, that rest belongs to those who can afford it, has the logic exactly backwards. The Sabbath was given to slaves, by a God who had just freed them, to keep them from rebuilding Egypt with their own hands.

Look at how far the law pressed this into the structure of the society. The Sabbath was the seventh day, but the principle did not stop at the week. Every seventh year the land itself was to rest, the fields left unsown, and whatever grew of its own accord belonged to the poor and the wild animals alike (Leviticus 25:4-7 ESV). And every fiftieth year, the year after seven sevens, the trumpet sounded the Jubilee, and debts were released, and slaves went free, and land sold in desperation returned to the family that had lost it. The Sabbath was the seed of an entire economy of release. A society that stops one day in seven is being trained, week by week, to believe that the world is not a closed system of scarcity in which you must grab and hold and never let go. It is being trained to believe in a God who provides, who gives the double portion of manna on the sixth day so that no one has to gather on the seventh (Exodus 16:29 ESV). Take that seriously and you see that the Sabbath is not a pause in the economy. It is a different economy breaking into the old one, one day at a time, until the whole thing is leavened.

And we have rebuilt it. This is where I have to stop pointing at the skeptic and put myself inside the indictment, because I am as captured as anyone. Trace the history and you can almost watch the chains go back on. For most of human existence, work ended when the light did. The sun set the terms. Then in 1879 Edison demonstrated the incandescent bulb at Menlo Park, and within a generation the factory could run all night, the shift could be split, the day could be cut into pieces and sold around the clock. The sociologist Murray Melbin called this the colonization of the night, the slow conquest of the one stretch of time the body had always kept for itself, a frontier opened after dark the way the American West was opened after dark fell on the older world (Melbin 1987). The clock came first, the factory bell that the historian E. P. Thompson traced through the early industrial towns, training a generation of farmers off the rhythm of the seasons and onto the rhythm of the machine (Thompson 1967). Then the light. Then, in our own lifetime, the final piece. In 2007 the first iPhone, and the factory we had pushed into the night, we now carry in our pockets and lay on the nightstand beside our sleep. There is no closing time anymore. The brick count never goes to zero. Pharaoh moved into the phone.

I feel this in my own house. I have five sons. I know what it is to lie in bed having stopped working only in the sense that my hands stopped, while the machine in my head kept running the angles, kept counting bricks. I have stood in my own kitchen at eleven at night answering a message that could have waited until morning and called it diligence. It was not diligence. It was fear. It was the quiet refusal to believe that the church, the family, the world would survive my stopping. The Sabbath names that fear and calls it what it is. Idolatry. Not the idolatry of a golden statue but the older one underneath it, the belief that I am the one keeping things alive.

And here is the part of the indictment I feel most, as a father. My sons are watching what I cannot stop doing, and they are learning from it what a man is. They are learning that a man is what he produces, that his worth is the size of his output, that rest is what you take when you have earned it and most days you have not. I can preach the Sabbath from a pulpit and unteach it in my own kitchen in a single distracted evening. The day was given for them as much as for me, your son and your daughter named directly in the command, and when I will not stop, I am not only wearing myself out. I am handing my children the yoke of Egypt and calling it a work ethic. The Sabbath is the one inheritance I most want to leave them and the one I am most tempted to withhold by example.

Josef Pieper saw the philosophical root of this before the smartphone existed to prove him right. Writing in the rubble of postwar Germany, he argued that we have come to believe a person is justified by work alone, that the worker is the only real human being and rest is merely the refueling that makes more work possible (Pieper 1948). On that account you do not rest in order to live, you rest in order to produce. Even your leisure is conscripted. The vacation exists to make you a better employee. The sabbath of the wellness app exists to optimize your performance. Pieper called the alternative leisure, but he did not mean idleness. He meant a stance of receiving rather than seizing, an openness to a world you did not make and cannot finally control. Rest, in this sense, is the moment you admit the universe is a gift and not a product. That is why a culture that can only produce cannot truly rest. It has forgotten how to receive.

There is a reversal hidden in all of this that we miss because we read the command as a restriction. We hear the Sabbath as a no, a day of cannot, a list of forbidden things. But the deepest thing the Sabbath says is yes. It says you are allowed to stop. You have permission to be a creature and not the Creator, to be small, to be held. The exhausted modern person does not actually want more freedom in the sense the culture sells, the freedom to do anything at any hour with no closing time. That freedom is precisely the prison. What the soul wants is permission to be finite, and the Sabbath is the only institution left that grants it. The world will give you infinite options and call it liberty. The Sabbath gives you a wall, a fence around one day, and inside that fence is the only real freedom most of us will ever taste, the freedom of having nothing to prove for twenty-four hours. The restriction is the gift. The fence is the field.

Now carry the one text I want to hold through all of this, the spine of the whole argument. When Jesus is challenged for letting his disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, he says a sentence that has been used to abolish the day and was meant to save it. The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27 ESV). Hear what he is actually doing. The religious leaders had turned the gift into a test, the emancipation into a new slavery, the day of freedom into thirty-nine categories of forbidden labor you could fail. Jesus does not say the Sabbath is abolished. He says it is a gift, and you have turned the gift into a weapon, and you have it upside down. The Sabbath was made for you. It is not one more brick. It is the day the brick-making stops.

There is a danger I have to name before I say what the Sabbath is for us, because the church has made the opposite mistake from the culture and it is just as deadly. The culture abolished the Sabbath. The religious turned it into a cage. By the time of Jesus, the rabbis had built a hedge around the day, thirty-nine categories of forbidden labor, and the hedge that was meant to protect the gift had strangled it. The day made for freedom had become the most surveilled day of the week, the day you could be caught and condemned for healing a man or feeding yourself. Marva Dawn warns that we are perfectly capable of repeating this, of turning Sabbath-keeping into a new legalism, a performance we use to feel superior and to measure others (Dawn 1989). If your Sabbath becomes one more arena in which you succeed or fail, one more way to rank yourself against the family that does it worse, you have rebuilt the cage. The Sabbath is not a test you pass. It is a gift you receive, and the moment it becomes a test, it has stopped being the Sabbath and become Egypt with a religious accent.

So what is it, finally, and why do you need it. The Sabbath is a weekly act of trust that the world will hold together while you stop. It is the practiced, embodied, twenty-four-hour confession that you are not God, that you are not Pharaoh, that the sky has another keeper. Eugene Peterson, who pastored for decades and watched the disease up close, said the Sabbath is the one day we deliberately do nothing that justifies our existence (Peterson 1989). That is the whole offense of it. Every other day you can point to what you made and say, see, I earned my place. On the Sabbath you point at nothing. You stop, and the ground does not open, and slowly, over years of stopping, the lie in your chest begins to die. The lie that says you are what you produce.

Let me say plainly that grace does not come last here by accident. The law of the Sabbath does real work first. It exposes you. The first time you genuinely try to keep it, you will discover how much of your identity was riding on your output, because the withdrawal is brutal. You will reach for the phone like a man reaching for a drink. You will feel useless, and then you will feel afraid, and then, if you stay in it, you will feel the floor of grace underneath the panic. The Sabbath is where the gospel stops being a doctrine and becomes something your body knows. You did not make yourself. You cannot keep yourself. You are held.
