The cross did that work on a Friday and the tomb stayed shut through a Saturday, a Sabbath, while the disciples could do nothing at all, and the salvation of the world was accomplished entirely without their help. They rested on the Sabbath according to the commandment (Luke 23:56 ESV), and while they rested, everything that mattered was being done for them. That is the pattern. That is always the pattern.

I am not going to give you a method here. That is for another day and another essay. I am going to leave you where the command leaves us, with a choice we make once a week and mostly decline. The world will tell you that you cannot afford to stop. It told the slaves the same thing. It was lying then. Augustine wrote that our hearts are restless until they rest in God (Augustine 397), and we have built a civilization to prove him right, a civilization that has abolished the night and colonized the day and cannot, for all its power, give a tired person one hour of true rest. The Sabbath is the standing refusal of all of it. One day. No bricks. The sky held by someone else.

You will not believe that until you try it. And you will not try it until you are tired enough to stop pretending you are God.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 397. Confessions. Translated by Henry Chadwick. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991.

Brueggemann, Walter. 2014. Sabbath as Resistance: Saying No to the Culture of Now. Louisville: Westminster John Knox Press.

Heschel, Abraham Joshua. 1951. The Sabbath: Its Meaning for Modern Man. New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux.

Melbin, Murray. 1987. Night as Frontier: Colonizing the World After Dark. New York: The Free Press.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1989. The Contemplative Pastor: Returning to the Art of Spiritual Direction. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Pieper, Josef. 1948. Leisure: The Basis of Culture. Translated by Gerald Malsbary. South Bend: St. Augustine's Press, 1998.

Thompson, E. P. 1967. Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism. Past and Present 38: 56 to 97.

title: How to Rest in a Culture of Exhaustion
excerpt: Exhaustion is not a scheduling problem and it will not be fixed by better scheduling, because the tiredness underneath our tiredness is the kind a vacation cannot reach, and Scripture offers something we have nearly stopped believing is real.
body:
A man comes to me exhausted, and he has tried everything the culture told him to try. He took the vacation. He bought the better mattress and the sunrise alarm and the app that tracks his sleep and scolds him in the morning. He cut his screen time and started the cold plunge and read the book about deep work. He is doing all of it, and he is more tired than when he started, and he cannot understand why. I have been that man. I know exactly why.

The reason is that he treated his exhaustion as a logistics failure when it is a spiritual condition, and you cannot reschedule your way out of a spiritual condition. There is a tiredness that sleep fixes. And there is a tiredness underneath the tiredness that sleep cannot touch, the weariness of a soul that has not stopped, in any real sense, in years. The first kind is in the body. The second kind is in the place where you decide what you are for. We keep applying body solutions to a soul problem, and then we wonder why the rest does not take.

Let me steel-man the alternative, because it is reasonable and it is everywhere. The optimization answer says exhaustion is a resource problem. You have finite energy, you are spending it badly, so audit your inputs, protect your sleep, batch your tasks, and the deficit closes. There is real truth in this. Most of us are genuinely sleep-deprived and over-scheduled, and the basic physiology is not wrong. A person who sleeps five hours and drinks at midnight will be tired in a way that no theology will fix, and pretending otherwise is its own dishonesty. The optimizers are right that the body has limits and that we routinely violate them. So far, so good.

But watch what the optimization answer does underneath. It treats you as a machine whose output you are trying to maximize, and it treats rest as maintenance, the downtime that keeps the machine running. On that logic you are never actually resting. You are recovering in order to produce. Your sabbath is conscripted into your labor. Josef Pieper named this in postwar Germany, when he watched a whole society rebuild itself around the idea that the worker is the only real human being and rest is merely the refueling of the worker (Pieper 1948). The optimization answer cannot give you rest because it does not believe rest is real. It only believes in better-managed work. And the soul knows the difference. The soul will not be fooled by a vacation that is secretly a tune-up.

Hold one text through this. It is the most familiar invitation in the Gospels, and familiarity has sanded the strangeness off it. Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, and you will find rest for your souls (Matthew 11:28-29 ESV). Notice what Jesus does not say. He does not say come to me and I will remove your yoke. He offers a different yoke. The promise of rest is not the absence of work, it is a change of master. The exhausted man assumes rest means nothing on his shoulders. Jesus says the problem was never that you carried something, the problem is what you were carrying and who put it there.

What were we carrying. We were carrying the weight of justifying our own existence, and that is a weight no scheduling app can lift. Eugene Peterson translated the next line of that passage in a way that has stayed with pastors for a generation, the unforced rhythms of grace (Peterson 2002). Unforced. The exhaustion we live in is forced rhythm, the cadence of a machine that never stops because it was built never to stop. Trace it back. The factory bell came first, the industrial clock the historian E. P. Thompson described training farmers off the seasons and onto the shift (Thompson 1967). Then Edison's bulb in 1879 abolished the natural close of the day. Then the smartphone in 2007 put the factory in our hands and on our nightstands. We did not drift into exhaustion. We engineered it, decade by decade, and then sold ourselves the cure inside the same machine that caused the disease. The app that fixes your screen time runs on the screen.

So how do you actually rest. Not as a tip. As a turning. The first move is to stop trying to earn the rest, because earned rest is a contradiction the soul sees through immediately. Marva Dawn, who wrote about keeping the Sabbath with more honesty than most, said the discipline begins with ceasing, and ceasing means ceasing not only from work but from the anxiety that drives the work, from the need to produce, to accomplish, to be the one who holds it together (Dawn 1989). You do not schedule that. You repent of it. You confess that you have been functioning as a small god, keeping your small world spinning by force of will, and you lay it down, and you discover the world keeps spinning, which is both humbling and the first real relief you have felt in years.

The second move is to receive instead of seize. Dallas Willard argued that the spiritual life is built on practices, and that rest is not the absence of discipline but one of its hardest forms, because to truly rest you must trust, and trust is a muscle most of us have let go slack (Willard 1988). Try it concretely. Take one day, or if a day feels impossible, take three hours, and do nothing in them that justifies your existence. Do not catch up. Do not get ahead. Do not optimize the rest itself into a productivity ritual. Sit with people you love and do not check your phone. Walk without a podcast telling you how to improve. Eat slowly. Pray badly. Let the silence be uncomfortable until it stops being uncomfortable. You are not refueling. You are practicing trust. You are letting your body learn what your mind keeps forgetting, that you are held by someone who never sleeps so that you are free to.

I will not hide the cost, because the optimizers at least promise quick results and I will not. The first several times you genuinely cease, you will feel worse. The anxiety does not leave quietly. It rises, because you have removed the activity that was medicating it, and now it has nothing to do but be felt. This is not the practice failing. This is the practice working. You are detoxing from a drug, and the drug was your own usefulness. Wendell Berry, watching the same machine eat the rhythms of rural life, wrote that we have given up the great possibility of being at home in our own lives, of being present where we are (Berry 1990). The rest you are looking for is not somewhere else, in a vacation or a retreat or a better year. It is in the unbearable, healing experience of being fully where you already are, with nothing to prove and nothing to produce.

The cross does the deepest work here, and the law has to land before the grace does. The law of rest exposes you. It shows you, in the panic of the first quiet hour, exactly how much of your worth was riding on your output. That exposure is grace disguised as discomfort, because once you see it, you can finally stop carrying it. Jesus did not say take a break. He said come to me. The rest he offers is not a state you manufacture, it is a person you come to with empty hands. On the cross he did the one work that ends all the frantic working, and he said it is finished, and the most countercultural sentence a tired person can say is to believe him and stop.

You will not rest by managing your energy better. You will rest when you stop believing the lie that the world is yours to hold up. Lay it down. It was never yours.

### Works Cited

Berry, Wendell. 1990. What Are People For? Essays. New York: North Point Press.

Dawn, Marva J. 1989. Keeping the Sabbath Wholly: Ceasing, Resting, Embracing, Feasting. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Peterson, Eugene H. 2002. The Message: The Bible in Contemporary Language. Colorado Springs: NavPress.

Pieper, Josef. 1948. Leisure: The Basis of Culture. Translated by Gerald Malsbary. South Bend: St. Augustine's Press, 1998.

Thompson, E. P. 1967. Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism. Past and Present 38: 56 to 97.

Willard, Dallas. 1988. The Spirit of the Disciplines: Understanding How God Changes Lives. San Francisco: HarperOne.

title: Prayer When You Do Not Feel Like It
excerpt: The advice to pray only when you feel moved to has quietly emptied more prayer lives than open unbelief ever did, and the people who pray for decades almost all share one secret about feeling that no one tells the beginner.
body:
I did not pray for the first twenty years of my life because I did not believe anyone was listening, and that, at least, was honest. What surprised me after I came to faith was discovering a second kind of not-praying, quieter and more respectable, that runs through the lives of people who believe completely. They believe God hears. They simply do not pray, because they are waiting to feel like it, and the feeling, week after week, does not come. They have been told that prayer should be spontaneous, that forced prayer is fake prayer, that God wants the heart and not the recitation. So they wait for the heart to show up. And while they wait, the prayer life dies of natural causes, and no one ever names the cause of death.

Let me give that view its due, because it is not stupid and it is partly true. The case against praying when you do not feel like it goes like this. God is not interested in performance. He sees the heart, not the mouth. Jesus condemned the people who prayed to be seen and who heaped up empty phrases thinking they would be heard for many words (Matthew 6:7 ESV). So to drag yourself through prayers you do not feel is to risk the exact hypocrisy Jesus attacked, mouthing words to a God who wants truth in the inward being. Better, the argument says, to wait until you mean it. Better honest silence than dishonest noise. There is real conviction in this, and a real fear of becoming a Pharisee, and I respect both.

Here is what that view gets right and where it goes wrong. It is right that God wants the heart. It is wrong about how the heart gets there. It assumes the heart leads and the body follows, that you feel devotion first and then you pray. But that is not how a human being is built, and it is not how Scripture treats us, and it is not how anyone who has prayed for forty years got there. The feeling does not lead. Usually the feeling follows. You do not pray because you feel like it. You feel like it, eventually, sometimes, because you prayed.

Hold the one text that breaks this open, and it is not a teaching, it is a body of evidence. The Psalms. The prayer book Jesus himself prayed, and the striking thing about it, once you actually read it through, is how much of it is prayed against the feelings. The psalmist commands his own soul. Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me. Hope in God (Psalm 42:11 ESV). Read that carefully. He is not reporting a feeling. He is talking back to his feelings, preaching to himself, telling his own downcast soul what to do. Eugene Peterson spent years living inside the Psalms and concluded that they teach us prayer is not the language of our feelings but the discipline that re-forms our feelings, that we learn to pray by praying words we did not generate until they generate something in us (Peterson 1989). The Psalms are not spontaneous outbursts. They are mostly someone praying through the absence of the feeling, on the far side of which the feeling sometimes returns.

Now the history, because this notion that real prayer must be felt is younger than we think. For most of Christian history, prayer was understood as a practice, an appointed thing, done at appointed hours whether the heart was warm or cold. The monastic hours, the daily office, the fixed prayers of the morning and the evening, all of it assumed that you would often not feel like it and built a structure precisely for those times. The structure was the point. Then came a long shift, accelerating after the Romantic movement of the early 1800s, in which feeling became the measure of the real. The genuine was the spontaneous. The true act was the unforced one. And the church, breathing the same air, slowly absorbed the idea that scripted prayer was dead prayer and only the heart-felt counted. We inherited a piety that cannot survive a dry season, because we threw out the very forms that were designed to carry us through dry seasons. We kept the feeling and discarded the scaffolding, and then we wondered why our prayer lives collapse the moment the feeling does.

I am inside this. I have knelt with nothing in my chest, no warmth, no sense of presence, the ceiling as blank as it was when I was an atheist, and I have wanted to get up and call it honesty. The flesh is weak, Jesus said to the disciples who could not stay awake to pray with him in the one hour he asked, and he did not excuse them with it, he named it and told them to watch and pray anyway (Matthew 26:41 ESV). The weakness is not a disqualification from prayer. It is the human condition prayer is for.

So how do you pray when you do not feel like it. You pray anyway, and you let the not-feeling become part of the prayer instead of a reason to stop. Dallas Willard insisted that the spiritual disciplines work indirectly, that you cannot will yourself to feel devotion any more than you can will yourself to fall asleep, but you can arrange your life around the practices that make devotion possible, the way you cannot force sleep but you can lie down in a dark room (Willard 1988). Praying when you do not feel like it is lying down in the dark room. You are not manufacturing the feeling. You are putting yourself where the feeling can find you.

Concretely, this means three things, and only because the thinking actually produces three. First, use words that are not your own when your own have run out. Pray a psalm. Pray the Lord's Prayer slowly, one line a breath. The given words carry you when your heart cannot generate any. Second, keep the appointment regardless. Set a time, the same time, and show up to it the way you show up to a job you cannot skip on the days you feel like it, because a friendship sustained only by spontaneous visits is not a friendship, it is an acquaintance. Third, tell God the truth about the absence. The driest prayer I have ever prayed began, I do not want to be here and I feel nothing, and that sentence, it turned out, was prayer of the realest kind, because it was honest and it was addressed to him. The Psalms are full of exactly that sentence.

The grace under all of this is the part the performance-anxiety never reaches, and the law has to clear the ground first. The law says pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17 ESV), and that command will crush you if you hear it as a demand to generate constant feeling. Hear it instead as permission. You are allowed to come empty. The whole basis of Christian prayer is that we do not approach God on the strength of our fervor. We approach on the strength of Christ, who prayed the prayers we cannot pray, who in the garden prayed with such anguish that the sweat fell like blood, who intercedes for us now even when we have no words. The Spirit helps us in our weakness, for we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26 ESV). Read that and feel the weight lift. On the days you cannot pray, prayer is still happening, underneath you, on your behalf, in a language deeper than feeling.

That is why you pray when you do not feel like it. Not to perform. Not to earn. You pray because prayer was never riding on your feelings in the first place, and the sooner you stop waiting for the warmth before you kneel, the sooner you will be kneeling on the day the warmth returns. Augustine, who knew the restless heart better than any of us, said our hearts find no rest until they rest in God (Augustine 397), and the resting is not a mood you wait for. It is a practice you enter, mostly in the dark, until one morning, without announcement, the light is already in the room.

Do not wait to feel like it. The feeling is on the other side of the praying, and the only way through is through.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 397. Confessions. Translated by Henry Chadwick. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1989. Answering God: The Psalms as Tools for Prayer. San Francisco: HarperOne.

Willard, Dallas. 1988. The Spirit of the Disciplines: Understanding How God Changes Lives. San Francisco: HarperOne.

title: The Examined Life: Spiritual Practices That Hold
excerpt: We have been sold the spiritual disciplines as techniques for self-improvement, which is the one thing they were never meant to be, and the difference between a practice that holds and a practice that quietly hollows you out comes down to a single question about what you are actually doing.
body:
Socrates said the unexamined life is not worth living, and we have repeated it so often that we no longer hear how much it leaves out. Examine the life, fine. But with what, and toward what. A man can examine his life relentlessly and become nothing but more anxious about himself, more curved inward, a connoisseur of his own faults. The examined life can become the most exhausting form of self-absorption there is. The question is never only whether you examine your life. The question is what you bring the life under examination toward, and whether the practices you use to examine it open you up or close you in.

I want to talk about the spiritual disciplines, the old practices the church has carried for two thousand years, prayer and fasting and silence and confession and Scripture and the Sabbath. And I want to start by admitting that they have been badly sold. In the last forty years they were repackaged for a self-improvement market, offered as techniques for a better, calmer, more productive you. Fasting for focus. Silence for stress. Meditation for the cortisol. There is a version of the disciplines on every wellness platform now, stripped of God and aimed at the self, and the strange thing is they sometimes work on their own terms. You will feel calmer. That is exactly the danger.

Let me steel-man that approach, because it is sincere and it helps people. The pragmatic case says, who cares about the theology, the practices produce measurable goods. Meditation lowers blood pressure. Gratitude raises baseline happiness. Fasting sharpens the mind. The contemplative traditions stumbled onto real technologies of human flourishing, and we can keep the technologies and drop the metaphysics. People are less anxious, more present, kinder. What could be wrong with that. And the honest answer is that nothing is wrong with calmer and kinder, and a great deal of real suffering is eased by these practices even when God is nowhere in the frame. I will not pretend otherwise. The disciplines do have natural effects, and those effects are good.

But here is what the technique approach cannot see about itself. When you aim a spiritual discipline at the self, you make the self the destination, and the self is precisely the thing the disciplines were designed to dethrone. A practice aimed at your own improvement leaves you, at the center, exactly where you started, only better managed. You become a more serene version of the same self-curved-inward person you were before. Dallas Willard cut straight to this. The disciplines, he wrote, are not ways of earning anything or of impressing God or of improving the self as a project. They are ways of placing ourselves in the presence of God so that he can do in us what we cannot do for ourselves (Willard 1988). The whole orientation is outward and upward. The moment it turns back on the self, the same action becomes its opposite. The fast that was meant to make you hungry for God becomes a diet. The silence that was meant to make you available to God becomes a spa.

Hold one text through this, and let it judge every practice. Whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it (Matthew 16:25 ESV). That sentence is the whole logic of the disciplines in one line. They are not techniques for saving your life, for securing it, optimizing it, holding it together. They are practiced ways of losing it, of handing it over, of dying a little to the project of self so that something truer can live. A discipline that helps you save your life is working against the gospel even when it calms you down. A discipline that helps you lose your life is the real thing, even when it leaves you raw. That is the test, and it is a hard one, because the two can look identical from the outside. Same fast, same silence, same kneeling. The difference is the direction of the heart.

The history matters here, because the modern self that the disciplines must reckon with is a recent thing. The philosopher Charles Taylor traced how we became what he calls buffered selves, sealed off, self-defining, taking our own inner experience as the final court of meaning, a sense of self that simply did not exist for most of human history (Taylor 2007). The ancient and medieval Christian came to the disciplines assuming the self was porous, open, in need of being acted upon from outside, formed by powers greater than itself. We come to the same disciplines assuming the self is the sovereign center and the practices are tools it deploys for its own ends. Same practices. Opposite anthropology. And the practices quietly conform to the anthropology of the one performing them. Give a buffered self the disciplines and it will use them to reinforce the buffer. That is why the technique version hollows you out. It takes practices designed to open the self and uses them to fortify it.

So what makes a practice hold. Three things, and I offer them because the structure of the disciplines genuinely produces three. A practice that holds is aimed at God and not at the self, it is sustained when it stops feeling good, and it is done in a body and not just a mind. Take them in turn.

Aimed at God. The simplest test of any practice is to ask who it is for. When I fast and the question in my mind is how I am doing, the fast has already curdled. When I fast and the hunger drives me toward God, becomes a prayer my stomach is praying, the fast holds. Same act. The aim decides. James K. A. Smith has argued that we are formed not mainly by what we think but by what we love, and that our loves are trained by practices, by the embodied things we do over and over until they shape the orientation of the heart (Smith 2009). Which means the disciplines are not neutral tools. They are forming you toward something with every repetition. The only question is toward what. Toward God, or toward a more polished self.

Sustained past the feeling. A practice that you keep only while it feels good is not a discipline, it is a mood you are indulging. The desert fathers, the early monastics who fled to the Egyptian wilderness in the fourth century, built their whole lives on the conviction that you keep the rule especially on the days the rule feels dead, because those are the days it is actually doing its work, scraping away the part of you that only obeys when obedience is pleasant. The practice that holds is the one you kept through the dry month.

Done in the body. We are not brains piloting flesh. We are bodies, and the disciplines know it, which is why they are so physical, the empty stomach, the bent knee, the closed mouth, the cleared day. Marva Dawn wrote that the Sabbath in particular must be embodied, ceased into with the whole self and not merely agreed with as an idea, because an idea changes nothing and a practiced body changes everything (Dawn 1989). You will not think your way into a new heart. You will be formed into one, slowly, through what you repeatedly do with your actual body in actual time.

Now the grace, and the law before it. The law of the disciplines is real and it will expose you fast. Try to keep a simple rule of life, a fixed time of prayer, a weekly Sabbath, a regular fast, and you will discover within two weeks how undisciplined you are, how enslaved to comfort, how unable to do the very things you said you wanted. That exposure is not the practices failing. It is the first thing they were meant to do, to show you that you cannot save your own life, that the self-improvement project was doomed from the start because the self cannot improve the self. And right there, at the bottom of your own inability, is where grace finally has room to work. The disciplines do not earn God. They empty your hands so they are open to receive him. Augustine examined his life more searchingly than Socrates ever did, and what he found at the bottom was not a better Augustine but a restless heart that no practice could satisfy and only God could (Augustine 397). The practices that hold are the ones that bring you, again and again, to the end of yourself.

The examined life is not worth living if all you ever find is yourself. Examine the life until you reach the end of it, and then look up. That is the only examination that holds.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 397. Confessions. Translated by Henry Chadwick. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991.

Dawn, Marva J. 1989. Keeping the Sabbath Wholly: Ceasing, Resting, Embracing, Feasting. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Smith, James K. A. 2009. Desiring the Kingdom: Worship, Worldview, and Cultural Formation. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge: Harvard University Press.

Willard, Dallas. 1988. The Spirit of the Disciplines: Understanding How God Changes Lives. San Francisco: HarperOne.

title: How to Read the Bible Devotionally
excerpt: Most people who quit reading the Bible quit because they were taught to read it the way they read everything else, fast and for information, and the oldest tradition of Christian reading is built on the exact opposite instinct.
body:
I came to the Bible the way a former atheist comes to anything, to master it. I read it to find the contradictions, then, after I believed, I read it to find the arguments, the doctrines, the proof texts I could deploy. I read it fast, the way I read everything, mining it for information I could carry out and use. And for a long time I could not understand why a book I now believed was the word of God left me so unchanged. I was reading it correctly by every standard I knew. The standards were the problem.

There is a way of reading the Bible that gathers information, and it is good and necessary and the church needs more of it, not less. But there is an older way, nearly lost, that the tradition called reading for formation rather than information, reading not to get something out of the text but to let the text get something out of you. And almost no one teaches it anymore, because almost everything in our world trains us in the opposite direction. We read to extract. We skim, we scan, we pull the takeaway and move on. Bring that habit to Scripture and you will treat the living word like a feed to be consumed, and you will get exactly what you get from a feed. Nothing that stays.

Let me give the strongest case for the other approach, the study-first approach, because I hold it too and I do not want to caricature it. The serious reader says the Bible is an ancient text in foreign languages from cultures three thousand years gone, and to read it devotionally without first reading it carefully is to read your own reflection back to yourself. You will make it say whatever you already feel. Better to learn the history, the grammar, the context, to understand what the author meant before you ask what it means for you, or you will turn the Bible into a mirror and call your reflection God. This is true. I have watched devotional reading become exactly that, a warm fog in which people find divine endorsement of whatever they already wanted. The guardrail of careful study is not optional, and I am not arguing against it.

But here is what careful study cannot do by itself, and what the study-only reader sometimes forgets. You can understand a text completely and remain untouched by it. Knowledge of Scripture is not the same as formation by Scripture, and the most informed reader in the room can be the least changed. Jesus said this to the most expert Bible readers of his day. You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life, and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me (John 5:39-40 ESV). They had the text mastered. They had memorized it. And they walked straight past the One it was pointing to, because they were reading for information about God and never let it become an encounter with him. That is the warning hanging over every careful reader, myself most of all. You can win the argument about the text and lose the thing the text was for.

Hold that text as the spine. The Scriptures bear witness, they point, they are not the destination but the finger pointing at the destination. Read for information and you stop at the finger. Read devotionally and you follow it to the face.

The history here is encouraging, because the way of reading we have lost was the normal way for most of Christian history. The monastic tradition formalized it under a Latin name, lectio divina, sacred reading, and it had four slow movements that ran exactly counter to how we read now. You read the text slowly, lectio. You stopped on the word or phrase that arrested you and turned it over, meditatio. You let it become prayer, oratio. And you fell silent and let God act, contemplatio. The whole thing assumed that the point of reading was not coverage but encounter, not how many chapters but whether you met God in one verse. Eugene Peterson recovered this for the modern church and gave it a memorable image, that we are to read Scripture the way a dog works a bone, not racing through it but staying with it, gnawing, returning, getting the marrow out, what the old writers called rumination (Peterson 2006). We have become readers who swallow whole and digest nothing.

Then the printing press changed how everyone reads, and Scripture got swept up in it. After Gutenberg in the 1450s, and far more after mass literacy, reading became fast, silent, private, and extractive, a tool for gathering information at speed. That was a gift to the world and to the spread of the Bible itself. But a side effect was that the slow, communal, ruminative reading that had formed Christians for a thousand years came to feel inefficient, even strange. And then the screen finished what the press began. The smartphone, arriving in 2007, trained us to read in fragments, to scan for the relevant line and bounce away, attention shattered into seconds. Bring that shattered attention to the Psalms and you will get nothing, not because the Psalms have failed but because you are reading a deep thing with a shallow instrument. We do not have a Bible problem. We have an attention problem, and it follows us onto the page.

So how do you read devotionally. Slowly, and three small turns make the difference, because the practice really does have three. Read less and stay longer. Read it as addressed to you. And let it become prayer.

Read less and stay longer. Abandon the chapters-per-day arithmetic. Take five verses, or one. Read them three times, the third time aloud, because the ear catches what the racing eye skips. Stop on the word that snags you and stay there until it gives something up. You are not trying to cover the Bible. You are trying to let one true sentence go all the way down.

Read it as addressed to you. Not as a document about ancient people but as a letter that has reached its recipient. When the text says fear not, hear it spoken to you, in your kitchen, on the Tuesday you are afraid. This is where the study guardrail matters, so that you receive what the text actually says and not what you wish it said, but once you understand it rightly, you must let it speak to you and not only to the Israelites. The word is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword, and it discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Hebrews 4:12 ESV). A sword you study on a shelf cuts nothing. Let it be drawn.

Let it become prayer. The moment a verse opens, stop reading and start praying it back. If the text says the Lord is my shepherd, pray it, tell him you have wandered, ask him to lead you. The reading was always meant to turn into conversation. That turn, from reading about God to speaking with God, is the whole hinge of devotional reading, and the page is just where the conversation starts.

The law and the grace are both in this practice, and the law comes first as it always does. When you slow down and let the word actually read you, it will expose you. The verse you stayed with will name the thing in you that you were reading fast to avoid. That is the sword doing its work, and it will hurt, and it is supposed to. But the One the Scriptures bear witness to did not come to leave you cut open. He came to heal the thing the word exposed. The whole canon is a finger pointing at a cross, and the cross is where the indictment the text raises against you is answered, fully, by him, in your place. Augustine was undone not by mastering Scripture but by a single sentence of it read at the right moment in a garden, take up and read, and he took it up, and it read him, and he was never the same (Augustine 397). That is devotional reading. Not information carried out. A self handed over.

Stop trying to get through the Bible. Let one verse get through to you. That is the whole of it, and most of us have never once done it.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 397. Confessions. Translated by Henry Chadwick. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991.

Peterson, Eugene H. 2006. Eat This Book: A Conversation in the Art of Spiritual Reading. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

title: How to Build a Healthy Church Staff Culture
excerpt: The staff culture you actually have is the one you tolerate on a Tuesday, not the one you describe in the elder retreat.
body:
A staff meeting opens with prayer, and three of the five people praying are afraid of the person leading it. They are not afraid he will yell. They are afraid of something quieter than that. They are afraid of the look that crosses his face when someone disagrees, the way the temperature in the room drops two degrees, the email that comes at nine that night with the subject line that just says 'Quick thought.' So they pray, and they smile, and they keep the real conversation for the parking lot. The culture of that staff is not the printed values on the breakroom wall. The culture is what happens in the parking lot.

Most pastors think they are building a healthy staff culture when what they are building is a comfortable one. The two are not the same. A comfortable culture is a place where nobody contradicts the leader and everyone leaves on time and the conflict goes underground where it ferments. A healthy culture is a place where the hardest thing on the table gets said by the person least afraid to say it, and nobody loses standing for saying it. I have run both kinds. I know the difference from the inside, because for years I mistook the silence in my own staff meetings for peace, and it was not peace. It was the absence of trust dressed up as agreement.

Let me steel-man the comfortable manager, because he is not a villain and he is often me. He has read the studies. He knows that turnover in ministry is brutal, that pastors burn out, that a church split can take a decade to heal. So he protects the calm. He smooths the friction. He tells himself that a peaceful staff is a faithful staff, that unity is a fruit of the Spirit, that he is shepherding tender people through a hard calling. And he is right about the tenderness. He is right that people in ministry carry wounds that the corporate world does not see. The instinct to protect them is a good instinct that has been pointed in the wrong direction.

Here is what he gets wrong. He has confused the absence of conflict with the presence of trust, and Patrick Lencioni spent a career showing that these are nearly opposites (Lencioni 2002). Trust is what makes conflict survivable. Where trust is high, people fight about ideas in the open and walk out of the room intact. Where trust is low, people agree in the room and undermine in the hallway. The peaceful staff the comfortable manager is so proud of is not a sign of trust. It is a sign that trust is so thin nobody dares to test it. He is not protecting his people. He is starving them of the one thing that would let them tell him the truth.

The spine text here is the night before the cross, and it is stranger than we let it be. 'Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist' (John 13:3-4 ESV). Read the logic of that sentence. John tells us first that Jesus knew the full extent of his authority, that everything had been placed in his hands, and then, because of that knowledge and not in spite of it, he got on the floor and washed twelve sets of dirty feet. The security came first. The service came out of the security. He could kneel because there was nothing left to prove.

That is the engine of a healthy staff culture, and almost nobody runs on it. The leader who knows where his standing comes from can take the lowest seat in the room without losing himself. The leader who does not know is the one who needs the meeting to affirm him, who cannot let a critique pass without correcting the record, who washes nobody's feet because he is still waiting for someone to wash his. A church staff inherits the anxiety of the person at the top. If the senior leader is grasping, the whole staff grasps. If he can kneel, he gives them permission to stop performing.

We did not get here by accident, and the history matters. The modern church staff is a young invention. For most of Christian history the local congregation had a pastor and perhaps a sexton, and the idea of an executive pastor, a creative director, a connections coordinator, and a discipleship pastor reporting through an org chart would have been unintelligible. The multi-staff church as we know it is largely a product of the church growth movement that took shape in the nineteen seventies and eighties, when Donald McGavran's work at Fuller and the rise of the seeker-sensitive megachurch taught a generation to think of the congregation as an organization to be scaled. We imported the org chart from the corporation, and with it we imported the corporation's diseases, the politics, the performance reviews, the quiet anxiety of people whose livelihood depends on a manager's mood.

None of that is wrong in itself. Structure is a gift. But we adopted the structure without adopting the safeguard, and the safeguard is theological, not managerial. Edwin Friedman, a rabbi who spent his life studying leadership in congregations and families, named the missing piece. He called it self-differentiation, the capacity of a leader to stay connected to people while staying clear about his own convictions, to hold steady in the presence of someone else's anxiety without absorbing it or reacting to it (Friedman 2007). The differentiated leader does not need the staff to be calm in order to be calm himself. That is what lets him invite the hard conversation. He can hear it without coming apart.

So what do you actually do. Begin with the thing you can control, which is your own face in the room. Watch what happens to the temperature when someone disagrees with you, and learn to keep it level on purpose, because the staff is reading you for permission and you are giving it whether you mean to or not. Then make the disagreement count for something. When a junior staff member tells you a plan will not work and she is right, change the plan in front of everyone and say out loud who changed your mind. Nothing teaches a staff that candor is safe faster than watching candor win once. Bonhoeffer warned that the leader who arrives with a vision of the perfect community and demands that the real people conform to it will end up destroying both the vision and the people (Bonhoeffer 1954). Lead the staff you have, not the one in your head.

And ration your reactions. Henri Nouwen wrote that the great temptation of Christian leadership is the temptation to be relevant, to be spectacular, to be powerful, and that the antidote is a leadership that descends rather than climbs, that is willing to be led where it would rather not go (Nouwen 1989). A healthy staff culture is built by a leader who has made peace with not being the most impressive person in the room. He does not need the win in every exchange. He has already washed feet. He has nothing to prove and therefore everything to give.

There is a test for whether the culture is actually changing, and it is a quiet one. Listen for what your newest and least powerful staff member is willing to say in front of the room. The intern, the part-time administrator, the young hire who joined six months ago and has the most to lose by speaking. When that person disagrees with you out loud, without lowering her voice and without checking the faces of the older staff first, you have built something real. Until that day, every assurance that your people feel free to speak is a thing you are telling yourself, not a thing they have shown you. The health of a staff is measured at its bottom, not its top, the same way Jesus measured greatness on the night he reached for the towel.

The culture you have is the one your people describe in the parking lot. You will not change it with a values document or a ropes course or a verse on the wall. You will change it the first time someone says the dangerous true thing in the meeting and watches you receive it without flinching. That is the whole work, and it never ends. The towel does not stay tied. You pick it up again every Tuesday.

A healthy staff is not a quiet one. It is a brave one.

### Works Cited

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Friedman, Edwin H. 2007. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

Lencioni, Patrick. 2002. The Five Dysfunctions of a Team. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

title: When to Fire Someone in Ministry
excerpt: The cruelest thing a pastor can do to a staff member is keep him on a year past the point where everyone but him already knows.
body:
The conversation everyone is dreading has already happened a hundred times. It has happened in the car on the way home, when the executive pastor's wife asked how it went and he said nothing and stared at the road. It has happened in the elder meeting, in the long pause after someone says his name. It has happened in the worship leader's own gut at two in the morning. The only place it has not happened is the one place it needs to happen, which is across a desk, in daylight, with the words said plainly. We will keep almost anyone for almost any length of time to avoid that one room.

Firing someone in ministry is harder than firing someone anywhere else, and we should say why instead of pretending otherwise. In a normal job, the relationship is contractual. In a church, the relationship is covenantal, or it feels that way. You prayed together. You buried his father. His kids call you by a nickname. You stood in front of the congregation and said God had called this person to this work, and now you are sitting across from him preparing to say it is over. The language of calling and the language of employment are tangled together, and we use the tangle as an excuse to do nothing.

Let me give the case for patience its full strength, because it is a strong case and I have hidden behind it. Grace is the center of what we preach. We believe people can change. We believe the Spirit is not finished with anyone. We have all known a leader who was struggling in month eight and thriving in month twenty, and we are right to fear the kind of pastor who fires fast and prays slow. Scripture is full of restoration, of Peter rebuilt on a beach after he had failed at the worst possible moment. A church that cuts its people loose at the first sign of weakness is not a church, it is a firm with a steeple. The patient pastor is protecting something real.

But grace and clarity are not enemies, and we treat them as if they were. The patient pastor has performed a sleight of hand on himself. He has decided that keeping the failing staff member is the gracious choice, when in fact it is often the cowardly one wearing grace as a costume. Grace toward the underperforming worship leader is not the only grace in the room. There is also the grace owed to the volunteers he is exhausting, the grace owed to the congregation he is no longer serving, the grace owed to the man himself, who deserves to know the truth while he is still young enough to find the thing he is actually built for. By calling my avoidance grace, I was spending other people's grace to protect my own comfort.

The text I want to carry is the appointing of the seven in Acts, because it shows that ministry roles exist for a function and not as a reward. The widows were being neglected in the daily distribution, and the apostles did not say the men currently failing at the task deserved patience. They said the work had to be done, and they sought out men full of the Spirit and of wisdom to do it (Acts 6:3 ESV). The role served the people. When the role stops serving the people, the role has to change hands, and the kindness is owed first to the people the role exists for. We have inverted this. We treat the staff position as belonging to the staff member, a possession we would be cruel to take away, when it was never his. It was the congregation's, on loan.

So when. Not for one bad season, and not for a personality you find tiring, and never for telling you the truth you did not want to hear. Fire for a sustained gap between the work and the person that prayer and coaching and time have not closed, when you have named it clearly more than once and given a real path and watched the path go unwalked. Fire for character, faster than you want to, because a gifted manipulator does more damage in a church than an honest underperformer ever will. Fire when keeping someone requires you to lie, to the elders about how it is going, to the congregation about why numbers are slipping, to the person himself about a future that is not coming. The lie is the signal. When you are lying to keep the peace, the peace is already gone.

The history of how we got so timid is worth tracing. The professionalization of ministry, which gathered speed across the twentieth century and accelerated after the church growth movement of the nineteen seventies built the multi-staff church, gave us employees without giving us the stomach to manage them. We borrowed the human resources department's vocabulary, the performance plan and the documented warning, but we kept a theology of the pastorate that treats every staff member as an ordained brother whose removal is a kind of excommunication. So we freeze. We have the corporate tools and the covenantal nerves, and the two cancel out, and the failing leader stays for three years while everyone suffers and calls it love.

Edwin Friedman saw this paralysis everywhere he looked, and he named its real cause. He said the chronically anxious system will always pressure the leader to relieve its anxiety, and the most anxious members will set the agenda, so the leader who cannot tolerate someone else's pain will be ruled by whoever is most willing to inflict it on him (Friedman 2007). The pastor who cannot fire is not more loving. He is less differentiated. He has let the discomfort of one hard conversation hold an entire church hostage. The failure of nerve does not look like failure. It looks like patience. That is what makes it so durable.

Here is the reversal that took me too long to learn. The kindest thing is almost always the earlier thing. The longer you wait, the worse the eventual conversation gets for everyone, especially the person you are protecting. Keep a man two years past the point of fit and you have not given him grace, you have given him two years of failing publicly, two years of his confidence eroding, two years of a marriage straining under a job he cannot do, before you finally say what you could have said with dignity at month nine. Delay does not soften the blow. It compounds it and then delivers it anyway, with interest he had no idea he was accruing.

Before the day comes, the cross has to do its work on you, and it does it as law before it does it as grace. The law first. The reason you cannot have this conversation is that you need this man to walk out still thinking well of you, and that need is an idol, the same idol the apostles refused when they would not let the neglected widows go on being neglected to spare anyone's feelings. You have made your own reputation as a kind employer into a small god, and it is costing the very people the role exists to serve. That is sin, and naming it as sin is the only thing that breaks its grip. The grace second. The cross says your standing was settled by Another before you ever managed a single staff member, bought in blood you did not spill, so you do not have to purchase this man's approval with one more year of his slow failure. You are free to tell the truth precisely because the verdict over you is not his to give. The leader who has heard that law and received that grace can deliver hard news from a settled place and not from anger, because he is no longer secretly trying to make the other person agree that he is fair. Tell the truth plainly. Own your part in waiting too long. Be generous with severance and time and a real reference, because how you end a tenure preaches to everyone still on staff about what you actually believe. Ruth Haley Barton writes that leaders have to attend to their own souls precisely so that their decisions flow from God and not from their own unexamined fear (Barton 2008). The firing done from a settled soul is a different act than the firing done from panic, even when the words are the same.

There is one more place we hide, and it is the holiest-sounding excuse of all. We say we are waiting on the Lord. We say we have not yet received clarity, that we are praying for wisdom, that we do not want to run ahead of God. And sometimes that is true and good. But often the language of discernment is the language of paralysis with a stained-glass window in front of it. Ruth Haley Barton writes that we have to be honest about the difference between genuine waiting on God and the spiritualized procrastination that lets us avoid a decision we already know we have to make (Barton 2008). The Spirit who gave us wisdom also gave us the courage to act on it. When the clarity has been sitting in your chest for six months and you are still calling it discernment, the thing you are waiting on is not God. It is your own willingness to be disliked.

The goal was never to be a man who can fire easily. The goal is to be a man who can tell the truth in love when love and truth both cost something. Most of us are not too quick to let people go. We are too slow, and we baptize the slowness, and the people we claim to be protecting pay for our comfort.

Grace tells the truth in time. Cowardice waits for it to die.

### Works Cited

Barton, Ruth Haley. 2008. Strengthening the Soul of Your Leadership: Seeking God in the Crucible of Ministry. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press.

Friedman, Edwin H. 2007. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

title: Leading Through Conflict on a Church Team
excerpt: A church team does not get into trouble because it fights, it gets into trouble because it learned to call avoidance peace.
body:
Two staff members have not directly spoken to each other in four months, and everyone knows it, and nobody says it. They are professionals. They pass each other in the hall. They sit on the same row in the all-staff meeting and route every actual message through a third person who has become an unwilling diplomat between two people who used to be friends. The team is functioning. The calendar fills, the services happen, the bulletin gets printed. And underneath the function a low current of avoidance is running through everything, and the longer it runs the more the whole team organizes itself around not setting it off.

We have a strange relationship with conflict in the church. We treat it as a failure of sanctification, as if a mature team would simply never disagree, as if the presence of friction proves the absence of the Spirit. So when conflict shows up, and it always shows up, we feel ashamed of it and we hide it. We swallow the disagreement and call the swallowing humility. We let the resentment build and call the building patience. And the conflict does not go anywhere. It just moves down, out of the meeting and into the body, into the headaches and the clipped emails and the Sunday smiles that do not reach the eyes.

Let me steel-man the peacemaker, because he is quoting Jesus and he is not wrong about much. Blessed are the peacemakers. A quarrelsome church is a poor witness, and the world is watching how we treat each other, and Paul begged the Philippians to be of the same mind. The peacemaker has seen what unchecked conflict does, has watched a church split over a building program and never recover, has buried friendships that died in a business meeting. His instinct to protect the unity of the team is not cowardice. It is the scar tissue of someone who has seen the alternative. He is guarding something he has watched bleed out before.

But he has misread the text he is standing on, and the misreading is costing him the very thing he wants. Peacemaking is not peacekeeping. The peacemaker in the Sermon on the Mount is an active figure who goes into the broken place and makes something, the way a steelworker makes a beam, through heat and pressure and joining. The peacekeeper is a different creature entirely. He keeps the peace by keeping the lid on, and the lid is not peace, it is a delay. What he calls unity is two people not speaking for four months while a third carries their mail. Jesus did not bless that. He blessed the harder and braver thing, the one that walks into the conflict on purpose and stays until something is actually mended.

The spine text is plainer than we admit, and it is from Jesus' own mouth. 'If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone' (Matthew 18:15 ESV). Go. The movement is toward the person, not away. Alone, which means not to the third party, not to the prayer chain disguised as concern, not to the spouse over dinner, not to the loose coalition you are quietly building in the hallway. The most disobeyed verse in church staff life is not about money or sex or doctrine. It is this one, the simple command to take the problem to the person and nobody else, and our entire architecture of avoidance exists to get around it.

Watch what triangulation actually does to a team, because it is the disease underneath most church conflict. Edwin Friedman built his whole understanding of congregations on the way anxiety moves through relationships, and he showed that when two people cannot tolerate the tension between them, they will reliably pull in a third to stabilize it (Friedman 2007). The third person feels useful, even chosen, carrying messages and absorbing complaints. But the triangle does not resolve the conflict. It preserves it. It lets two people stay angry indefinitely because the pressure that would have forced them to deal with each other is being bled off through someone else. Every staff has these triangles. Most pastors are sitting inside several of them and feeling needed instead of feeling alarmed.

We did not invent this avoidance. We inherited it, and the history clarifies the grip it has. The therapeutic turn in American culture, which the sociologist Philip Rieff diagnosed as early as nineteen sixty-six in his account of the triumph of the therapeutic, taught us to read every relational difficulty as a matter of feelings to be managed and validated rather than truths to be told (Rieff 1966). The church drank deeply from that stream. We learned to prize emotional comfort above honest correction, to fear hurting someone more than we feared leaving them in sin, to mistake niceness for love. A whole generation of church teams now treats the avoidance of hard words as the highest relational virtue, and we cannot find the verse that taught us that, because there is no such verse.

Here is the reversal. The conflict you are avoiding is not the threat to the team. The avoidance is the threat. Lencioni mapped this with uncomfortable precision when he showed that teams which cannot engage in honest conflict do not become more unified, they become less committed, because people will not buy into a decision they were never allowed to argue with (Lencioni 2002). The silence you are protecting is producing the disengagement you are about to complain about. The meeting where nobody pushes back is not a sign of alignment. It is the sound of people who have stopped believing their voice changes anything, saving their real opinions for the parking lot where the decisions get quietly unmade.

So lead into it. When you sense the four-month silence, name it out loud and decline to be the third corner of the triangle, sending the two people back to each other with your blessing and your expectation. When someone comes to complain about a colleague, the most pastoral question you can ask is whether they have said this to the person directly, and the most pastoral answer to no is to walk with them until they do. Set the table so that conflict in the meeting is normal and conflict in the hallway is not. The team that fights well in the open is the team that does not need to fight in the dark.

And remember that the alternative to honest conflict is not peace but a burden no single person can carry. In the wilderness Moses came apart under exactly this weight. The people quarreled and complained and routed every grievance through him, and he cried out to God that he was not able to carry all this people alone, that the load was too heavy, that he would rather die than keep bearing it by himself (Numbers 11:14 ESV). The Lord's answer was not to make the conflict disappear. It was to spread the weight, to take of the Spirit on Moses and put it on seventy elders so that they would bear the burden of the people with him and Moses would not bear it alone (Numbers 11:17 ESV). Read what God refuses to do. He does not promise Moses a quiet camp. He gives him shared leadership, a body of people willing to stand inside the tension with him rather than route it around him. The leader who absorbs every conflict alone, who lets himself become the third corner of every triangle, is not being strong. He is doing the very thing God told Moses to stop doing, and it will crush him the same way. Nouwen called the alternative the downward movement of Christian leadership, the refusal to escape conflict through power, the choice to remain present and bear the weight together where it would be easier to dominate or disappear (Nouwen 1989).

I have to name my own part in this, because I led a team for years that I was proud of for never fighting, and I have since come to understand that I was proud of the wrong thing. The reason nobody fought in my meetings was not that we had achieved some rare maturity. It was that I had made disagreement expensive, in a hundred small ways I never noticed, and my people had done the arithmetic and decided silence was cheaper. The peace I prized was the peace of a room that had given up on changing my mind. It took a staff member leaving, and telling me on the way out the things she had never felt safe to say while she stayed, before I understood that the quiet I had treated as a trophy was actually the bill coming due. I had mistaken the absence of conflict for the presence of unity, and the two had never been further apart.

A team that has learned to fight honestly and stay is more unified than a team that has never fought at all, the way a bone that healed is stronger than a bone that was never tested. We keep protecting our teams from the one thing that would actually bind them together. We keep choosing the quiet, and the quiet keeps costing us the thing the quiet was supposed to save.

Peace is not the absence of conflict. It is conflict carried all the way through.

### Works Cited

Friedman, Edwin H. 2007. A Failure of Nerve: Leadership in the Age of the Quick Fix. New York: Seabury Books.

Lencioni, Patrick. 2002. The Five Dysfunctions of a Team. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

Rieff, Philip. 1966. The Triumph of the Therapeutic: Uses of Faith After Freud. New York: Harper and Row.

title: How to Develop Leaders, Not Just Recruit Volunteers
excerpt: A church can run a hundred volunteers through its slots for a decade and produce not a single leader, and most of them do.
body:
Every September the same announcement goes up on the screen and into the bulletin and across the platform. We need volunteers. The nursery is short, the parking team is thin, the connections desk has two people doing the work of five, and so the ask goes out, and a few tired saints raise their hands again because they always do. The church fills its slots. The machine runs another year. And if you stood at the back of that room and asked who among these faithful people is being formed into a leader who could one day carry weight, the honest answer would be almost none of them, because nobody is trying to.

There is a difference between recruiting and developing, and most churches have collapsed it without noticing. Recruiting fills a need that the church has. Developing meets a need that the person has, the need to grow into the fullness of what God made them to carry. Recruiting asks what the volunteer can do for the ministry. Developing asks what the ministry can do for the volunteer, what God might be building in a human being through the assignment. We say we want to develop leaders. What we usually want is to fill the schedule, and the schedule, once filled, has no reason to develop anyone.

Let me make the recruiter's case honestly, because the work is real and the recruiter is not lazy. The services do have to happen. The children do have to be safe. Someone does have to count the offering and run the slides and stack the chairs, and a church that romanticizes development while the practical work falls apart is not deep, it is just disorganized. The recruiter is keeping the lights on. He looks at the gap between the work and the workers and he closes it the only way he knows how, week after week, and the church owes him more thanks than it gives. His instinct to staff the need is not wrong.

But he has accepted a quiet exchange that is hollowing his church out from the inside. By treating people as labor to be deployed, he gets the slot filled this week and loses the leader who would have filled a hundred slots over twenty years. He is harvesting and never planting. And there is a deeper cost, because people can tell when they are being used rather than formed. The volunteer who senses that the church only wants his hands and not his growth eventually burns out, not from the labor but from the meaninglessness of labor that leads nowhere. We wonder why we cannot keep volunteers. It is because we never made them into anything. We just spent them.

The text I want to carry is the way Jesus made leaders, because it is almost the opposite of how we do it. 'And he appointed twelve, so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach' (Mark 3:14 ESV). Read the order. With him first. Sent out second. The being with came before the doing for, and the doing flowed out of the being with. Jesus did not recruit twelve volunteers to staff a movement. He drew twelve men into his life, let them watch him pray and weep and argue and rest, and only out of that shared life did he send them to do anything. The formation was relational before it was functional. We have inverted the order, and the inversion is the whole problem.

The history of how we lost this is the history of the church learning to think like a business, and the year markers are not subtle. When the church growth movement took hold across the nineteen seventies and eighties, and Peter Drucker, the most influential management thinker of the century, began consulting with megachurch pastors and teaching them to run congregations as organizations to be scaled, we gained efficiency and lost apprenticeship. The org chart replaced the rabbi. We built systems to process volunteers at scale, intake forms and ministry placement matrices and the language of human capital, and a system that processes people efficiently is structurally incapable of doing the slow, inefficient, deeply personal work of forming one leader at a time. The factory cannot raise a child.

Here is the reversal that costs the most to accept. Developing leaders will always look less efficient than recruiting volunteers, and it will always produce more in the end. Pouring eighteen months into one person who might lead a ministry someday is a worse use of a Tuesday than filling six open slots, by every metric your dashboard tracks. But the six slots are filled by people who will leave, and the one person becomes someone who fills slots you will never see, who develops others, who is still leading when you are gone. The kingdom does not scale the way a corporation scales. It scales the way a vineyard scales, slowly, through roots, one planting at a time, and you will not see the harvest in the quarter you planted it.

What does developing actually require of us, and why do we avoid it. It requires proximity, the willingness to let people close enough to watch you lead and to be coached inside the real work rather than in a classroom. Ruth Haley Barton argues that leaders can only give away what they themselves have received, that an unformed leader produces unformed followers, that the inner life of the one doing the developing is the ceiling on everyone he develops (Barton 2008). This is why we avoid it. Developing a leader means being watched up close, and being watched up close means being known, and being known means our own gaps come into view. Recruiting keeps people at arm's length. Developing brings them inside, where they can see us, and that is precisely the cost we do not want to pay.

It also requires that we hand over real authority before the person is fully ready, which terrifies the recruiter, because real authority handed over means real mistakes made in public. But there is no other way it has ever worked. Jesus sent the twelve out while they still misunderstood almost everything, and they came back having done the work badly and well, and the sending was the school. We hoard the meaningful decisions and then wonder why nobody around us has grown. You cannot develop a leader by letting him stack chairs. You develop him by letting him lead, and then standing close enough to debrief the wreckage and the wins, week after week, until the day he is leading better than you.

The deepest part is the part we are most tempted to skip, the formation of the person beneath the function. Bonhoeffer reminded us that Christian community is not an ideal we impose but a reality we receive, that the goal is never to build the impressive thing but to serve the actual person God has placed in front of us (Bonhoeffer 1954). Developing a leader is finally an act of love for that specific human being, not a strategy for staffing the church. The moment it becomes a strategy, the person feels it, and the formation dies. We must want the volunteer to grow even if it means he grows right out of our church and into a calling we never get the credit for.

The oldest picture of this is not Jesus and the twelve. It is Moses in the wilderness and the day his father-in-law watched him work. Jethro found Moses sitting alone from morning to evening while the people stood around him waiting, judging every dispute himself, and he said the thing every overfunctioning leader needs to hear, what you are doing is not good, you and the people will wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you and you are not able to do it alone (Exodus 18:17-18 ESV). Then he told Moses to develop leaders, to look for able men out of the people and place them over thousands and hundreds and fifties and tens, to teach them the statutes and let them carry the lighter cases so that they would bear the burden with him (Exodus 18:21-22 ESV). Read what the cure for Moses was. Not a better schedule. Not a more efficient docket. Other leaders, formed and trusted and handed real weight, because the work was never meant to live or die on one man. You will not develop leaders from behind a desk handing out assignments. You develop them the way Jethro told Moses to, by raising up able people, teaching them, and giving them the cases that are too small for your ego and exactly the right size for their growth.

There is a final cost most of us never count, and it is the cost to our own ego. The leader who develops other leaders is signing up to be eclipsed. The people you raise well will, if you have done it faithfully, eventually preach better than you preached at their age, lead larger than you led, see things you cannot see. And a great deal of what passes for a shortage of leaders in our churches is actually a senior leader's quiet unwillingness to be surpassed, a hoarding of the spotlight dressed up as a concern for readiness. We keep people in the volunteer pool because a developed leader is a threat to the man at the top in a way a chair-stacker never will be. Nouwen warned that the descending way of Jesus runs directly against the climbing instinct that lives in every leader, that we are forever tempted to grasp at relevance and visibility instead of giving them away (Nouwen 1989). You cannot develop a leader and protect your own prominence at the same time. You have to choose, and most of us choose ourselves and call it prudence.

This is where the cross has to do its work, and it does it as law before it does it as grace. The law first. The reason you will not raise leaders who might surpass you is that you need to be the indispensable one, the source the church cannot do without, and that need is not humility wearing thin, it is idolatry, the determination to be a small savior to people who already have a real one. You have made your own irreplaceability into a god, and like every idol it demands that everyone around you stay smaller than you so that you can keep feeling large. That is sin, and naming it as sin is the only thing that loosens its grip. The grace second. The cross says the one indispensable work was already finished by the only indispensable Man, accomplished in blood you did not spill while you contributed nothing but the sin he carried, and your standing was settled there before you developed a single leader. You do not have to be the source. You were never the source. The man who has heard that law and received that grace can pour himself into people who will eclipse him and rejoice when they do, because his worth was never riding on being the largest one in the room. He is free to give his power away, because the verdict over him was never his to earn and is no longer his to lose.

A church that only recruits will always be short of volunteers. A church that develops will one day have more leaders than it knows what to do with. Almost all of us are running the first kind and praying for the results of the second.

Stop filling slots. Start raising leaders.

### Works Cited

Barton, Ruth Haley. 2008. Strengthening the Soul of Your Leadership: Seeking God in the Crucible of Ministry. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press.

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. 1954. Life Together. Translated by John W. Doberstein. New York: Harper and Row.

Nouwen, Henri J. M. 1989. In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership. New York: Crossroad.

title: The Lonely Seat: Power and the Senior Leader
excerpt: The loneliness of the senior seat is real, and the way most pastors try to cure it is exactly what makes it worse.
body:
A pastor stands at the door after the third service, and forty people tell him it was exactly what they needed, and he drives home and cannot think of a single person he could call to say he is not okay. He leads a staff of twelve. He has elders who pray for him by name. He is surrounded all week by people who depend on him, who admire him, who would say without hesitation that they love him. And he is alone in a way that none of them can see, because the seat he sits in has put a pane of glass between him and everyone who reports to him, and he installed the glass himself and forgot he did it.

The loneliness of the senior leader is one of the most documented and least discussed facts of ministry. Pastors leave the work in great numbers, and when Barna asked those who had considered quitting what weighed on them, more than two in five named loneliness and isolation among the reasons (Barna 2021). We acknowledge this loneliness with a kind of sympathy that does nothing, the way we acknowledge that the work is hard. What we rarely do is look at where the loneliness comes from, because the source is uncomfortable. The loneliness of the senior seat is not only something done to the leader. It is largely something the leader does to himself, through power, and the cure he reaches for makes it worse.

Let me steel-man the leader who keeps his distance, because his reasons are not foolish and I have used every one of them. He will tell you, correctly, that he cannot be fully transparent with people he supervises, that there are confidences he must keep, that a leader who falls apart in front of his team destabilizes the whole team. He will tell you that authority requires a measure of separateness, that the captain cannot drink with the crew, that someone has to carry what cannot be shared. And he is right about all of it. The seat does require a real and necessary solitude. Some of the distance is the cost of the office, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of dishonesty.

But he has done something with that legitimate truth that turns it into a prison. He has taken the necessary solitude of the role and quietly expanded it into a total isolation that serves his power rather than his people. There is a difference between the loneliness that comes from carrying confidences and the loneliness that comes from never letting anyone see you need anything. The first is the cost of leadership. The second is the fruit of pride dressed as duty. He has confused them on purpose, because the second kind protects an image, and the image has become more precious to him than the relationships, and he calls the whole thing the loneliness of command when half of it is the loneliness of self-protection.

The text I want to carry is the long, sad arc of Saul, the first king of Israel, because no story in Scripture shows more plainly what power does to a man who uses it to protect himself. Saul began among the people, hiding among the baggage on the day he was chosen, a head taller than everyone and somehow still shy of the seat (1 Samuel 10:22-23 ESV). But once the crown was on him the seat began to close around him. When the women sang that David had struck down his ten thousands and Saul his thousands, the king eyed David from that day on (1 Samuel 18:9 ESV), and the eyeing never stopped. He grew suspicious of his own son, of his own servants, of the one man at court who loved him most, until he sat in his hall with a spear in his hand and no friend left in the room. Read what isolated him. Not the office. The office did not have to do this to him. What isolated Saul was a power he used to guard his standing instead of to serve his people, and the more he guarded it the more alone he became, until the lonely seat had swallowed him whole. That is the medicine taken in reverse, the warning written across a king's whole reign.

Because here is what power does to most of us, and the social science is as old as the church's amnesia about it. Edwin Friedman observed that leaders become isolated not primarily because others push them away but because they stop being honestly engaged, hiding behind the role, managing impressions, surrounding themselves with people who will not contradict them (Friedman 2007). The lonely leader has often, without admitting it, selected for agreement.
